There is no specific antiviral; a vaccine, Ixchiq, has been licensed in some countries for people at high risk, and control rests on Aedes control.
Sources: WHO — Chikungunya <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya>

### Chlamydia trachomatis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/chlamydia-trachomatis/
TL;DR: A bacterium that infects the eye, and after repeated episodes scars the eyelid so lashes scrape the cornea and cause blindness.
Summary: Trachoma is caused by specific serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis. Repeated eye infections in childhood provoke inflammation that scars the conjunctiva; over decades the scarred eyelid turns inward and the lashes rub the cornea — trichiasis — which is painful and causes irreversible blindness. It is the leading infectious cause of blindness and is concentrated in the poorest, driest and most water-scarce communities.
Sources: WHO — Trachoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Dengue virus
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/dengue-virus/
TL;DR: Four related mosquito-borne viruses that cause a severe, bone-aching fever and occasionally a life-threatening plasma leak.
Summary: Dengue virus has four serotypes (DENV-1 to 4). Infection with one gives lifelong immunity to that serotype but only transient protection against the others, and a second infection with a different serotype raises the risk of severe dengue — the plasma leakage, bleeding and shock that can be fatal. It is the world's fastest-spreading mosquito-borne viral infection, driven by urbanisation, travel and the Aedes aegypti mosquito.
Sources: WHO — Dengue and severe dengue <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Dracunculus medinensis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/dracunculus-medinensis/
TL;DR: The guinea worm — a metre-long parasite that emerges through the skin of the leg, and the disease closest to eradication in history.
Summary: Guinea worm infection is contracted by drinking water containing copepods that carry the larvae. A year later a painful blister forms, usually on the leg, and a worm up to a metre long emerges over weeks. There is no drug and no vaccine; elimination rests entirely on safe water, filtering and containing every case. Cases have fallen from an estimated 3.5 million a year in the 1980s to a small number, making it the next candidate for eradication after smallpox and polio.
Sources: WHO — Dracunculiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dracunculiasis-(guinea-worm-disease)>; The Carter Center — Guinea worm disease <https://www.cartercenter.org/programs/guinea-worm/>

### Echinococcus species
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/echinococcus/
TL;DR: Tapeworms from dogs that grow into slow, cyst-like masses in the human liver and lungs — hydatid disease.
Summary: Echinococcus granulosus causes cystic echinococcosis, in which a fluid-filled cyst grows for years in the liver or lungs; Echinococcus multilocularis causes alveolar echinococcosis, an invasive, tumour-like disease with a high fatality rate if untreated. People are accidental intermediate hosts, infected by eggs from the faeces of dogs (or foxes, for E. multilocularis). Control depends on deworming dogs and stopping livestock and dogs from sharing a cycle of infection.
Sources: WHO — Echinococcosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/echinococcosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Foodborne trematodes
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/foodborne-trematodes/
TL;DR: Flukes caught from eating raw or undercooked fish, shellfish, aquatic plants or crustaceans; some raise the risk of bile-duct cancer.
Summary: The foodborne trematodiases include clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis (liver flukes), paragonimiasis (lung fluke) and fascioliasis (liver fluke of livestock). People are infected by eating raw fish, crab, watercress or other freshwater plants. Chronic Clonorchis and Opisthorchis infection is a Group 1 carcinogen for cholangiocarcinoma, the bile-duct cancer, making these worms a cancer risk as well as a parasitic disease.
Sources: WHO — Foodborne trematode infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/foodborne-trematode-infections>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Leishmania species
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/leishmania/
TL;DR: Parasites spread by sandflies that cause skin sores, disfiguring mucosal damage, or a fatal infection of internal organs.
Summary: Leishmania species cause three main syndromes: cutaneous leishmaniasis (skin ulcers that heal with scars), mucosal leishmaniasis (destruction of the nose and mouth), and visceral leishmaniasis, which attacks the spleen, liver and bone marrow and is fatal without treatment. Roughly 20 species infect people; over 90 sandfly species transmit them. Treatment is long, toxic and increasingly failing in South Asia, and there is no approved vaccine.
Sources: WHO — Leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Lymphatic filarial worms
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/lymphatic-filarial-worms/
TL;DR: Filarial worms spread by mosquitoes that block the lymph system, causing the swelling of elephantiasis and the pain of hydrocele.
Summary: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori are mosquito-borne filariae that live in the lymphatic vessels. Most infections are asymptomatic, but in a minority the lymph channels become blocked and the limbs or scrotum swell permanently — the disfigurement long stigmatised as elephantiasis. Lymphatic filariasis is a leading global cause of disability, and its endosymbiotic Wolbachia bacteria is both part of the pathology and a drug target.
Sources: WHO — Lymphatic filariasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Mycetoma-causing organisms
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/mycetoma-agents/
TL;DR: Fungi and bacteria that enter through a skin injury and grow into a painless, steadily enlarging swelling that destroys tissue and bone.
Summary: Mycetoma is a chronic infection caused either by fungi (eumycetoma, most often Madurella mycetomatis) or by bacteria (actinomycetoma, including Nocardia and Actinomadura). The organism enters through a thorn prick or a small injury, most commonly on the foot, and over years the swelling enlarges and drains grains through sinuses. It is concentrated in the 'mycetoma belt' around the Sahel, where barefoot agricultural work is common. Treatment is long, and fungal mycetoma responds poorly to current drugs.
Sources: WHO — Mycetoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Mycobacterium leprae
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/mycobacterium-leprae/
TL;DR: The bacterium that causes leprosy, which damages skin and peripheral nerves and can leave permanent disability if treated late.
Summary: Mycobacterium leprae grows extremely slowly and prefers the cooler parts of the body — skin and peripheral nerves. The result is patches of numb skin and, in the severe forms, nerve damage, deformity and blindness. It is not highly contagious; most people who are exposed never develop the disease. Multidrug therapy cures the infection, but the damage done before diagnosis is often irreversible, so early detection is everything.
Sources: WHO — Leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Mycobacterium tuberculosis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/mycobacterium-tuberculosis/
TL;DR: The bacterium that causes tuberculosis — slow-growing, hard to kill, and the source of the world's most drug-resistant epidemic.
Summary: Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, divides inside macrophages, and has a waxy cell wall that makes it resistant to many drugs and to the immune system. It can persist in the body for years without causing illness, which is why a quarter of humanity is estimated to carry latent infection. Its ability to acquire resistance to each new drug in turn — and to survive months of treatment — is why tuberculosis has produced multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Mycobacterium ulcerans
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/mycobacterium-ulcerans/
TL;DR: A bacterium related to leprosy and tuberculosis that produces a toxin destroying skin and fat, causing the painless Buruli ulcer.
Summary: Mycobacterium ulcerans grows in warm, slow-moving water and releases mycolactone, a toxin that destroys fat and skin tissue and suppresses the local immune response — so the ulcer is painless and the surrounding area does not hurt. Without treatment the ulcer expands and leaves severe scarring and contractures, sometimes requiring amputation. It is concentrated in West and Central Africa and parts of Australia.
Sources: WHO — Buruli ulcer <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/buruli-ulcer>; TB Alliance — telacebec trial in Buruli ulcer <https://www.tballiance.org/news-new-clinical-trial-examines-use-novel-compound-telacebec-buruli-ulcer-patients/>

### Onchocerca volvulus
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/onchocerca-volvulus/
TL;DR: A filarial worm spread by blackflies that causes intense itching and can blind people — river blindness.
Summary: Onchocerca volvulus is a filarial nematode transmitted by the bite of blackflies that breed in fast-flowing rivers, which is why the disease is called river blindness. Adult worms live in nodules under the skin and release millions of microfilariae that migrate through the skin and eye. The result is severe dermatitis and, after years of exposure, irreversible blindness. Ivermectin mass treatment transformed the disease from a cause of mass blindness to a target for elimination.
Sources: WHO — Onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Orthoebolavirus (Ebola virus)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/ebolavirus/
TL;DR: A filovirus that causes haemorrhagic fever with a case fatality rate that has reached 90%, spread by contact with the bodily fluids of the sick and the dead.
Summary: Ebola viruses are filamentous RNA viruses of the family Filoviridae. Several species cause disease in people; Zaire ebolavirus is the most lethal and the one for which vaccines and antibody treatments are licensed. The virus enters through mucous membranes or broken skin and attacks the immune system and blood vessels, causing the haemorrhage and multi-organ failure that give the disease its reputation. Fruit bats are implicated as the reservoir, and outbreaks begin with spillover from animals into people.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Plasmodium species
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/plasmodium/
TL;DR: Single-celled parasites transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes; five species infect people and one of them causes almost all the deaths.
Summary: Plasmodium falciparum causes the great majority of malaria deaths, dominating in sub-Saharan Africa; P. vivax is the most widespread outside Africa and can relapse from dormant liver stages; P. malariae, P. ovale and P. knowlesi account for the rest. The parasite has a complex life cycle alternating between mosquito and human, with a liver stage that is invisible to most diagnostics and a blood stage that causes disease. Its genetic diversity and its ability to develop resistance make both drugs and vaccines hard.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Rabies virus
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/rabies-virus/
TL;DR: A virus that travels from a bite up the nerves to the brain, where it causes almost uniformly fatal encephalitis once symptoms begin.
Summary: Rabies virus is a lyssavirus transmitted mainly by dog bites. It travels along peripheral nerves to the central nervous system and, once symptoms appear, is almost always fatal — but it is entirely preventable by prompt wound washing and post-exposure vaccination, with rabies immunoglobulin for severe bites. Most human deaths are in Africa and Asia and are linked to poor access to vaccines and immunoglobulin, not to a lack of science.
Sources: WHO — Rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### Sarcoptes scabiei
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/sarcoptes-scabiei/
TL;DR: The microscopic mite that burrows into skin and causes scabies, an intensely itchy rash that spreads easily in crowded homes.
Summary: The scabies mite burrows into the outer layer of skin and lays eggs, causing an itch that is often worst at night and a rash that invites bacterial infection. Ordinary scabies may carry a few dozen mites, but in crusted (Norwegian) scabies there are thousands, and it is highly transmissible. Impetigo and, in severe cases, post-streptococcal kidney disease and rheumatic heart disease follow scabies outbreaks in tropical communities.
Sources: WHO — Scabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies>; WHO — scabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/scabies>

### Schistosoma species
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/schistosoma/
TL;DR: Blood flukes that live in the veins around the bladder or gut and release eggs that damage organs; people catch them wading or swimming in fresh water.
Summary: Schistosoma mansoni, S. haematobium and S. japonicum are water-borne trematodes whose larvae, released by freshwater snails, penetrate human skin. Adult worms live in the veins and lay eggs that lodge in the bladder or intestine, driving chronic inflammation and scarring. S. haematobium causes bladder disease and is a major risk factor for bladder cancer; S. mansoni causes liver fibrosis and portal hypertension. More than 200 million people are infected, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.
Sources: WHO — Schistosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Snake venom
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/snake-venom/
TL;DR: A mixture of toxins injected in a bite that can destroy tissue, paralyse muscles or make blood clot uncontrollably.
Summary: Snakebite envenoming is not an infection but belongs in the NTD group because of who it affects: agricultural workers, children and poor rural communities with no reliable access to antivenom. Venoms differ by species — some cause coagulopathy and bleeding, some paralyse the respiratory muscles, some destroy local tissue — which is why antivenom must match the snakes present in a region. Most deaths are preventable with the right antivenom, given quickly.
Sources: WHO — Snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO — snakebite envenoming strategy <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515993>

### Soil-transmitted helminths
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/soil-transmitted-helminths/
TL;DR: Roundworm, whipworm and hookworm — gut worms spread through contaminated soil that affect hundreds of millions of children.
Summary: The main soil-transmitted helminths are Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) and the hookworms Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale. They spread where sanitation is poor and people walk barefoot or eat unwashed food. Heavy infections cause anaemia, stunting, poor school performance and, for hookworm, chronic blood loss. They are the classic target of school-based deworming, which is one of the cheapest interventions in public health.
Sources: WHO — Soil-transmitted helminth infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Taenia solium
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/taenia-solium/
TL;DR: The pork tapeworm — eating undercooked pork causes gut tapeworm, but swallowing its eggs causes cysts in the brain and epilepsy.
Summary: Taenia solium has an unusual double burden. The adult tapeworm, acquired by eating undercooked pork containing cysts, lives in the human gut. But if a person swallows the tapeworm's eggs — from contaminated food, water or hands — the larvae form cysts in the brain, causing neurocysticercosis, which is a leading preventable cause of epilepsy worldwide. Pigs are the intermediate host and free-roaming pigs that eat human faeces complete the cycle.
Sources: WHO — Taeniasis/cysticercosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/taeniasis-cysticercosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/treponema-pallidum-pertenue/
TL;DR: The bacterium that causes yaws — disfiguring skin and bone lesions in children that a single dose of azithromycin can cure.
Summary: Yaws is a chronic bacterial infection of skin and bone that mainly affects children under 15 in warm, humid, poor rural communities. It begins with a painless skin lesion and progresses, if untreated, to destructive lesions of the skin, bone and cartilage years later. Yaws is closely related to the bacterium that causes syphilis but is spread by skin contact in childhood rather than sexually. A single oral dose of azithromycin cures it, which is why a global eradication effort is under way.
Sources: WHO — Yaws <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/yaws>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Trypanosoma brucei
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/trypanosoma-brucei/
TL;DR: A single-celled parasite carried by the tsetse fly that causes sleeping sickness in people and nagana in cattle.
Summary: Trypanosoma brucei is an extracellular protozoan that lives in blood, lymph and eventually the brain. Two subspecies cause human disease: T. b. gambiense in West and Central Africa, which runs a slow chronic course over years, and T. b. rhodesiense in East and Southern Africa, which is acute and can kill within weeks. It evades the immune system by repeatedly changing its surface coat, which is why a vaccine has never worked.
Sources: WHO — Human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Trypanosoma cruzi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/trypanosoma-cruzi/
TL;DR: The parasite carried by blood-sucking triatomine bugs that causes Chagas disease, which can damage the heart decades after infection.
Summary: Trypanosoma cruzi infects an estimated six to seven million people in Latin America. The acute phase is usually mild and unnoticed; the chronic phase can follow years later with cardiomyopathy, heart failure and sudden death in about a third of those infected. It is also transmitted by blood transfusion, organ transplant and from mother to child, which is why blood-bank screening matters even outside endemic areas.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Zika virus
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/pathogens/zika-virus/
TL;DR: A flavivirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes that is usually harmless in adults but causes severe birth defects when it infects a pregnant woman.
Summary: Zika virus belongs to the same genus as dengue, yellow fever and West Nile virus, and it is transmitted by the same Aedes mosquitoes. In most people it causes a mild illness or none at all, which allowed it to spread silently. Its danger is in pregnancy: infection can reach the fetus and cause congenital Zika syndrome, with microcephaly and serious brain abnormalities. It can also be transmitted sexually, which is unusual for an arbovirus and complicated the response.
Sources: WHO — Zika virus (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/zika-virus>


## Vectors

### Aedes aegypti
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/aedes-aegypti/
TL;DR: The yellow-fever mosquito — a day-biting city dweller that is the main transmitter of dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
Summary: Aedes aegypti is the most important urban mosquito for viral disease. It bites during the day, breeds in small containers of clean water — tyres, buckets, flower pots, water tanks — and lives in and around houses, so it is not controlled by bed nets. Because it prefers people and breeds in domestic water storage, it follows urbanisation and unreliable piped water.
Sources: WHO — dengue and Aedes control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Aedes albopictus
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/aedes-albopictus/
TL;DR: The Asian tiger mosquito — a hardier relative of Aedes aegypti that has spread into temperate regions and carries the same viruses.
Summary: Aedes albopictus transmits dengue, chikungunya and Zika and, unlike Aedes aegypti, tolerates cooler temperatures and survives winters as eggs. That has let it establish in southern Europe, North America and China, where it causes the sporadic outbreaks that were once confined to the tropics. It breeds in both natural and artificial containers, including tree holes and discarded plastics.
Sources: ECDC — Aedes albopictus <https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/disease-vectors/facts/mosquito-factsheets/aedes-albopictus>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Anopheles mosquitoes
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/anopheles-mosquito/
TL;DR: The night-biting mosquitoes that transmit malaria — the vector whose control has saved more lives than any drug.
Summary: Anopheles gambiae and its relatives are the principal malaria vectors in Africa, and Anopheles species transmit the disease worldwide. Unlike Aedes aegypti, they bite mainly between dusk and dawn and breed in a wide range of water bodies rather than domestic containers — which is why insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying work against them, and why those two tools have driven nearly all the decline in malaria since 2000. The same two properties make resistance to the insecticides used in both a serious threat.
Sources: WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>; WHO — Global Malaria Programme <https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme>

### Blackflies (Simulium)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/blackfly/
TL;DR: Day-biting flies that breed in fast-flowing rivers and transmit river blindness.
Summary: Simulium blackflies breed in turbulent, well-oxygenated rivers and bite during the day, which is why onchocerciasis is concentrated along the rivers that these flies use as breeding grounds — the same rivers communities depend on for water and land. Larvicides applied to the river can suppress the fly, and this was the foundation of the original West African control programme before ivermectin existed.
Sources: WHO — Onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Culex mosquitoes
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/culex-mosquito/
TL;DR: Night-biting mosquitoes that breed in stagnant water and transmit lymphatic filariasis.
Summary: Culex quinquefasciatus is the main lymphatic filariasis vector in urban and peri-urban settings, breeding in polluted, stagnant water — latrines, open drains, septic tanks. Because it bites at night, insecticide-treated nets do reduce transmission, but the breeding sites are extensive where sanitation is poor, which links filariasis control to sanitation and drainage.
Sources: WHO — Lymphatic filariasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Freshwater snails
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/freshwater-snails/
TL;DR: The intermediate hosts of schistosomes — the worms cannot complete their cycle without the right snail species.
Summary: Schistosoma species each need a specific snail intermediate host: Bulinus for S. haematobium, Biomphalaria for S. mansoni, Oncomelania for S. japonicum. Infected snails release cercariae that penetrate human skin in fresh water. Because the parasite cannot reproduce without the snail, the snail is a bottleneck that can be attacked with molluscicides, environmental management, or by changing the habitat — which is why snail control is being revisited as an elimination tool alongside praziquantel.
Sources: WHO — Schistosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Sandflies (Phlebotomus and Lutzomyia)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/sandfly/
TL;DR: Small, silent, night-biting flies that transmit leishmaniasis.
Summary: Sandflies are about a third the size of a mosquito and bite at dusk and at night with little sound, so people are often unaware they were bitten. Phlebotomus species transmit Old World leishmaniasis in Africa, Asia and southern Europe; Lutzomyia species transmit New World disease in Latin America. Their breeding sites are moist organic matter — animal burrows, cracks in walls, soil — which makes them harder to attack than container-breeding mosquitoes.
Sources: WHO — Leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Triatomine bugs (kissing bugs)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/triatomine-bug/
TL;DR: Blood-sucking bugs that live in the cracks of poor rural houses and transmit Chagas disease through their faeces.
Summary: Triatomine bugs — Rhodnius, Triatoma and Panstrongylus — feed at night and defecate close to the bite, transferring Trypanosoma cruzi when the person scratches. They colonise cracks in mud walls, thatched roofs, and behind furniture, so housing quality determines risk. House spraying and improved housing have interrupted transmission in much of the Southern Cone, but the bug persists in the Amazon and in the Gran Chaco.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Tsetse fly (Glossina)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/vectors/tsetse-fly/
TL;DR: The blood-feeding fly of Africa that transmits sleeping sickness to people and nagana to cattle.
Summary: Tsetse flies are found only in sub-Saharan Africa and are unusual among insects in that females give birth to live larvae one at a time. Both sexes feed on blood and transmit Trypanosoma brucei. Control has historically used baited traps, insecticide-treated targets and the sterile insect technique; the fly's restricted range is the main reason sleeping sickness transmission has been pushed down so far.
Sources: WHO — Human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>


## Treatments

### Acoziborole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/acoziborole/
TL;DR: The first single-dose, one-day oral cure for sleeping sickness — approved in 2026 and registered first in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Summary: Acoziborole is a benzoxaborole developed by DNDi and Sanofi that cures Gambiense sleeping sickness with a single oral dose in both stages of disease, removing the need for lumbar-puncture staging, hospitalisation or a cold chain. It inhibits the trypanosome's CPSF3, an RNA-processing enzyme, and trials reported cure rates up to 96%. The European Medicines Agency approved it in 2026, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo — the country with the largest burden — registered it in June 2026, with other endemic countries expected to authorise importation. For a disease that once required weeks of intravenous treatment in hospital, it is the difference between a referral and a tablet.
Sources: DNDi — DRC approves acoziborole <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2026/drc-approves-use-acoziborole-breakthrough-one-day-oral-treatment-against-sleeping-sickness/>; DNDi — sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Albendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/albendazole/
TL;DR: A broad deworming tablet donated for mass treatment of gut worms and lymphatic filariasis, and used for cystic worm disease.
Summary: Albendazole is a benzimidazole that binds worm beta-tubulin, blocking microtubule assembly so the worm cannot absorb nutrients. It is one of the most widely used medicines on earth, donated by GSK for lymphatic filariasis and soil-transmitted helminth control, and given in mass campaigns that treat hundreds of millions of children a year. It also treats hydatid disease and neurocysticercosis, where prolonged courses are needed.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Ansuvimab
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ansuvimab/
TL;DR: A single monoclonal antibody that improved survival in Ebola, and one of the first treatments ever licensed for the disease.
Summary: Ansuvimab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds the Ebola virus glycoprotein and blocks it from entering cells. It was one of two antibody products shown in a randomised trial during the 2018–2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo to reduce mortality substantially compared with the standard of care, and it was subsequently licensed. It marked the point at which Ebola became a disease with specific treatment rather than supportive care alone — a rare advance for a haemorrhagic fever.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Arpraziquantel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/arpraziquantel/
TL;DR: A child-friendly dispersible tablet that finally treats schistosomiasis in preschool-aged children, who were excluded from the standard medicine.
Summary: Arpraziquantel is a paediatric formulation of praziquantel's active enantiomer, developed by the Pediatric Praziquantel Consortium for children from 3 months to 6 years — a group that carries a heavy schistosome burden but was almost never treated, because the standard tablet is large, bitter and of unestablished dosing in small children. It is a 150 mg dispersible tablet with an acceptable taste and stability in hot, humid climates, and is active against both Schistosoma mansoni and S. haematobium. The European Medicines Agency adopted a positive scientific opinion in December 2023 and WHO prequalified it in 2024, and the first preschool-aged child was treated in Uganda in early 2025 through an implementation study.
Sources: WHO — EMA positive scientific opinion on arpraziquantel <https://www.who.int/news/item/07-02-2024-european-medicines-agency-(ema)-adopts-a-positive-scientific-opinion-on-arpraziquantel>; Pediatric Praziquantel Consortium <https://www.pediatricpraziquantelconsortium.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Artemether-lumefantrine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/artemether-lumefantrine/
TL;DR: The most widely used artemisinin-based combination therapy — a three-day oral course that has cured hundreds of millions of people.
Summary: Artemisinin-based combination therapy pairs a fast-acting artemisinin, which kills most parasites in the first three days, with a slower partner drug that clears what remains. Artemether-lumefantrine is the most used combination worldwide. The combination model exists specifically to delay resistance: the artemisinin reduces the parasite population so fast that the partner drug rarely faces a resistant mutant. It only works if the partner drug is still effective, which is why losing partners to resistance is such a serious prospect.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>

### Artesunate
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/artesunate/
TL;DR: The first-line treatment for severe malaria, derived from the Chinese herb qinghao, and the reason severe malaria stopped being a death sentence.
Summary: Artesunate is a derivative of artemisinin, the antimalarial discovered in China in the 1970s from Artemisia annua and recognised with the 2015 Nobel Prize. Given intravenously it is the standard treatment for severe falciparum malaria, clearing parasites faster than any alternative and reducing mortality compared with quinine. Its limitation is that artemisinins are cleared quickly and must always be used in combination for uncomplicated disease to protect against resistance.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Azithromycin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/azithromycin/
TL;DR: A single-dose oral antibiotic used to wipe out trachoma and yaws through mass treatment.
Summary: Azithromycin is a broad-spectrum macrolide antibiotic that, given as a single oral dose, cures the eye infection that causes trachoma and the bacterium that causes yaws. Both programmes use mass administration of single doses to entire communities, which is far more practical than the topical and injectable alternatives. In trachoma it is the 'A' in the SAFE strategy; in yaws it underpins the eradication effort begun in 2012.
Sources: WHO — trachoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Bedaquiline (for leprosy)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/bedaquiline/
TL;DR: A tuberculosis drug with a very long half-life and strong activity against the leprosy bacillus, in a Phase 3 trial as a shorter treatment.
Summary: Bedaquiline was developed for drug-resistant tuberculosis and blocks mycobacterial ATP synthase. Its half-life of about five and a half months and its greater activity against Mycobacterium leprae than rifampicin make it attractive for leprosy, where the treatment course is long and people stop taking it. A Phase 2 trial in Brazil found that bedaquiline monotherapy cleared M. leprae in multibacillary patients, and a Phase 3 active-controlled trial of bedaquiline with rifampicin and clofazimine is under way. It is also being tested as post-exposure prophylaxis, which would make it the first new preventive agent for leprosy since single-dose rifampicin.
Sources: Leprosy research updates — bedaquiline <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12010777/>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Benzathine penicillin G
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/benzathine-penicillin/
TL;DR: A long-acting penicillin injection that cures yaws and syphilis with a single dose.
Summary: Benzathine penicillin G is a long-acting intramuscular penicillin that maintains bactericidal levels for weeks, so a single injection cures yaws and early syphilis. It is the alternative to azithromycin in yaws eradication where azithromycin resistance or contraindication matters, and it remains the standard treatment for syphilis and for preventing congenital syphilis. Its limits are that it requires injection and a functioning cold chain.
Sources: WHO — yaws <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/yaws>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Benznidazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/benznidazole/
TL;DR: The first-line treatment for Chagas disease — effective in the acute and early phases, but less so in established chronic disease.
Summary: Benznidazole is a nitroimidazole that kills Trypanosoma cruzi. It cures most people treated in the acute phase and in congenital infection, and it reduces progression in young children and in early chronic disease. In adults with longstanding cardiac disease the benefit is less certain, and the 60-day course causes side effects — rash, neuropathy, bone-marrow suppression — in a substantial minority, which leads many to stop treatment. Access has historically been poor outside Latin America.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Chloroquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/chloroquine/
TL;DR: The cheap, effective antimalarial that resistance destroyed — a case study in how fast a wonder drug can be lost.
Summary: Chloroquine cured malaria cheaply for decades and was the backbone of early eradication efforts. Widespread resistance in Plasmodium falciparum, driven by mutations in the parasite's transporter gene, made it useless across most of Africa and Asia by the 1990s, and it was replaced by artemisinin-based combination therapy. It remains effective against P. vivax in many places and is still used for some non-malarial conditions. Its history is the clearest warning of what could happen to artemisinins.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Clofazimine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/clofazimine/
TL;DR: The third drug in leprosy multidrug therapy, which also suppresses the inflammatory reactions the disease causes.
Summary: Clofazimine is a fat-soluble dye-derived antibiotic that is part of leprosy multidrug therapy. Besides killing Mycobacterium leprae it has anti-inflammatory activity that helps control leprosy reactions, the immune episodes that cause nerve damage. It stains the skin a reddish-brown, which is cosmetically noticeable but reversible. It is also used in Buruli ulcer regimens.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Dapsone
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/dapsone/
TL;DR: One of the three drugs in multidrug therapy for leprosy, and the drug that resistance made obsolete as a solo treatment.
Summary: Dapsone is a sulfone antibiotic that blocks folate synthesis in Mycobacterium leprae. Given alone for decades it selected resistant bacteria, which is why leprosy is now treated with multidrug therapy — rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine together. Dapsone also treats dermatitis herpetiformis and is used in some other skin conditions; it can cause anaemia and, rarely, a severe hypersensitivity syndrome.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/diethylcarbamazine/
TL;DR: A filarial drug combined with albendazole for mass treatment of lymphatic filariasis.
Summary: Diethylcarbamazine kills microfilariae and is a component of the albendazole-plus-DEC combination that is the main mass-treatment regimen for lymphatic filariasis outside Africa. It cannot be used where onchocerciasis or loiasis co-circulate, because it can cause severe reactions in those infections, which is why African programmes use albendazole plus ivermectin instead. It is donated by Eisai.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Doxycycline (antifilarial use)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/doxycycline/
TL;DR: An antibiotic that kills the Wolbachia bacteria inside filarial worms, sterilising and eventually killing them.
Summary: Doxycycline is an ordinary tetracycline antibiotic that happens to be lethal to Wolbachia, the endosymbiotic bacteria filarial worms depend on. A four-to-six week course sterilises adult worms and leads to their death, giving a durable effect that single-dose antifilarials do not. The problem is the course length: it is impractical for mass campaigns, so its use is targeted at individuals and in research settings, while programmes use shorter, higher-dose regimens in trials.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis and Wolbachia <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Eflornithine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/eflornithine/
TL;DR: A treatment for late-stage sleeping sickness, now given in combination with nifurtimox (NECT).
Summary: Eflornithine blocks ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme the trypanosome needs to divide. Given as an intravenous infusion over days it cured late-stage Gambiense sleeping sickness, but the regimen was burdensome; combined with oral nifurtimox as NECT it became far more practical. Its development is a classic case of a drug with no commercial market being kept alive by public and philanthropic funding.
Sources: DNDi — sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Emodepside
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/emodepside/
TL;DR: A veterinary dewormer being developed as a new human treatment for river blindness and gut worms, acting on a different channel from ivermectin.
Summary: Emodepside has been used in veterinary medicine for years and is now in clinical development for human onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths. It opens the SLO-1 potassium channel in worm nerve and muscle, a mechanism distinct from ivermectin's, so it offers a fallback where ivermectin cannot be used — including in areas where Loa loa co-circulates and ivermectin carries a risk of severe reactions. DNDi is leading the human development.
Sources: DNDi — onchocerciasis and emodepside <https://dndi.org/diseases/onchocerciasis/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Ethambutol
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ethambutol/
TL;DR: The fourth drug in standard tuberculosis treatment, included mainly to prevent resistance developing to the others.
Summary: Ethambutol inhibits the synthesis of arabinogalactan in the mycobacterial cell wall. It is not the most powerful drug in the regimen, but it protects the others: including a fourth drug makes it much harder for the bacterium to acquire simultaneous resistance during the long months of treatment. Its characteristic toxicity is optic neuritis, which requires monitoring vision at higher doses.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Fexinidazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/fexinidazole/
TL;DR: The first all-oral cure for sleeping sickness — a ten-day tablet course that replaced days of intravenous treatment.
Summary: Fexinidazole was developed by DNDi with Sanofi and approved in 2019 for both stages of Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis: a 10-day oral course covers early and late disease, removing the need for lumbar puncture staging and hospital infusions. It is not effective enough in the severe form of Rhodesiense disease. Its approval was a proof of concept that a non-profit partnership can take an abandoned compound to registration for a disease with no commercial market.
Sources: DNDi — fexinidazole <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Fosravuconazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/fosravuconazole/
TL;DR: The first drug tested against fungal mycetoma in a randomised trial — safe and once-weekly, but it did not beat itraconazole.
Summary: Fosravuconazole is a triazole antifungal designed for onychomycosis and repurposed for eumycetoma. In the first randomised, double-blind clinical trial for the disease, run at a single centre in Sudan by the Mycetoma Research Centre with DNDi and Eisai, it was compared at two once-weekly doses against daily itraconazole, with surgery at six months. Neither dose was superior to itraconazole, and both had numerically lower efficacy — but fosravuconazole showed no new safety concerns and its once-weekly dosing is far easier for patients who travel long distances to a clinic. That combination of a negative efficacy result and a real practical advantage is the honest outcome of the trial.
Sources: First randomised mycetoma trial results (The Lancet Infectious Diseases) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39098321/>; A balancing act: the pioneering mycetoma trial in Sudan (PLOS NTD) <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371/journal.pntd.0013000>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Isoniazid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/isoniazid/
TL;DR: One of the four drugs in standard tuberculosis treatment, and the mainstay of preventive treatment for people at high risk.
Summary: Isoniazid has been a cornerstone of tuberculosis treatment since 1952 and is unusual in being highly specific to mycobacteria, which is why it is well tolerated. It kills actively dividing bacteria and is the drug most used for preventive treatment in people with latent infection — a single drug taken for months to stop the disease developing. Resistance, common in multidrug-resistant strains, is detected through mutations in the katG and inhA genes.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Ivermectin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ivermectin/
TL;DR: A once-a-year tablet that transformed river blindness and lymphatic filariasis, and is donated free for as long as it is needed.
Summary: Ivermectin paralyses parasitic worms by opening glutamate-gated chloride channels that vertebrates do not have, which is why it is so safe. A single dose suppresses microfilariae for months, and repeated annual mass treatment broke transmission of river blindness across much of Africa and Latin America. Merck has donated it free for onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis since 1987, making it one of the largest drug donation programmes in history. It is also a treatment for scabies and strongyloidiasis.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Ixchiq (chikungunya vaccine)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ixchiq/
TL;DR: The first licensed chikungunya vaccine, whose use was paused in people aged 60 and over in 2025 after serious adverse events.
Summary: Ixchiq is a live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine and the first product of any kind licensed against the disease, given as a single dose. In 2025 the FDA and CDC recommended a pause in its use in people aged 60 and older while they investigated post-marketing reports of serious neurological and cardiac events — seventeen in total, including two deaths, in recipients aged 62 to 89 — and the FDA issued a further safety update later that year. The vaccine remains available for younger people, but the pause removed it from the age group most vulnerable to severe chikungunya, which is a substantial limitation for a disease spread by the same mosquitoes as dengue and with no specific treatment.
Sources: FDA/CDC — pause in use of Ixchiq in people 60 and older <https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/safety-availability-biologics/fda-and-cdc-recommend-pause-use-ixchiq-chikungunya-vaccine-live-individuals-60-years-age-and-older>

### Linezolid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/linezolid/
TL;DR: An oxazolidinone antibiotic that is effective against resistant tuberculosis, and also active against the leprosy bacillus.
Summary: Linezolid blocks the bacterial ribosome and is one of the most effective drugs in the BPaLM regimen for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Its problem is toxicity: prolonged use causes bone-marrow suppression, peripheral neuropathy and optic nerve damage, so it needs monitoring and patients often need dose adjustment. It illustrates the trade-off in resistant tuberculosis, where effective drugs are scarce enough that toxicity is accepted as the price of a cure.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Liposomal amphotericin B
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/liposomal-amphotericin-b/
TL;DR: A single-dose infusion that cures visceral leishmaniasis in South Asia, and the most effective treatment for it.
Summary: Liposomal amphotericin B packages the antifungal amphotericin B in fat spheres that concentrate in the organs where Leishmania lives, killing the parasite while reducing the kidney toxicity of the free drug. In South Asia a single dose can cure visceral leishmaniasis, which transformed treatment from weeks of injections to one visit. Its limits are cost, the need for a cold chain and infusion equipment, and the logistics of supporting it — which is why combination regimens have been explored to stretch supply.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### LXE408
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/lxe408/
TL;DR: A novel oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis, developed with Novartis, that could remove injections from treatment entirely.
Summary: LXE408 is a first-in-class oral compound developed by DNDi with Novartis as a potential new treatment for visceral leishmaniasis. It completed two Phase II proof-of-concept studies in India and Ethiopia in 2025 with promising efficacy and safety, and it represents the field's best hope of moving away from injected regimens — including the toxic antimonials that WHO's 2026 guideline update began to retire. It belongs to a class new to leishmaniasis, which also makes it useful if resistance to current drugs emerges.
Sources: DNDi — LXE408 with Novartis for visceral leishmaniasis <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/lxe408-novartis-visceral-leishmaniasis/>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Mebendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/mebendazole/
TL;DR: A chewable deworming tablet used in school programmes against roundworm, whipworm and hookworm.
Summary: Mebendazole is the other main benzimidazole dewormer alongside albendazole, donated by Johnson & Johnson for soil-transmitted helminth control. Chewable formulations make it practical for young children, and it is a mainstay of school-based deworming, which reduces anaemia and improves growth and school attendance at very low cost.
Sources: WHO — deworming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Melarsoprol
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/melarsoprol/
TL;DR: An arsenic-based treatment for late-stage sleeping sickness that is effective but can itself be lethal.
Summary: Melarsoprol has been the mainstay for late-stage sleeping sickness for decades, and it is still needed for Rhodesiense disease that has reached the brain. It is an arsenic compound given by intravenous injection, and it causes a fatal post-treatment encephalopathy in a small proportion of patients — a risk that made a safer alternative urgent and drove the development of NECT, fexinidazole and acoziborole.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Miltefosine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/miltefosine/
TL;DR: The first oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis, but its long course and teratogenicity limit its use.
Summary: Miltefosine is an oral alkylphosphocholine that kills Leishmania by disrupting its membrane and metabolism. It was a major advance as an oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis, especially in South Asia, and is also used for cutaneous disease. Its drawbacks are a 28-day course, gastrointestinal side effects, teratogenicity (so pregnancy must be excluded and prevented), and declining efficacy in South Asia, likely from resistance.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Mosnodenvir (JNJ-1802)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/mosnodenvir/
TL;DR: A dengue antiviral that protected volunteers in a human challenge study, but whose Phase 2 field trial was discontinued in 2025.
Summary: Mosnodenvir is a small-molecule antiviral that blocks dengue virus replication and, unusually for the field, demonstrated protection in a controlled human infection model — a strong early signal that a preventive dengue drug might be possible. It was safe and well tolerated in Phase 1 and Phase 2a studies. In 2025 the developer discontinued the Phase 2 field study, leaving dengue without an approved antiviral and illustrating a recurring problem: a promising mechanism validated in a challenge model still needs a large, expensive field trial, and there is no commercial logic for funding one in the countries where dengue kills most people.
Sources: Johnson & Johnson — discontinuation of the Phase 2 dengue study <https://www.jnj.com/media-center/press-releases/johnson-johnson-to-discontinue-phase-2-field-study-evaluating-investigational-antiviral-for-the-prevention-of-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Moxidectin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/moxidectin/
TL;DR: A longer-acting relative of ivermectin, approved in 2018 for river blindness, that suppresses microfilariae for longer.
Summary: Moxidectin is a macrocyclic lactone that works on the same glutamate-gated chloride channel as ivermectin but stays in the body longer, so a single dose suppresses onchocercal microfilariae for a full year or more. The FDA approved it for onchocerciasis in 2018 on the basis of a trial showing better and more sustained skin microfilarial suppression than ivermectin. It has not yet displaced ivermectin in mass programmes, where the free donation of ivermectin is decisive.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Nifurtimox
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/nifurtimox/
TL;DR: A Chagas and sleeping-sickness drug; as part of NECT it made late-stage sleeping sickness far easier to treat.
Summary: Nifurtimox is a nitrofuran active against both Trypanosoma cruzi and T. brucei. It is a second-line option for Chagas disease (a 60-day course with significant side effects), but its landmark role is in NECT — nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy — which replaced weeks of melarsoprol infusions for late-stage sleeping sickness with a simpler, safer regimen. It is on the WHO essential medicines list.
Sources: DNDi — sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Nitazoxanide (as a fascioliasis alternative)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/nitazoxanide/
TL;DR: The only plausible alternative to triclabendazole for fascioliasis, and a poor one — cure rates around 30% in the patients who need it most.
Summary: Nitazoxanide is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic used for intestinal infections, and it has been tested as a fallback for fascioliasis when triclabendazole fails. The evidence is discouraging: in an Egyptian series of patients who had already failed two doses of triclabendazole, nitazoxanide cured about 30%; in a Peruvian case series it was ineffective. It is included here because it defines the problem rather than solving it — triclabendazole is the only recommended medicine for human fascioliasis, resistance is emerging, and there is no established alternative behind it.
Sources: Triclabendazole treatment failure for Fasciola hepatica (EID) <https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/7/20-3900_article>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Olorofim
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/olorofim/
TL;DR: A new antifungal from the tuberculosis-style pipeline that has excellent activity against the main mycetoma fungus in the laboratory.
Summary: Olorofim is an orotomide antifungal that inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and is in development for multidrug-resistant mould infections. It has shown excellent in vitro activity against Madurella mycetomatis, the main cause of eumycetoma, which makes it one of the most promising compounds for a disease with no reliably effective drug. It is not being developed for mycetoma — the market cannot support it — so the field's route is to follow the antifungal pipeline and find funding to test such compounds where the disease occurs.
Sources: The antifungal pipeline — fosmanogepix, ibrexafungerp, olorofim <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8501344/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Oxamniquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/oxamniquine/
TL;DR: An older drug that worked only against Schistosoma mansoni and has largely been abandoned.
Summary: Oxamniquine was developed as a schistosomiasis treatment but is active only against Schistosoma mansoni. It fell out of use because praziquantel covers all three main schistosome species in a single dose and was easier to supply. Its story is a warning about reliance on a single drug: when the only remaining medicine fails, the alternatives have already been retired.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Oxfendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/oxfendazole/
TL;DR: A veterinary dewormer being developed as a treatment that could kill the adult worms of river blindness, lymphatic filariasis and loiasis.
Summary: Oxfendazole is a benzimidazole used for decades in animals, now in clinical development for human filarial disease by DNDi and partners. What makes it interesting is the possibility of macrofilaricidal activity — killing adult worms rather than only suppressing their offspring — which would shorten elimination programmes that currently must run for the 10–15 year lifespan of the adult parasite, and would treat the patient rather than only the community. Phase II work is running across several infections: the eWHORM partnership's basket trial in Africa, where trichuriasis recruitment is complete and onchocerciasis and loiasis sites have opened, and a Phase IIa proof-of-concept trial for lymphatic filariasis started in India by the ICMR in 2025. A commercialisable tablet formulation is in development.
Sources: DNDi — oxfendazole <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/oxfendazole/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Paromomycin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/paromomycin/
TL;DR: An injectable antibiotic that kills Leishmania and is used, often in combination, for visceral leishmaniasis.
Summary: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that disrupts the parasite's ribosomes and mitochondria. Given intramuscularly for 21 days it cures visceral leishmaniasis, and in combination with liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine it shortens and cheapens treatment. It is also used topically for some cutaneous forms. Its main limitations are injection-site pain and the need for daily injections over weeks.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Pentamidine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pentamidine/
TL;DR: An old injected drug for early-stage sleeping sickness, and still a first-line option there.
Summary: Pentamidine is used for the first stage of Gambiense sleeping sickness, before the parasite reaches the brain. It is given by intramuscular injection over about a week. Its limitations — injections, and poor efficacy once the parasite is in the central nervous system — are why oral treatments such as fexinidazole and acoziborole matter so much.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Pentavalent antimonials
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/antimonials/
TL;DR: The original leishmaniasis drugs — cheap and effective, but toxic to the heart and now failing in South Asia.
Summary: Sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate have treated leishmaniasis for over seventy years. They remain widely used for cutaneous disease and in some regions for visceral disease, because they are cheap. Their problems are a long course of painful injections and serious toxicity, including heart-rhythm disturbance and pancreatitis, plus widespread treatment failure in Bihar, India, where resistance became so common that antimonials were abandoned there.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Permethrin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/permethrin/
TL;DR: A topical insecticide cream that kills scabies mites, and the same chemical class used to treat bed nets.
Summary: Permethrin is a synthetic pyrethroid. As a 5% cream washed off after 8–14 hours it kills scabies mites, and it is the first-line topical treatment for ordinary scabies. It is also applied to clothing and bed nets as an insecticide. For crusted scabies and for whole-community treatment, oral ivermectin is often preferred because topical treatment of a whole household or village is impractical.
Sources: WHO — scabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Praziquantel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/praziquantel/
TL;DR: A single-dose tablet that kills adult schistosomes and tapeworms, and the only drug used at scale against schistosomiasis.
Summary: Praziquantel is the backbone of schistosomiasis treatment worldwide. A single oral dose kills adult worms by opening a calcium-permeable ion channel, causing paralysis and damage to the worm's surface. It is cheap, safe and on the WHO essential medicines list. Its weaknesses are that it works poorly against immature worms, requires repeated treatment to prevent reinfection, and is the only option — which makes resistance a serious concern if it emerges.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>

### Pretomanid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pretomanid/
TL;DR: One of the three drugs in the six-month, injection-free regimen that transformed treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis.
Summary: Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole that, like delamanid, is activated by the mycobacterial enzyme Ddn. Given with bedaquiline and linezolid — the BPaLM regimen — it allows multidrug-resistant tuberculosis to be cured in six months without injections, replacing regimens that took up to two years and included injectable drugs with severe toxicity. It is one of the clearest recent gains in tuberculosis care, and it exists because of a non-profit drug developer working where the market did not.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Primaquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/primaquine/
TL;DR: The drug that clears the dormant liver stages of vivax malaria and blocks transmission — with one dangerous exception, G6PD deficiency.
Summary: Primaquine has two distinct jobs: it kills the hypnozoites, the dormant liver forms that cause relapses in Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale malaria, and it kills the mature gametocytes that transmit the parasite to mosquitoes. It is the only widely available drug that does the first. Its danger is that it causes haemolysis in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, a common genetic condition in malaria-endemic countries, so testing is recommended before use — which is itself a barrier where laboratory capacity is thin.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Pyrazinamide
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pyrazinamide/
TL;DR: The drug that shortened tuberculosis treatment from nine months to six — and whose mechanism took decades to explain.
Summary: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug that is only active in acidic conditions, which is why it works against bacteria in inflamed tissue that other drugs reach poorly. Adding it to the regimen in the 1970s shortened treatment from nine months to six, one of the largest single gains in tuberculosis care. Its mechanism was settled only recently, and it remains central to both drug-susceptible and newer resistant-disease regimens.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/rabies-postexposure-prophylaxis/
TL;DR: Wound washing plus a course of rabies vaccine, with immunoglobulin for severe bites — it prevents the disease completely if given in time.
Summary: Rabies PEP is the combination of immediate wound washing, a series of rabies vaccine doses, and — for category III exposures — rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound. Given promptly after a bite it prevents disease essentially every time. The global problem is access: deaths happen where vaccine and immunoglobulin are unavailable, unaffordable or require travel that victims cannot make in time. Intradermal dose-sparing regimens and monoclonal antibodies are ways to stretch scarce supplies.
Sources: WHO — rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Rifampicin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/rifampicin/
TL;DR: The most important drug in leprosy and Buruli ulcer treatment, and the one that makes single-dose prevention possible.
Summary: Rifampicin kills mycobacteria by blocking RNA polymerase. It is the key bactericidal component of leprosy multidrug therapy, part of the antibiotic combination that cures Buruli ulcer, and the basis of single-dose post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts of leprosy patients. Because it is also a first-line tuberculosis drug, rifampicin resistance in either disease is a shared threat and its use is carefully stewarded.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Snake antivenom
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/snake-antivenom/
TL;DR: Antibodies from hyper-immunised animals that neutralise venom — the only specific treatment for snakebite, and often in short supply.
Summary: Snake antivenom is made by immunising horses or sheep with venom and harvesting the antibodies, which are then given intravenously to neutralise circulating venom. It must match the snakes of the region, so a shortage in one country cannot be filled from another's stock. Problems include cost, cold-chain requirements, a risk of allergic reactions, and a long history of poor-quality products; WHO maintains a list of prequalified antivenoms to address the last of these.
Sources: WHO — snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Suramin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/suramin/
TL;DR: An injected drug for first-stage Rhodesiense sleeping sickness, the form of the disease that kills within weeks.
Summary: Suramin treats the early stage of Rhodesiense sleeping sickness, which is acute and must be treated urgently. It is given by intravenous injection after a test dose, because of a risk of immediate reactions. It does not cross into the brain, so late-stage disease needs a different drug — historically melarsoprol.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Tafenoquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/tafenoquine/
TL;DR: A single-dose alternative to primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria, but with the same G6PD danger.
Summary: Tafenoquine does what primaquine does — clearing dormant liver stages of Plasmodium vivax — but in a single dose rather than a 5 to 14 day course, which matters enormously for adherence in people who feel well after their fever has gone. It shares primaquine's contraindication in G6PD deficiency and therefore requires a quantitative G6PD test before use, making the diagnostic a prerequisite for the drug.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Telacebec (Q203)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/telacebec/
TL;DR: A tuberculosis drug with exceptional potency against the Buruli ulcer bacterium, in trials that could shorten treatment from eight weeks to a few doses.
Summary: Telacebec is an imidazopyridine developed for tuberculosis that blocks QcrB in the mycobacterial respiratory chain. Against Mycobacterium ulcerans it has the lowest minimum inhibitory concentration of any drug tested — far below rifampicin or clarithromycin — and in mouse models it sterilised the infection after only sixteen doses, which would translate into an ultrashort regimen. TB Alliance initiated a Phase 2 proof-of-concept trial (TREAT-BU) in mid-2024. It is the clearest example in the NTD field of the repurposing strategy: take a molecule whose safety is already established for one mycobacterial disease and prove it works for another, rather than inventing a new drug for a market that cannot pay.
Sources: TB Alliance — telacebec trial in Buruli ulcer <https://www.tballiance.org/news-new-clinical-trial-examines-use-novel-compound-telacebec-buruli-ulcer-patients/>; TREAT-BU trial (ClinicalTrials.gov) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06481163>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Tribendimidine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/tribendimidine/
TL;DR: A deworming drug developed in China that is active against gut worms, including some that resist the standard drugs.
Summary: Tribendimidine is a broad-spectrum anthelmintic developed in China and used there for years. Trials have shown good activity against Ascaris, hookworm and Trichuris, and it appears effective against some benzimidazole-resistant worms, making it a candidate for combination or rotation where resistance bites. It acts on nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Triclabendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/triclabendazole/
TL;DR: A deworming tablet particularly effective against liver flukes, used for fascioliasis and paragonimiasis.
Summary: Triclabendazole is a benzimidazole that is unusually active against the liver fluke Fasciola, killing both immature and adult worms, and it also treats Paragonimus lung flukes. It is on the WHO essential medicines list and was added to WHO's donated-donation programme for foodborne trematodiases. As with other benzimidazoles, its target is parasite beta-tubulin.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — foodborne trematode infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/foodborne-trematode-infections>


## Diagnostics

### Antibody rapid diagnostic tests
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/antibody-rdt/
TL;DR: Finger-prick strip tests that detect the body's antibody response, widely used to map who has been exposed to an NTD.
Summary: Antibody RDTs are the workhorse of NTD mapping: they are cheap, need no laboratory and are used to survey whole villages for exposure to lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis and other infections. Their fundamental limitation is the antibody response itself — it persists after infection clears, so a positive result indicates exposure, not necessarily active infection, and cannot be used to decide whether someone needs treatment. A newer generation of tests targets parasite antigens instead.
Sources: FIND — diagnostics for neglected diseases <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Brugia Test Plus (BT+)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/brugia-test-plus/
TL;DR: A second-generation rapid test for the Brugia species that the standard filariasis antigen test cannot detect.
Summary: Brugia malayi and B. timori cause a large share of lymphatic filariasis in South and Southeast Asia, and the standard circulating-filarial-antigen test does not see them. The alternative — antibody tests — cannot distinguish current from past infection. Brugia Test Plus detects IgG4 antibodies against two Brugia antigens simultaneously, was independently evaluated in Malaysia, the United States and Indonesia, and performed reproducibly in high-temperature, high-humidity field conditions. It is an example of a diagnostic built to fill a specific hole in the elimination toolkit rather than a general improvement.
Sources: Drugs & Diagnostics for Tropical Diseases — lymphatic filariasis <https://www.ddtd.org/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/catt/
TL;DR: A field test for Gambiense sleeping sickness that detects antibodies and has driven decades of active screening.
Summary: CATT mixes the patient's blood with stained trypanosomes that agglutinate in the presence of specific antibodies. It made mass screening for sleeping sickness possible in remote settings without a laboratory. Because it detects antibodies it cannot distinguish current from past infection, so a positive CATT is followed by parasite confirmation. It works for Gambiense disease but not for Rhodesiense, for which there is no comparable rapid test.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Cartridge-based molecular tests
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/gene-cartridge-test/
TL;DR: Self-contained cartridges that run a molecular test at the point of care, like the platforms built for tuberculosis.
Summary: Cartridge platforms automate sample preparation and DNA amplification inside a sealed disposable, so a molecular result can be obtained with minimal training outside a laboratory. The tuberculosis cartridge is the best-known example and has been adapted for NTDs and for detecting drug resistance. For NTD programmes their promise is sensitive diagnosis where it is needed; their obstacles are cost per test, the need for a powered instrument, and the fact that different diseases need different cartridges.
Sources: FIND — cartridge-based molecular diagnostics <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Chagas serology and blood-donor screening
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/chagas-serology/
TL;DR: Two different antibody tests are needed to confirm Chagas disease, and every blood donor in affected regions should be screened.
