Summary: Because Trypanosoma cruzi is hard to see in blood during chronic infection, diagnosis rests on detecting antibodies — and because those tests are imperfect, WHO requires two different serological methods to agree before calling a case confirmed. The same tests screen blood donors and pregnant women, which is how transfusion transmission has been largely stopped in Latin America and how congenital cases are found. Screening is also required in non-endemic countries receiving migrants from affected regions.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Cysticercosis serology (EITB and rT24H)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/cysticercosis-serology/
TL;DR: Antibody tests that confirm exposure to the pork tapeworm, used alongside imaging to diagnose brain cysts.
Summary: Diagnosing neurocysticercosis combines imaging with serology. The enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB, also called the LLGP-EITB) detects antibodies against specific Taenia solium glycoproteins and is highly specific; the rT24H assay uses a recombinant antigen and is easier to standardise and deploy. Both indicate exposure rather than active disease and cannot show whether a lesion in the brain is alive, so they are read together with CT or MRI and with the clinical picture. Detecting the tapeworm carrier — the person actually shedding eggs — is a separate and harder problem, relying on stool examination or coproantigen tests that are insensitive at low burdens. A point-of-care test for active infection and for the carrier state is one of the field's clearest unmet needs.
Sources: WHO — taeniasis/cysticercosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/taeniasis-cysticercosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Direct agglutination test (DAT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/direct-agglutination-test/
TL;DR: A laboratory test for visceral leishmaniasis that detects antibodies by visible clumping, and works well in East Africa.
Summary: DAT mixes the patient's serum with stained Leishmania promastigotes; antibodies cause the parasites to clump, which is read visually. It is inexpensive and works better than rK39 in East Africa, where that strip underperforms. Its drawbacks are that it needs a cold chain, a laboratory and overnight incubation, so it is not a village-level test.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Dual rapid diagnostic test for yaws
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/yaws-dual-rdt/
TL;DR: A rapid test that combines a treponemal and a non-treponemal line, helping separate active yaws from past infection — and from syphilis.
Summary: Yaws is caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue, and the antibodies it provokes cross-react with those of venereal syphilis, so a simple treponemal test cannot tell the two apart or distinguish active infection from old. Dual rapid diagnostic tests address this by combining a treponemal line, which detects any exposure, with a non-treponemal line, which is more indicative of active infection — the same approach used in syphilis screening. WHO and partners have also developed a target product profile for a second, harder test: one that detects the macrolide resistance mutations that would compromise azithromycin, the antibiotic the entire eradication strategy depends on. That resistance test does not yet exist as a field product.
Sources: Diagnostics to support the eradication of yaws — target product profiles <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9473620/>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Ebola RT-PCR
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/ebola-rt-pcr/
TL;DR: The molecular test that confirms Ebola infection, and the test on which outbreak response depends.
Summary: Ebola is confirmed by detecting viral RNA in blood, usually by RT-PCR. Because viral load rises over the first days of illness, an early negative test does not exclude infection, and patients are retested. The test defines who is a case, who must be isolated and whose contacts must be traced — so its availability, speed and accuracy shape the entire response. During outbreaks, laboratory capacity is often established from scratch, frequently in tents near treatment centres.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Filarial test strip (FTS)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/filarial-test-strip/
TL;DR: A rapid antigen test for lymphatic filariasis that falls after the worms die, so it can show whether transmission has actually stopped.
Summary: The FTS is a lateral-flow test for circulating filarial antigen from adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms. Its crucial advantage over antibody tests is behaviour after cure: because it detects the parasite's own antigen rather than the host's antibody response, it falls when the adult worms die, so a negative result means something about the present rather than the past. It is used for mapping, for assessing the impact of mass treatment and for post-validation surveillance, and it is far more practical than night blood films, which require a sample taken when microfilariae are in the bloodstream. It does not detect Brugia species, which is why a brugian test was developed separately.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Formol-ether concentration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/formol-ether-concentration/
TL;DR: A stool concentration technique that makes light worm infections easier to see under a microscope.
Summary: The formol-ether (or formol-ethyl acetate) concentration method separates parasite eggs and cysts from stool debris by centrifugation, so more of the sample can be examined and light infections that a direct smear would miss become visible. It is a workhorse of diagnostic parasitology, though it is less quantitative than Kato-Katz for measuring infection intensity.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminth diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Kato-Katz stool smear
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/kato-katz/
TL;DR: The standard microscope method for counting worm eggs in stool — cheap, quantitative and the benchmark for schistosomiasis and gut worms.
Summary: A measured sample of stool is sieved, pressed through a template onto a slide and examined under a microscope; the egg count is expressed as eggs per gram. It needs only a microscope and a trained technician, which is why it is used almost everywhere. Its weaknesses are declining sensitivity when infection intensity is low — exactly the situation at the end of an elimination campaign — and the need for a fresh sample examined within about an hour for hookworm.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/molecular-lamp/
TL;DR: A DNA test that runs at one warm temperature, bringing molecular detection closer to the field.
Summary: LAMP amplifies parasite DNA at a constant temperature of around 60–65°C without a thermal cycler, so it can run on a simple heat block. For schistosomiasis and other NTDs it offers much greater sensitivity than microscopy for light infections, which matters for verifying elimination. Its practical limits are reagent cost, strict contamination control, and the need for reliable electricity and a cold chain for some reagents.
Sources: FIND — molecular diagnostics <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Malaria rapid diagnostic test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/malaria-rdt/
TL;DR: A finger-prick strip that detects malaria parasite antigens in fifteen minutes, and that made test-and-treat possible in villages.
Summary: Malaria rapid diagnostic tests detect parasite proteins — usually histidine-rich protein 2 for Plasmodium falciparum — on a lateral-flow strip, with no microscope or electricity. They transformed malaria care by allowing a health worker to confirm infection before treatment, which is what makes test-and-treat policy workable and prevents the blind prescribing that drives resistance. Their weaknesses are heat sensitivity, the deletion of the hrp2 gene in some parasite populations that makes them falsely negative, and their inability to quantify parasite density — which microscopy and molecular testing still provide.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>

### Mini-FLOTAC
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mini-flotac/
TL;DR: A stool concentration technique more sensitive than the standard smear for counting worm eggs, and easier to standardise.
Summary: Mini-FLOTAC is a flotation-based method for counting helminth eggs in stool. It detects more low-intensity infections than the standard Kato-Katz smear and uses a closed, standardised apparatus that reduces operator variability and exposure to faecal material. As soil-transmitted helminth programmes move from controlling disease to eliminating it as a public health problem, they need diagnostics sensitive enough to certify that moderate and heavy infections have fallen below the target threshold, and Mini-FLOTAC is one of the practical options — alongside molecular methods, which are more sensitive still but cost more.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminth infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Molecular tuberculosis test with rifampicin resistance (Xpert MTB/RIF)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/xpert-mtb-rif/
TL;DR: A cartridge-based test that detects tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in under two hours, from a sputum sample.
Summary: This test automated molecular tuberculosis diagnosis and made resistance detection routine. It amplifies the bacterium's DNA and simultaneously identifies mutations in the rifampicin-resistance gene, so a patient can be started on the right treatment the same day rather than waiting weeks for culture. It is also a marker for multidrug resistance, since rifampicin resistance usually accompanies isoniazid resistance. Its limits are cost, the need for an instrument and power, and lower sensitivity in people with HIV and in children, who produce fewer bacteria in sputum.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Mycolactone detection
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mycolactone-detection/
TL;DR: A test for the toxin the Buruli ulcer bacterium produces, which could allow diagnosis at a district clinic rather than a reference laboratory.
Summary: Mycobacterium ulcerans causes disease entirely through mycolactone, its toxin, so detecting the toxin is a direct way to diagnose the infection. Fluorescent thin-layer chromatography has been evaluated at district level, and other assay formats are in development. The value is practical: PCR requires a reference laboratory and a sample transport chain, whereas a toxin test could be done where the patient presents, allowing treatment to start before the lesion extends. A point-of-care test is one of WHO's stated research priorities for Buruli ulcer precisely because late diagnosis is the main driver of disability.
Sources: WHO — Buruli ulcer research priorities <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/buruli-ulcer/research-priorities>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (POC-CCA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/point-of-care-cca/
TL;DR: A urine strip test for schistosomiasis that gives a result in minutes, without a microscope or a stool sample.
Summary: POC-CCA is a lateral-flow test that detects an antigen released by adult schistosomes into urine. It requires no electricity, no microscope and no stool, and it detects most moderate and heavy Schistosoma mansoni infections well. It tends to read positive for weeks after successful treatment, which limits its use for test-of-cure, and its sensitivity for light S. haematobium infection is debated. It remains a research-grade product rather than a WHO-prequalified device.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/molecular-pcr/
TL;DR: The most sensitive way to detect a parasite's DNA, used for confirmation, low-intensity infection and surveillance.
Summary: PCR copies a specific DNA sequence many times over so that even trace amounts can be detected, and quantitative PCR can estimate the parasite load. It is valuable exactly where microscopy fails: light infections, post-treatment monitoring and pooled surveillance samples. In most NTD settings it is a laboratory and reference test, limited by cost, equipment, clean facilities and trained staff — the constraints that field-friendly molecular platforms are trying to remove.
Sources: WHO — molecular diagnostics for NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### rK39 rapid test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/rk39-rapid-test/
TL;DR: A finger-prick strip test for visceral leishmaniasis that gives an answer in fifteen minutes in a village clinic.
Summary: The rK39 immunochromatographic strip detects antibodies to a Leishmania antigen and is the main field test for visceral leishmaniasis. In South Asia it is highly sensitive and specific on symptomatic patients, which is why it underpins case detection there. Its performance is lower in East Africa, and because it detects antibodies it can stay positive for years after cure and cannot be used to confirm relapse.
Sources: WHO — visceral leishmaniasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Skin snip for onchocerciasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/skin-snip/
TL;DR: A tiny bloodless skin sample examined for microfilariae — the traditional way to confirm river blindness infection.
Summary: In a skin snip, a small sliver of skin is taken with a corneoscleral punch and incubated in saline so that emerging microfilariae can be counted. It is the classical confirmatory and quantitative test for onchocerciasis and was used to assess how well treatment suppressed the parasite. It is invasive, needs a laboratory and has largely been superseded for programme decisions by antibody testing and molecular methods.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Thick blood smear and microscopy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/microscopy-thick-smear/
TL;DR: Examining a stained drop of blood under a microscope to see trypanosomes directly — the confirmation that a patient is really infected.
Summary: Direct microscopic examination of a stained thick blood film, or of a lymph-node aspirate, confirms trypanosome infection after a positive antibody test. It is specific but not sensitive at low parasite loads, so programmes pair it with concentration methods (the capillary tube centrifugation and the mini anion exchange centrifugation technique). Its strength is certainty: an antibody test can be wrong, a visible parasite cannot be.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Tuberculin skin test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/tuberculin-skin-test/
TL;DR: The century-old skin test for tuberculosis infection, still used despite its inability to distinguish infection from vaccination.
Summary: The tuberculin skin test measures the immune response to injected mycobacterial antigens. It indicates that a person has been infected at some point, but cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease, and it produces false positives in people vaccinated with BCG — which is most people in high-burden countries. Interferon-gamma release assays were developed to avoid that problem, though they have their own limitations and cost more. Both are tests of infection, not of disease, and are used mainly to decide who should receive preventive treatment.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Ultrasound for mycetoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mycetoma-ultrasound/
TL;DR: A bedside scan whose 'dot-in-circle' sign identifies mycetoma and helps distinguish the fungal form from the bacterial one.
Summary: Ultrasound has become a key diagnostic for mycetoma because the grains the organism forms in tissue produce a characteristic 'dot-in-circle' appearance. It is cheap, needs no laboratory, can be done in a district hospital, and helps determine how far the disease has spread through soft tissue and bone — which shapes whether surgery is feasible. Identifying whether the infection is fungal or bacterial still needs the grains themselves, examined by microscopy, culture or molecular methods, but ultrasound is what makes an early working diagnosis possible where a reference laboratory is not.
Sources: WHO — mycetoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### WHO simplified trachoma grading
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/trachoma-grading/
TL;DR: A standard set of visual signs that lets a trained grader decide in the field whether someone has active or blinding trachoma.
Summary: The WHO simplified grading system defines five signs — follicular and intense inflammation, conjunctival scarring, trichiasis and corneal opacity — that a grader can assess with a torch and a loupe. It is the basis for population prevalence surveys that decide whether a district needs mass azithromycin treatment. Its limitation is subjectivity: grader agreement varies, which is why photographic grading and, more recently, artificial-intelligence grading are being evaluated.
Sources: WHO — trachoma grading <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Zika RT-PCR
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/zika-rt-pcr/
TL;DR: A molecular test that confirms Zika during the short window when the virus is detectable, and is the only reliable way to diagnose it.
Summary: Zika is confirmed by reverse-transcription PCR on blood or urine, and the window is narrow: the virus is detectable for only about a week after symptoms begin, so a negative test later does not rule out infection. Serology is the fallback but cross-reacts heavily with dengue and other flaviviruses, which makes it unreliable in exactly the places where both circulate. In pregnancy this matters enormously, because a definitive diagnosis shapes counselling and monitoring.
Sources: WHO — Zika virus (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/zika-virus>


## Targets

### Bacterial ribosome (50S subunit)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/bacterial-ribosome/
TL;DR: The protein factory that oxazolidinones and macrolides block to stop bacteria making proteins.
Summary: The bacterial ribosome is the most successful antibiotic target in medicine, and the reason is selectivity: the bacterial 50S subunit differs enough from its human counterpart that drugs can bind it without harming the patient. Linezolid and azithromycin act here by different mechanisms — linezolid blocks initiation of translation, macrolides block elongation — which is why they are not interchangeable despite sharing a target.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Bacterial RNA polymerase
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/rna-polymerase/
TL;DR: The enzyme that copies DNA into RNA, and the target of rifampicin, the cornerstone of leprosy and Buruli ulcer treatment.
Summary: Rifampicin binds bacterial RNA polymerase and blocks transcription, killing mycobacteria including Mycobacterium leprae and M. ulcerans. It is so effective that a single dose is used for leprosy post-exposure prophylaxis, and it anchors multidrug therapy. Rifampicin resistance is the main threat to leprosy control, and it is also a first-line drug for tuberculosis, which makes stewardship of the drug a shared concern.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Chikungunya virus glycoprotein
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/chikungunya-glycoprotein/
TL;DR: The surface protein that lets chikungunya virus enter cells and the antigen in the licensed vaccine.
Summary: The chikungunya envelope glycoproteins mediate attachment and entry and are the target of neutralising antibodies, which is why the licensed live-attenuated vaccine is built on them. As with Ebola, the disease has been addressed with a vaccine rather than an antiviral — and the 2025 pause in use of that vaccine in older adults shows that a well-chosen target does not remove the need for post-marketing safety surveillance.
Sources: WHO — chikungunya (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya>

### Cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 3 (CPSF3)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/cpsf3/
TL;DR: The newly identified target of acoziborole, the single-dose drug candidate for sleeping sickness.
Summary: CPSF3 is part of the machinery that matures messenger RNA. Acoziborole binds it in Trypanosoma brucei and shuts down RNA processing, killing the parasite with a single oral dose — a striking result for a disease whose older treatments required intravenous infusions over days. The target was identified using chemical genetics and genome-scale screening, and it illustrates how a modern antiparasitic target can be found even without a large commercial programme.
Sources: DNDi — acoziborole for sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Cruzain (T. cruzi cysteine protease)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/cruzain/
TL;DR: A digestive enzyme the Chagas parasite needs to survive in the blood; a long-pursued drug target.
Summary: Cruzain is the major cysteine protease of Trypanosoma cruzi and is required for the parasite to break down proteins, invade cells and evade the immune response. It is one of the oldest rationally pursued antiparasitic targets, with three decades of inhibitor chemistry behind it, yet no cruzain inhibitor has reached the clinic — a cautionary example of how a good target does not guarantee a usable drug.
Sources: Chagas disease drug discovery <https://dndi.org/diseases/chagas/>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Ddn (deazaflavin-dependent nitroreductase)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/ddn/
TL;DR: The enzyme that activates pretomanid and delamanid inside the tuberculosis bacterium.
Summary: Ddn is unusual among drug targets in that it does not need to be inhibited — it needs to work. It converts the prodrugs pretomanid and delamanid into their active forms, which then poison the mycobacterium. Loss of Ddn function therefore causes resistance. It is the mirror image of a conventional target, and understanding it was essential to developing the nitroimidazole class that now underpins the six-month regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Dengue NS2B-NS3 protease
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/dengue-protease/
TL;DR: The viral scissors that cut the dengue proteins apart so the virus can assemble; a target borrowed from hepatitis C research.
Summary: The NS3 protein is a protease that, with its NS2B cofactor, cleaves the viral polyprotein into functional pieces. Blocking it stops the virus from maturing. The target is attractive because hepatitis C yielded successful protease inhibitors, giving a roadmap; the difficulty for dengue is that the active site is flatter and more exposed, so inhibitor design has been harder than for hepatitis C.
Sources: Literature search: dengue NS2B-NS3 protease inhibitors <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=dengue+NS2B-NS3+protease+inhibitor>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Dengue NS4B
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/dengue-ns4b/
TL;DR: A dengue protein that helps assemble the viral replication machinery, and the target of the discontinued antiviral mosnodenvir.
Summary: NS4B is one of the non-structural dengue proteins and is involved in building the replication complex on host membranes. Mosnodenvir, formerly JNJ-1802, inhibits it and protected volunteers in a controlled human infection model — the strongest early signal any dengue antiviral has produced. The field trial was discontinued in 2025, so the target is validated biologically but has not yet yielded a licensed drug.
Sources: WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; PAHO — dengue <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/dengue>

### Dengue NS5 polymerase
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/dengue-ns5/
TL;DR: The viral enzyme that copies the dengue genome, and the main target for a dengue antiviral.
Summary: NS5 is the largest dengue protein and contains the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that replicates the viral genome, plus a methyltransferase that helps the virus disguise its RNA from the immune system. Its active site is distinct from human polymerases, and both nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors have shown activity in laboratory and animal studies. No dengue antiviral is approved, but NS5 is the most advanced target.
Sources: WHO — dengue <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Dihydropteroate synthase (FolP1)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/dihydropteroate-synthase/
TL;DR: A bacterial folate-synthesis enzyme, targeted by dapsone and the reason dapsone monotherapy bred resistance.
Summary: Dihydropteroate synthase builds folate in bacteria, a pathway humans do not use, so inhibiting it is selective — which is why sulfone and sulfonamide drugs have been useful for decades. Dapsone blocks it in Mycobacterium leprae, but used alone for years it selected for resistant bacteria, and that experience is why leprosy is now always treated with a combination. Resistance mutations in folP1 remain a monitored concern.
Sources: WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### DprE1 (decarprenylphosphoryl-β-D-ribose 2′-epimerase)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/dpre1/
TL;DR: An enzyme mycobacteria use to build their waxy cell wall; one of the most promising new drug targets from tuberculosis research.
Summary: DprE1 builds arabinogalactan, a key component of the mycobacterial cell wall that makes these bacteria tough and drug-resistant. Inhibitors of DprE1 — developed largely in tuberculosis drug discovery — kill mycobacteria including M. leprae, and because the target is absent from human cells they can be selective and well tolerated. The work shows how investment in one mycobacterial disease can benefit another, since leprosy and Buruli ulcer share the same genus.
Sources: Literature search: DprE1 as a tuberculosis and leprosy target <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=DprE1+inhibitor+tuberculosis+leprosy>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Ebola virus glycoprotein
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/ebola-glycoprotein/
TL;DR: The protein on the virus surface that lets it enter cells, and the target of both licensed vaccines and antibody treatments.
Summary: The Ebola glycoprotein mediates attachment and entry into host cells and is the only protein exposed on the viral surface, which makes it the sole practical target for antibodies and vaccines. In practice, the field has not needed a small-molecule drug: antibodies against this protein reduced mortality in human trials, and vaccines that present it generate protective immunity. It is one of the clearest cases in this corpus of a target addressed entirely by biologics rather than chemical drugs.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### EmbB (arabinosyl transferase)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/embb/
TL;DR: The enzyme ethambutol inhibits to stop the mycobacterium assembling its cell wall.
Summary: EmbB is an arabinosyl transferase that builds arabinogalactan, a structural polymer in the mycobacterial cell wall. Ethambutol inhibits it, weakening the wall and helping the other drugs in the regimen. Mutations in embB are associated with ethambutol resistance — which in practice often travels with resistance to other drugs, because the same wall structure is the target of several of them.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Ergosterol (fungal and leishmanial membranes)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/ergosterol/
TL;DR: The sterol fungi and Leishmania use to build their membranes, and the molecule amphotericin B binds to punch holes in them.
Summary: Ergosterol is the fungal and protozoal equivalent of cholesterol, and it is absent from human cell membranes — which is what makes it such a good target. Amphotericin B binds ergosterol and forms pores that kill the cell. Packaged in liposomes, it concentrates where Leishmania lives and can cure visceral leishmaniasis in a single dose in South Asia.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>; WHO — mycetoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>

### Fungal dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/fungal-dhodh/
TL;DR: An enzyme in pyrimidine synthesis that olorofim blocks — and whose parasite equivalent is a separate antimalarial target.
Summary: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is required for pyrimidine synthesis, and the fungal and parasite enzymes differ enough from the human one to allow selective inhibition. Olorofim, an orotomide antifungal in development for resistant mould infections, blocks the fungal enzyme and has shown good activity against Madurella mycetomatis in the laboratory. The same enzyme in Plasmodium is a target for a separate class of antimalarial candidates.
Sources: WHO — mycetoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>

### Glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluCl)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/glucl/
TL;DR: A channel in worm nerve cells that ivermectin opens, paralysing and killing the parasite.
Summary: GluCl is an invertebrate ion channel absent from vertebrates, which is why ivermectin can kill worms and lice while being remarkably safe for humans. Opening the channel lets chloride flood the nerve cell, silencing it, so the worm is paralysed and cannot feed. Ivermectin's discovery won the 2015 Nobel Prize and it remains the backbone of onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis control.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis and ivermectin <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Haem detoxification in the parasite digestive vacuole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/haem-detoxification/
TL;DR: The process by which the malaria parasite neutralises the toxic haem released when it digests haemoglobin — and the step the quinolines block.
Summary: Plasmodium digests host haemoglobin inside its digestive vacuole and releases free haem, which is toxic to the parasite. It detoxifies haem by crystallising it into inert haemozoin. Chloroquine and related quinolines concentrate in the vacuole and interfere with this process, leaving the parasite poisoned by its own meal — which is why chloroquine was so effective for so long, and why mutations in the transporter that lets it into the vacuole cause resistance.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Haem-mediated artemisinin activation
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/artemisinin-activation/
TL;DR: Artemisinins are activated by the iron in haem and then damage many parasite proteins at once — a mechanism resistance has found hard to defeat.
Summary: Artemisinins are prodrugs. Inside the parasite, iron from haem cleaves their endoperoxide bridge, generating reactive radicals that alkylate a wide range of parasite proteins. Because the drug has no single protein target, the parasite cannot escape it with a single point mutation, which is why resistance has emerged as slower clearance rather than outright failure — and why artemisinins remain the backbone of malaria treatment.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>

### InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase, M. tuberculosis)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/inha/
TL;DR: The enzyme isoniazid blocks after being activated, stopping the mycobacterium from building its fatty-acid wall.
Summary: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG; the activated form then inhibits InhA, an enoyl-ACP reductase needed for mycolic acid synthesis. Because the bacterium's waxy cell wall depends on this pathway, blocking it is lethal. Resistance typically arises through mutations that disable KatG — so the bacterium escapes by refusing to activate the drug rather than by altering the target.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Insect acetylcholinesterase
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/insect-acetylcholinesterase/
TL;DR: The enzyme that shuts off nerve signals in insects, and the target of several classes of insecticide used against vectors.
Summary: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to end a nerve signal. Insecticides in the organophosphate and carbamate classes inhibit it, so the signal never stops and the insect dies. It is one of the oldest insecticide targets and central to vector control, but resistance mutations in the enzyme and increased metabolic detoxification have made many populations insensitive — a reason vector control is diversifying toward new chemistries and non-chemical methods.
Sources: WHO — vector control and insecticide resistance <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Insect voltage-gated sodium channel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/insect-sodium-channel/
TL;DR: The nerve channel that pyrethroids hold open — the target of the insecticide class used on almost every bed net in the world.
Summary: Pyrethroids such as permethrin and deltamethrin keep the insect voltage-gated sodium channel open, so nerve signals fire repeatedly and the insect dies. Because the same class is used on bed nets, in indoor spraying and in agriculture, resistance mutations in this channel — known as knockdown resistance, or kdr — are now widespread and are one of the most serious threats to vector control. Note that acetylcholinesterase, a different nerve target, is what organophosphate and carbamate insecticides act on.
Sources: WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Kelch13 (artemisinin resistance marker)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/pfkelch13/
TL;DR: Not a drug target but a resistance marker: mutations here are how the world detects artemisinin partial resistance.
Summary: Kelch13 mutations do not cause resistance by themselves but mark the parasite populations in which artemisinin partial resistance emerges. That makes the gene the basis of molecular surveillance: programmes sequence or genotype it to detect resistance as it appears, because resistance shows up as slower parasite clearance before it shows up as treatment failure. It is an unusually clear example of a genetic marker functioning as an early-warning system rather than as a drug target.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — Global Malaria Programme <https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme>

### Kinetoplastid proteasome
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/parasite-proteasome/
TL;DR: The parasite's protein-recycling machine, which the leishmaniasis candidate LXE408 blocks.
Summary: The proteasome degrades proteins that the cell no longer needs, and blocking it kills Leishmania. LXE408 is a first-in-class oral compound developed by DNDi with Novartis that acts on the kinetoplastid proteasome and completed two Phase II proof-of-concept studies in 2025. Because the mechanism is new to the disease, it would also serve if resistance to current drugs emerges — and because proteasome inhibitors already exist for cancer, the class is chemically well understood.
Sources: DNDi — LXE408 for visceral leishmaniasis <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/lxe408-novartis-visceral-leishmaniasis/>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Leishmania ribosome
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/parasite-ribosome/
TL;DR: The parasite's protein factory, which the aminoglycoside paromomycin disrupts.
Summary: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that binds the Leishmania ribosome and also disrupts the parasite's mitochondrial membrane potential, killing it through two mechanisms at once. The selectivity over the human ribosome is narrower than for bacterial ribosomes, which is one reason aminoglycosides are not a larger part of antiparasitic therapy.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>; DNDi — leishmaniasis <https://dndi.org/diseases/leishmaniasis/>

### Mycobacterial ATP synthase (AtpE)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/atp-synthase/
TL;DR: The enzyme bedaquiline blocks to cut off the energy supply of mycobacteria, including the leprosy bacillus.
Summary: ATP synthase is the enzyme mycobacteria use to generate their energy, and bedaquiline binds its c-subunit (AtpE) to shut it down. Because the target is essential and the drug has a very long half-life — around five and a half months — bedaquiline is attractive for leprosy, where treatment is long and adherence is the weak point. It was developed for drug-resistant tuberculosis and is now in a Phase 3 trial for multibacillary leprosy, an example of tuberculosis investment flowing into a neglected mycobacterial disease.
Sources: Leprosy research updates — new therapies <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12010777/>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### N-myristoyltransferase (NMT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/nmt/
TL;DR: An enzyme that attaches a fatty acid to proteins — essential in Leishmania and Trypanosoma, and genetically validated as a drug target.
Summary: N-myristoyltransferase catalyses the attachment of myristate to proteins, a modification that controls where proteins go in the cell. Genetic studies showed that the Leishmania and Trypanosoma enzymes are essential — the parasite dies without them — and the human enzyme is different enough for selective inhibitors. The oxaborole drug candidate DNDi-0690 has been associated with this line of work, making NMT one of the more promising non-azole targets.
Sources: DNDi — leishmaniasis <https://dndi.org/diseases/leishmaniasis/>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Nematode beta-tubulin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/beta-tubulin/
TL;DR: The protein that builds the worm's cellular skeleton and the target of the deworming drugs albendazole and mebendazole.
Summary: Benzimidazole dewormers bind nematode beta-tubulin and prevent it from assembling microtubules, which stops the worm from absorbing nutrients and dividing cells. The drugs work across many worms — Ascaris, Trichuris, hookworm — which is why they are the workhorses of school deworming. The catch is resistance: a single point mutation in beta-tubulin reduces binding, and benzimidazole resistance in livestock worms signals what could happen in human programmes.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths and deworming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/nematode-nachr/
TL;DR: A worm nerve receptor that tribendimidine activates to paralyse the worm, offering a mechanism different from the benzimidazoles.
Summary: Tribendimidine acts on nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing paralysis. Because it is not a benzimidazole, it offers a different mechanism from albendazole and mebendazole — which matters given how poorly those drugs work against Trichuris and how long the field has relied on a single class. It was developed and used in China, and trials have shown activity against Ascaris, hookworm and whipworm.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminth infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Ornithine decarboxylase (ODC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/ornithine-decarboxylase/
TL;DR: The enzyme eflornithine blocks to stop the sleeping-sickness parasite dividing.
Summary: Ornithine decarboxylase starts the synthesis of polyamines, which cells need to divide. Eflornithine inhibits it irreversibly, and the trypanosome is unusually dependent on the pathway, which is why the drug works against late-stage sleeping sickness. Its later use as a cosmetic cream for unwanted facial hair kept it in production — an accident of commerce that helped keep a medicine for a fatal disease available.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Penicillin-binding proteins (T. pallidum)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/penicillin-binding-protein/
TL;DR: The enzymes penicillin blocks to stop the yaws and syphilis bacterium building its cell wall.
Summary: Penicillin-binding proteins cross-link the bacterial cell wall, and beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin irreversibly inhibit them. Treponema pallidum has never developed penicillin resistance, which is why a single long-acting injection of benzathine penicillin still cures yaws and syphilis after more than seventy years. Its limitation is not resistance but delivery: the drug must be injected and kept cold.
Sources: WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### PfATP4 (Plasmodium sodium pump)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/pfatp4/
TL;DR: A parasite ion pump that a new class of fast-acting antimalarials blocks, and the most promising non-artemisinin target.
Summary: PfATP4 is a sodium-transporting ATPase that maintains the parasite's ion balance. Blocking it kills the parasite quickly, in a way that is distinct from artemisinins, which makes it valuable precisely because artemisinin resistance is emerging. The spiroindolone, imidazolopyrazine and dihydroisoquinolone classes all act here, and several candidates are in clinical development as potential single-dose cures — the first genuinely new antimalarial mechanism in decades.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — Global Malaria Programme <https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme>

### PncA (pyrazinamidase, prodrug activator)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/pnca/
TL;DR: The enzyme that converts pyrazinamide into its active form — loss of it causes resistance.
Summary: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug that depends on the mycobacterial enzyme PncA to release its active form, pyrazinoic acid. Like Ddn for pretomanid, PncA is a target that has to work rather than one that must be blocked, and mutations in pncA are the main route to pyrazinamide resistance — one of the reasons some multidrug-resistant strains are harder to treat.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/pfor/
TL;DR: An energy enzyme found in anaerobic parasites and bacteria but not in people, targeted by nitazoxanide.
Summary: PFOR catalyses a step in anaerobic energy metabolism that humans do not use, which makes it an attractive target. Nitazoxanide inhibits it, which is how it works against intestinal protozoa and helminths. Its poor efficacy against fascioliasis — the one place the field most needs an alternative — illustrates the difference between having a plausible target and having an effective drug.
Sources: WHO — foodborne trematode infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/foodborne-trematode-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### QcrB (cytochrome bc1 complex subunit)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/qcrb/
TL;DR: The enzyme subunit that telacebec blocks, cutting off the mycobacterium's energy supply — a target shared with tuberculosis.
Summary: QcrB is part of the cytochrome bc1 complex, which mycobacteria use to generate energy. The drug telacebec binds it and shuts down respiration, which is rapidly lethal to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and, at extremely low concentrations, to Mycobacterium ulcerans. Because the target is conserved across mycobacteria, the extensive work done on QcrB for tuberculosis can be mined for Buruli ulcer and leprosy — a rare case where investment in one disease delivers a validated target for two others with almost no market.
Sources: TB Alliance — telacebec for Buruli ulcer <https://www.tballiance.org/news-new-clinical-trial-examines-use-novel-compound-telacebec-buruli-ulcer-patients/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Rabies glycoprotein (G)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/rabies-glycoprotein/
TL;DR: The protein on the virus surface that lets it enter nerve cells and the antigen every rabies vaccine is built around.
Summary: The rabies glycoprotein mediates attachment and entry into host cells and is the only viral protein exposed on the surface, so it is the target of neutralising antibodies and the antigen in all licensed vaccines. Because the virus has only five proteins and a slow, nerve-bound journey, the glycoprotein is also the focus of efforts to design a single-dose vaccine or a monoclonal antibody that could replace scarce rabies immunoglobulin.
Sources: WHO — rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### Schistosome histone deacetylase 8 (SmHDAC8)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/schistosome-hdac8/
TL;DR: A schistosome enzyme that controls which genes are active; a structural quirk makes it selectively druggable.
Summary: Histone deacetylases remove acetyl groups from histones and thereby switch genes on and off. SmHDAC8 is a schistosome isoform whose active-site structure differs from the human enzymes in a way that allows selective inhibitors. Blocking it disrupts the worm's development and survival, and it is one of the more biochemically validated non-praziquantel targets for schistosomiasis.
Sources: Literature search: SmHDAC8 and selective inhibitors <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=SmHDAC8+schistosome+histone+deacetylase+inhibitor>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Schistosome sulfotransferase
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/schistosome-sulfotransferase/
TL;DR: The enzyme that activates oxamniquine inside the worm — which is why susceptibility varies between strains.
Summary: Oxamniquine is a prodrug that must be sulfated by a parasite sulfotransferase before it can damage schistosome DNA. Strains and species with low enzyme activity are naturally less susceptible, which is one reason the drug was limited to Schistosoma mansoni and eventually abandoned in favour of praziquantel. It is a clean illustration of how a resistance mechanism can be built into a parasite's biology rather than selected by drug pressure.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Schistosome TRP ion channel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/schistosome-trp-channel/
TL;DR: The ion channel praziquantel opens; identifying it finally explained how the main anti-schistosomal drug works.
Summary: For forty years after praziquantel became the only drug used against schistosomiasis, no one knew what it bound. Work using the free-living relative Dugesia and then schistosomes themselves traced its action to a transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channel: the drug opens it, calcium floods into the worm, and the worm contracts and dies. Naming the target opens the door to designing new drugs that hit the same channel — important, because praziquantel is a single point of failure for treating 250 million people.
Sources: Praziquantel's target identified (Nature Communications) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=praziquantel+TRP+channel+schistosome>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### SLO-1 potassium channel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/slo-1/
TL;DR: The worm channel that the new deworming drug emodepside opens, paralysing parasites including the filariae.
Summary: SLO-1 is a large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channel found in nematode nerve and muscle. Emodepside, long used in veterinary medicine, activates it and paralyses the worm. Because SLO-1 is a different channel from the one ivermectin hits, emodepside offers an alternative for worms and settings where ivermectin cannot be used — and it is in clinical trials for onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths.
Sources: DNDi — emodepside development <https://dndi.org/diseases/onchocerciasis/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Snake venom toxins
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/venom-toxins/
TL;DR: The mixture of enzymes and peptides in venom that antivenom must neutralise — several targets at once, not one.
Summary: Venom is a cocktail: phospholipases, metalloproteinases, serine proteases, neurotoxins and more, and the composition differs between species and even within a species by region. Antivenom is therefore not a targeted drug but a polyclonal mixture that must cover many toxins at once, which is why it must be manufactured against local snakes and why a single universal antivenom has proved so hard to design. Recombinant product development faces the same problem — it needs an antibody against every important toxin, not one.
Sources: WHO — snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/cyp51/
TL;DR: An enzyme parasites need to build their cell membranes; the same enzyme the antifungal drug class attacks.
Summary: CYP51 builds ergosterol, the parasite's equivalent of cholesterol. Because the parasite cannot simply take up host sterol in the way it needs, blocking CYP51 is lethal — and because CYP51 is a well-understood antifungal target with a large library of existing inhibitors, it is one of the cheapest starting points for new antiparasitic drugs. Azole antifungals such as posaconazole and ravuconazole have been repurposed into Chagas and leishmaniasis trials.
Sources: Literature search: Trypanosoma cruzi CYP51 and inhibitors <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Trypanosoma+cruzi+CYP51+inhibitor>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Thioredoxin glutathione reductase (TGR)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/schistosome-tgr/
TL;DR: The schistosome enzyme that keeps the worm's internal environment chemically balanced; a candidate target for new drugs.
Summary: Schistosomes manage oxidative stress through a single enzyme, thioredoxin glutathione reductase, that performs several jobs other organisms split between separate enzymes. Inactivating it cripples the worm's defence against the oxidative burst host immune cells use, which is why it has been explored both as a target for small molecules and as a vaccine antigen.
Sources: Literature search: schistosome thioredoxin glutathione reductase <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=schistosome+thioredoxin+glutathione+reductase>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Trypanothione reductase
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/trypanothione-reductase/
TL;DR: The parasite's dedicated antioxidant enzyme — a system humans do not have, so a drug against it should spare the patient.
Summary: Trypanothione is a small molecule unique to trypanosomatids and leishmaniae that mops up oxidative damage. Trypanothione reductase regenerates it, and the parasite cannot survive without this antioxidant defence. Because humans use a different system (glutathione), the enzyme is an attractive target for selective drugs — though after decades of effort no inhibitor has yet proved itself in patients.
Sources: Literature search: trypanothione reductase as a drug target <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=trypanothione+reductase+drug+target>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Type I nitroreductase (trypanosome prodrug activator)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/trypanosome-nitroreductase/
TL;DR: The enzyme that activates benznidazole, nifurtimox and fexinidazole — the reason these nitro drugs kill trypanosomes but not human cells.
Summary: Benznidazole, nifurtimox and fexinidazole are all nitroheterocyclic prodrugs, and all three depend on a parasite type I nitroreductase to convert them into reactive intermediates that damage DNA and proteins. The enzyme is absent from human cells, which is what gives the drugs their selectivity — and its loss is a route to resistance. It is why three chemically different drugs share a mechanism and, to some degree, a fate.
Sources: DNDi — Chagas disease <https://dndi.org/diseases/chagas/>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Wolbachia endosymbiont
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/targets/wolbachia/
TL;DR: A bacterium living inside filarial worms that the worm cannot survive without — so an antibiotic becomes an antiparasitic drug.
Summary: Wolbachia is an intracellular bacterium found in most filarial worms, including those causing lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis. The worm depends on it for energy metabolism and reproduction, so a course of doxycycline eradicates the bacteria, sterilises adult worms and eventually kills them. This makes an ordinary antibiotic a slow-acting but durable antifilarial treatment, and it is the reason Wolbachia is both a drug target and a driver of the inflammatory reactions that cause some filarial disease.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis and doxycycline <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>


## Technologies

### AI microscopy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ai-microscopy/
TL;DR: Software that reads microscope images and slides, counting parasites or grading disease more consistently than a fatigued human eye.
Summary: AI microscopy analyses images from a conventional microscope or a phone camera to detect and count parasites — schistosome eggs, filarial worms, trypanosomes, mycetoma grains. It addresses two real problems: the shortage of trained microscopists, and the variability between them. Field-ready systems combine a low-cost microscope or phone attachment with an on-device model, and several have reached field trials.
Sources: WHO — diagnostic innovation for NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### AI vector identification
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ai-vector-identification/
TL;DR: Phone apps and image models that identify a mosquito or fly species from a photograph, so surveillance does not depend on a specialist.
Summary: Identifying vectors morphologically requires expert entomological training, which most endemic districts lack. Image-classification models running on a smartphone can name a species from a photograph of a trapped insect, and acoustic and wingbeat-based approaches are being tested too. The payoff is wider, cheaper surveillance: more places can report which vectors are present, and rising insecticide resistance can be tracked sooner.
Sources: WHO — vector surveillance <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### AI-driven drug discovery
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ai-drug-discovery/
TL;DR: Using machine learning to pick drug targets, design molecules and predict which compounds will work before anything is made in a lab.
Summary: AI is changing antiparasitic drug discovery in three ways: predicting protein structures and pockets where no experimental structure exists; generating and ranking candidate molecules; and triaging huge screening libraries to find the few compounds worth testing. For NTDs, where there is no profit to fund brute-force screening, this matters disproportionately — a small team can now explore a target that would previously have needed an industrial programme.
Sources: DNDi — discovery and AI <https://dndi.org/portfolio/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### BCG vaccine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/bcg-vaccine/
TL;DR: The only licensed tuberculosis vaccine, given to infants worldwide, and only partly effective.
Summary: BCG is a live attenuated mycobacterium given to around 100 million infants a year. It protects reliably against disseminated tuberculosis and meningitis in young children, which is why newborn vaccination is universal in high-burden countries, but its protection against pulmonary disease in adults is variable and wanes. It also confounds the tuberculin skin test used to diagnose infection. A century after it was introduced, replacing it is one of the field's biggest unmet needs.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Buruli ulcer early-warning hotspots
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/early-warning-hotspots/
TL;DR: An environmental and animal surveillance approach that flags emerging Buruli ulcer hotspots two to six years before human cases appear.
Summary: Buruli ulcer moves: incidence rises in some places and falls in others, and it appears in areas that were previously free of it. A tool developed by the Doherty Institute in Australia uses environmental sampling — including mosquito and possum surveillance where they are implicated in transmission — to identify emerging hotspots two to six years before human infections occur. The value is that prevention can be targeted before people are affected, rather than surveillance merely confirming an outbreak that has already happened. It is one of the few genuinely predictive tools in the NTD field, and it complements the search for a point-of-care diagnostic.
Sources: Doherty Institute — early warning for Buruli ulcer hotspots <https://www.doherty.edu.au/articles/early-warning-tool-detect-buruli-ulcer-hotspots-before-human-cases-occur/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Case containment
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/case-containment/
TL;DR: Finding every guinea worm case before the worm can release larvae into water — the intervention that makes eradication possible without a drug.
Summary: Guinea worm has no drug and no vaccine, so eradication depends on breaking the chain one case at a time. Containment means detecting a case as soon as the worm begins to emerge, preventing the person from entering any water source, dressing the wound, and treating the drinking water. It sounds simple and is operationally demanding: it requires surveillance in every village, community members motivated to report cases (often through a cash reward), and a rapid response when a case is found. Containment is why the campaign can succeed with ten reported cases a year, and why a single missed case can seed a village's infections the following year.
Sources: Carter Center — Guinea worm eradication <https://www.cartercenter.org/programs/guinea-worm/>

### Community health workers and community-directed treatment
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/community-health-workers/
TL;DR: Trained local people who distribute medicines and find cases, reaching villages that clinics never see.
Summary: Community-directed treatment, pioneered for onchocerciasis in Africa, has local people decide how and when medicines are distributed in their own villages. It is what makes mass administration possible in places with few health facilities, and it extends to case-finding, referral and surveillance. Its strength is reach and trust; its constraints are training, supervision, workload and the fact that volunteers doing complex work need support and recognition.
Sources: WHO — community-directed treatment <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### CRISPR-based diagnostics
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/crispr-diagnostics/
TL;DR: Tests that use gene-editing proteins to detect a pathogen's DNA with a colour change, combining molecular sensitivity with simple field use.
Summary: CRISPR diagnostic platforms pair an isothermal amplification step with a Cas enzyme that, on recognising the target sequence, cuts a reporter molecule and produces a visible signal. The result is near-molecular sensitivity without a laboratory, at a low cost per test. For NTDs the appeal is detecting light infections at the point of care; the barriers are validation, regulation and scaling manufacture.
Sources: FIND — CRISPR diagnostics <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Dengue vaccination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/dengue-vaccination/
TL;DR: Vaccines against the four dengue serotypes — powerful, but complicated by the fact that a second infection is more dangerous.
Summary: Dengue vaccination is unusually difficult because there are four serotypes and a second infection with a different one raises the risk of severe disease. A first vaccine required pre-screening for prior infection; a later vaccine (TAK-003) protects without screening, and a single-dose Brazilian vaccine (Butantan-DV) has reported strong efficacy. Chikungunya, spread by the same mosquito, now has a licensed vaccine too. Vaccination complements, but cannot replace, mosquito control.
Sources: WHO — dengue vaccines <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Drug repurposing for NTDs
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/drug-repurposing/
TL;DR: Testing medicines already approved for something else against a neglected disease, to skip years of safety testing.
Summary: Repurposing starts from a drug with a known safety profile and asks whether it also works against an NTD. Examples include doxycycline against the Wolbachia in filarial worms, azoles against trypanosomes and Leishmania, and azithromycin against yaws and trachoma. Because safety work is largely done, the path to patients can be much shorter — but a repurposed drug may still fail on efficacy, formulation or dosing for the new disease.
Sources: DNDi — repurposing <https://dndi.org/portfolio/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Ebola vaccines (ERVEBO and others)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ebola-vaccines/
TL;DR: Vaccines that protect against Zaire ebolavirus and turned outbreak response from containment into prevention.
Summary: ERVEBO, a single-dose vaccine based on a vesicular stomatitis virus vector carrying the Ebola glycoprotein, was shown in 2015 to protect contacts of cases and was licensed in 2019. During the 2018–2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo it was given to more than 300,000 people, in a response complicated by conflict and distrust. A two-dose regimen has since been licensed, and further candidates are in development for other ebolavirus species. An outbreak response today includes vaccination as a matter of course, which was not true a decade ago.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### EG95 sheep vaccine for echinococcosis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/eg95-sheep-vaccine/
TL;DR: A vaccine that protects sheep against the tapeworm cysts that infect dogs, breaking the transmission cycle at its source.
Summary: EG95 is a recombinant vaccine against Echinococcus granulosus in sheep, with 96–100% protection in trials. Its importance is that it interrupts transmission on the animal side of the cycle: if lambs do not develop cysts, dogs that eat sheep organs do not become infected, and the eggs that cause human disease are never shed. The vaccine is registered and commercially produced in China and Argentina and used extensively in China, and WHO's assessment is that combining lamb vaccination with deworming dogs at least four times a year and culling older sheep could eliminate human cystic echinococcosis in under ten years. It is the clearest case in the NTD field of a purely veterinary intervention solving a human disease.
Sources: WHO — echinococcosis prevention and control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/echinococcosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Foot hygiene, bandaging and footwear for podoconiosis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/foot-hygiene-and-bandaging/
TL;DR: The entire treatment for podoconiosis: washing, emollients, bandaging and, above all, shoes.
Summary: There is no drug for podoconiosis, and treatment is entirely physical: daily washing with soap and water, soaking, emollients, elevation, compression bandaging and treatment of secondary infection. Community-based care programmes in Ethiopia have shown this manages the swelling, reduces painful attacks and restores mobility, and that trained community members can deliver it. Prevention is simpler still — shoes. It is the clearest example in this corpus of a disease whose solution is a pair of shoes and a bucket of water, and whose persistence is therefore a question of poverty rather than of medicine.
Sources: Literature search: podoconiosis <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=podoconiosis>

### Gene-drive mosquitoes
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/gene-drive-mosquitoes/
TL;DR: Genetically modified mosquitoes engineered to spread a trait through a wild population that stops them transmitting disease.
Summary: A gene drive uses CRISPR gene editing to copy itself into the majority of offspring, so a trait — such as infertility or resistance to the parasite — spreads through a wild mosquito population far faster than normal inheritance allows. It is the most powerful and the most contested new vector-control idea: it could suppress a species durably without chemicals, but it is self-propagating, essentially irreversible once released, and raises governance questions that have kept field releases to contained trials so far.
Sources: WHO — guidance framework for gene drive <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241511988>; WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Genomic surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/genomic-surveillance/
TL;DR: Sequencing pathogen DNA to track strains, spot drug resistance and follow how a parasite moves between places.
Summary: Whole-genome sequencing of parasites and vectors reveals drug-resistance mutations, whether an infection is locally transmitted or imported, and how strains spread. For NTD elimination the last question is critical: proving that a residual case was imported rather than locally acquired is what allows a country to claim elimination. Genomic capacity is growing in endemic countries, but it is unevenly distributed and sample logistics remain hard.
Sources: WHO — genomic surveillance for NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Hookworm vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/hookworm-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Experimental vaccines that aim to stop hookworm by blocking the parasite's feeding and development, not just killing adults already in the gut.
Summary: Repeated deworming treats hookworm but does not prevent reinfection, so a vaccine that reduces the intensity of infection would add something drugs cannot. Candidates target enzymes the worm needs to feed and digest blood, and have been taken through early clinical trials. The challenge is that hookworm has evolved to modulate the human immune response, so inducing durable protection is hard.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Indoor residual spraying
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/indoor-residual-spraying/
TL;DR: Spraying the inside walls of houses with long-lasting insecticide so that resting vectors pick up a lethal dose.
Summary: Indoor residual spraying targets mosquitoes and bugs that rest on interior walls after feeding, such as the Anopheles and Culex mosquitoes and triatomine bugs. It can suppress transmission in a whole community from a small amount of insecticide. Its weaknesses are cost and logistics, community acceptance, and resistance — and for Chagas disease it must be combined with housing improvement, because the bugs live in the wall cracks themselves.
Sources: WHO — vector control <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Insecticide-treated nets
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/insecticide-treated-nets/
TL;DR: Bed nets treated with insecticide that kill or repel night-biting mosquitoes and vectors.
Summary: Insecticide-treated nets protect the sleeper and, at high community coverage, kill enough mosquitoes to reduce transmission for everyone. They are the single most effective vector-control tool for night-biting mosquitoes, which makes them central to lymphatic filariasis control, and they have some effect on sandflies. They do not work against day-biting Aedes aegypti, the dengue vector, which is a fundamental limitation.
Sources: WHO — vector control <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Ivermectin mass drug administration for scabies
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/scabies-mda/
TL;DR: Treating a whole community at once with oral ivermectin, which is the only approach that stops scabies coming straight back.
Summary: Scabies recurs relentlessly if only the patient is treated, because the mite is reintroduced by everyone around them. Mass drug administration — treating an entire community with oral ivermectin, with topical permethrin for those who cannot take it — reduces both scabies and impetigo prevalence, and has been delivered at scale in Pacific island countries and Ethiopia. A cluster-randomised trial suggested that a single round may be as effective as two, which matters for cost and logistics, and WHO's 2024 consultation on combining NTD mass-treatment regimens raised the prospect of giving scabies treatment alongside lymphatic filariasis or trachoma campaigns using the same delivery machinery.
Sources: WHO — scabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies>; WHO — scabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/scabies>

### Lateral-flow assays
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/lateral-flow-assays/
TL;DR: The paper-strip format behind rapid tests — a drop of sample flows along a membrane and a coloured line gives the answer.
Summary: Lateral-flow assays are the technology behind most point-of-care NTD tests: rK39 for visceral leishmaniasis, POC-CCA for schistosomiasis, and antibody strips for filariasis and exposure mapping. They are cheap, need no equipment and are easy to use. Their limits are well known — antibody strips stay positive after cure, heat degrades some reagents, and sensitivity for light infection is often inadequate for elimination programmes.
Sources: FIND — rapid diagnostic tests <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Leishmaniasis vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/leishmaniasis-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Vaccines for leishmaniasis, motivated by the fact that people who recover from the skin form are protected for life.
Summary: Recovery from cutaneous leishmaniasis confers lasting immunity, which is the strongest evidence that a vaccine is possible. Candidates include defined recombinant antigens, live attenuated parasites and viral-vectored vaccines. Progress has been slow because leishmaniasis is a family of diseases, immunity is species-specific, and there is no commercial market to fund late-stage trials.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis vaccine development <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/malaria-vaccines/
TL;DR: Two recommended vaccines against falciparum malaria, ending decades in which a malaria vaccine was assumed impossible.
Summary: For decades a malaria vaccine was considered impractical because the parasite has thousands of antigens and a complex life cycle, and the first candidate took thirty years to develop. WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 in 2021 for children in moderate-to-high transmission settings, and R21/Matrix-M in 2023. Both target the circumsporozoite protein and reduce clinical malaria by roughly a third to a half, which is not enough to eliminate malaria but is enough to save tens of thousands of lives a year — and R21 can be produced at much greater scale and lower cost.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Mass drug administration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/mass-drug-administration/
TL;DR: Treating an entire community on a schedule with safe donated medicines, whether or not each person is tested, to break transmission.
Summary: Mass drug administration is the delivery model behind preventive chemotherapy for five NTDs. Rather than test everyone, programmes treat the whole eligible population in a district once or twice a year with medicines that are safe enough to give without diagnosis. Repeated rounds reduce the reservoir of infection until transmission can no longer sustain itself. What determines success is coverage — WHO's target is at least 65% of the eligible population — and whether the same people are reached year after year.
