Sources: WHO — preventive chemotherapy <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Mobile health and digital surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/mhealth-surveillance/
TL;DR: Using phones and simple digital tools to report cases, track campaigns and map where disease is still occurring.
Summary: Mobile reporting lets community workers and clinics submit case data, campaign coverage and geolocated outbreak signals without a computer or a paper trail. For NTDs it supports case-based surveillance for guinea worm, coverage monitoring for mass administration, and rapid reporting of dengue or cholera-like clusters. Its value is timeliness and granularity; its risks are data quality, fragmentation across systems, and the digital divide in the poorest districts.
Sources: WHO — NTD surveillance <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Onchocerciasis vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/onchocerciasis-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Experimental vaccines for river blindness, explored because drug treatment is lifelong and cannot kill adult worms.
Summary: Mass ivermectin controls river blindness but does not cure it: adult worms live for years and treatment must continue until they die naturally. A vaccine would change that equation, and candidates have been tested in animal models with some reduction in worm burden. The field is early, and the regulatory and trial infrastructure for a vaccine in a disease already 'under control' is a significant obstacle.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### One Health NTD integration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/one-health-ntd-integration/
TL;DR: Running human and animal health programmes together, because several NTDs live in animals and cannot be stopped by treating people alone.
Summary: For zoonotic NTDs — rabies, echinococcosis, taeniasis/cysticercosis, foodborne trematodiases — human treatment cannot eliminate the infection while the animal or environmental reservoir remains. One Health integration means vaccinating dogs to stop rabies, deworming dogs and controlling slaughter to stop hydatid disease, and managing livestock and aquaculture to stop foodborne trematodes. The obstacle is institutional: ministries of health and agriculture rarely plan together, and funding is siloed.
Sources: WHO — One Health <https://www.who.int/health-topics/one-health>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Open-science drug discovery
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/open-science-drug-discovery/
TL;DR: Developing medicines for diseases with no market by publishing everything and collaborating across institutions, as DNDi does.
Summary: Because an NTD medicine cannot earn a commercial return, the product development partnership model develops it on public and philanthropic funding and then ensures affordable access. DNDi's portfolio — fexinidazole and acoziborole for sleeping sickness, benznidazole access for Chagas, DNDi-0690 and emodepside — shows the model can deliver approved drugs. Open science, virtual screening consortia and data sharing further reduce the cost of each candidate.
Sources: DNDi — portfolio <https://dndi.org/portfolio/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/pair/
TL;DR: A minimally invasive technique that collapses a hydatid cyst through a needle instead of open surgery.
Summary: PAIR is a procedure for treating echinococcal liver cysts without open surgery: the cyst is punctured under ultrasound guidance, its fluid aspirated, a scolicidal solution injected to kill the contents, and the fluid reaspirated. It is used alongside albendazole, which is given before and after to reduce the risk of the procedure spreading infection, and it shortens hospital stays and recovery compared with surgery. It is not suitable for every cyst — the WHO classification determines whether a cyst is better observed, drained this way, or operated on — which is why standardised imaging and staging matter so much.
Sources: WHO — echinococcosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/echinococcosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Protein structure prediction (AlphaFold)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/alphafold-structure-prediction/
TL;DR: Software that predicts the 3D shape of a protein from its sequence, giving drug hunters a structure for targets that were never crystallised.
Summary: Determining a protein's structure experimentally can take years. Deep-learning prediction, led by AlphaFold and open databases such as the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, produces a usable model from sequence alone. For NTD drug discovery this is transformative: many parasite proteins have no experimental structure, and a predicted model is enough to start virtual screening and to understand where a drug could bind.
Sources: AlphaFold Protein Structure Database <https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Rabies vaccination and dog vaccination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/rabies-vaccination/
TL;DR: Vaccinating dogs breaks human rabies at its source, and vaccinating people after a bite prevents the disease entirely.
Summary: Human rabies can be eliminated by vaccinating the dogs that cause almost all cases — a strategy proven in the Americas and pursued in Africa and Asia — combined with prompt post-exposure prophylaxis for anyone bitten. Progress is limited by the cost and access of human vaccine and immunoglobulin, and by the logistics of reaching enough dogs to maintain herd immunity.
Sources: WHO — rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### Recombinant and next-generation antivenoms
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/recombinant-antivenoms/
TL;DR: Antivenoms made from engineered antibodies instead of horse serum, aiming to end the shortages and reactions of today's products.
Summary: Conventional antivenoms are made by immunising horses, which yields variable products, requires a cold chain, and carries a risk of allergic reactions. Recombinant antivenoms built from human monoclonal antibodies could be produced consistently, at scale, without animals. The scientific challenge is that venom is a cocktail of many toxins, so a product must combine antibodies against several of them — a hard engineering problem now being pursued with support from WHO's snakebite programme.
Sources: WHO — snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO — snakebite envenoming strategy <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515993>

### Ring vaccination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ring-vaccination/
TL;DR: Vaccinating the contacts of every case and their contacts — a strategy borrowed from smallpox that ends Ebola outbreaks.
Summary: Ring vaccination means finding every new case, identifying everyone they had contact with, and vaccinating those contacts and their contacts. It creates a protective ring that stops the virus reaching anyone beyond it, and it works even without vaccinating a whole population. The strategy was inherited from smallpox eradication and proved itself against Ebola in the 2015 Guinea trial and then in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It depends entirely on contact tracing, which is why surveillance and community trust are the determinants of whether it succeeds.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Seasonal malaria chemoprevention
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/seasonal-malaria-chemoprevention/
TL;DR: Giving antimalarials to children during the rainy season, when transmission peaks, whether or not they are infected.
Summary: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention delivers monthly antimalarial treatment to children under five during the transmission season in the Sahel and sub-Saharan belt, where malaria is intensely seasonal. It does not treat existing infection as a diagnosis would; it keeps children protected through the months when they are most at risk, in the same way that preventive chemotherapy works for NTDs. It prevents a large share of cases and deaths, and it is one of the clearest examples of the NTD and malaria worlds using the same delivery logic — which is why integrating the two campaigns is now being explored.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Snail control
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/snail-control/
TL;DR: Reducing the freshwater snails that schistosomes need to complete their life cycle, using molluscicides or habitat management.
Summary: Because each schistosome species needs a specific snail host, removing the snail breaks the cycle before the parasite can infect anyone. Methods include the molluscicide niclosamide, clearing vegetation and modifying irrigation and water infrastructure, and biological approaches. Snail control was central to early schistosomiasis programmes, fell out of favour when praziquantel arrived, and is now being reconsidered for elimination, where stopping transmission needs more than treating people.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Sterile insect technique
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/sterile-insect-technique/
TL;DR: Releasing large numbers of sterilised male insects so that wild females mate with them and produce no offspring.
Summary: The sterile insect technique irradiates mass-reared male insects so they are sterile but still compete for mates; repeated releases collapse the wild population. It is species-specific, leaves no chemical residue and has been used for decades against agricultural pests and against the tsetse fly. For mosquitoes the practical barriers are the need to rear and sex-sort millions of insects and the fact that releases must be sustained.
Sources: WHO — sterile insect technique <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### The SAFE strategy for trachoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/safe-strategy/
TL;DR: Surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness and environmental improvement — a four-part strategy matched to each stage of trachoma.
Summary: SAFE is the intervention model that has taken trachoma to the edge of elimination. Surgery treats trichiasis in people whose eyelids have already turned inward; antibiotics — mass azithromycin — reduce the community pool of infection; facial cleanliness reduces transmission between children; and environmental improvement, meaning water supply and latrines, attacks the conditions that allow the infection to spread, including the flies that feed on eye and nose discharge. It is the clearest example in the NTD field of pairing a medical intervention with a development one, and the reason WHO now recommends combining preventive chemotherapy with water and sanitation rather than running them as separate programmes.
Sources: WHO — trachoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Tiny targets for tsetse control
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tiny-targets/
TL;DR: Low-cost insecticide-treated cloth targets that kill tsetse flies and cost a fraction of traps, letting programmes cover far more ground.
Summary: Tiny targets are small, insecticide-treated cloth panels that attract and kill tsetse flies. Their significance is cost and coverage: because they are cheap and simple, programmes can deploy them densely across the riverine and lakeside habitats where tsetse concentrate, suppressing a local fly population enough to interrupt transmission of human African trypanosomiasis without treating everyone at risk. They are typically deployed alongside case-finding, and they make vector control feasible in the remote, sparsely served areas where sleeping sickness persists.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Total community treatment (TCT) for yaws
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/total-community-treatment/
TL;DR: Treating every person in an endemic community with one dose of azithromycin, repeated until yaws transmission stops.
Summary: The Morges strategy for yaws eradication runs on total community treatment: mass administration of a single oral dose of azithromycin to everyone in an affected community, followed by total targeted treatment — cases and their contacts only — as prevalence falls. TCT is feasible because azithromycin is a one-dose cure that needs no injection and can be given by a community health worker, which is what distinguishes it from the injectable penicillin campaigns that nearly eradicated yaws in the 1950s. Its vulnerability is the same as its strength: the entire strategy depends on one antibiotic, and azithromycin-resistant yaws has already emerged in Papua New Guinea.
Sources: WHO — supporting countries to implement the yaws eradication strategy <https://www.who.int/activities/supporting-endemic-countries-to-implement-yaws-eradication-strategy>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Triple-drug therapy (IDA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/triple-drug-therapy-ida/
TL;DR: Ivermectin, DEC and albendazole given together in one dose, which clears filarial worms faster than two-drug regimens and can shorten elimination programmes.
Summary: IDA is a single co-administered dose of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole for lymphatic filariasis. Compared with the earlier two-drug regimens it removes microfilariae from the blood far more completely after the first round, and modelling and field experience suggest it can cut the number of annual treatment rounds a country needs to reach the elimination threshold. WHO recommended it in 2017, and programmes including Kenya's have used it to accelerate. Its limitation is geographic: DEC is unsafe in people who also carry onchocerciasis or Loa loa, so IDA cannot be used where those infections co-circulate — which excludes much of West and Central Africa.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis treatment <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Tsetse traps and targets
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tsetse-traps/
TL;DR: Cloth traps and insecticide-treated targets that attract and kill tsetse flies, cutting sleeping-sickness transmission.
Summary: Tsetse flies are attracted to certain colours and shapes that mimic a host; traps and insecticide-treated targets exploit this to kill them with minimal insecticide. Because tsetse reproduce slowly and live in defined habitats, targeted trapping can suppress a local population enough to interrupt transmission even without treating people. It was one of the tools that pushed Gambiense sleeping sickness to its lowest recorded levels.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### TSOL18 pig vaccine (Cysvax)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tsol18-vaccine/
TL;DR: A vaccine that stops pigs developing tapeworm cysts, breaking the cycle that gives people neurocysticercosis.
Summary: TSOL18 is a recombinant vaccine against Taenia solium in pigs. Because pigs are the intermediate host, preventing cysts in pigs removes the step that lets people acquire the adult tapeworm — and therefore removes the tapeworm carriers who contaminate the environment with the eggs that cause brain cysts. It is produced commercially as Cysvax by Indian Immunologicals and is named by WHO among the specific animal-side control measures for the disease. The vaccine prevents new cysts but does not clear existing ones, so it is used with oxfendazole, which kills established cysts; a trial in Uganda found that three-monthly vaccination combined with oxfendazole eliminated transmission by pigs.
Sources: WHO — Taenia solium prevention through animals, One Health approach <https://www.who.int/activities/promoting-prevention-and-control-of-taenia-solium-infection-through-animals-with-the-one-health-approach/promoting-prevention-and-control-of-taenia-solium-infection-through-animals-with-the-one-health-approach>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Tuberculosis preventive treatment
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tb-preventive-treatment/
TL;DR: Treating people with latent tuberculosis infection before they become ill — the closest thing to a strategy for eliminating the disease.
Summary: A quarter of the world is estimated to carry latent tuberculosis, and roughly a tenth of those will develop active disease. Preventive treatment gives one or two drugs for one to six months to people at highest risk — household contacts, young children, and people with HIV — to stop that happening. WHO recommends a cascade of testing and treatment, and shorter rifamycin-based regimens have made it far more practical than the old nine-month isoniazid course. It is the intervention that most resembles an NTD elimination strategy: treating people who are not ill to stop transmission and disease later.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Vector surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/vector-surveillance/
TL;DR: Systematically catching, counting and testing vectors to know where and when the risk is highest.
Summary: Vector surveillance includes trapping adult mosquitoes and flies, sampling larvae, mapping breeding sites, and testing captured insects for infection. It tells a programme whether transmission is rising or falling, where to spray, and whether resistance is appearing. It is chronically underfunded relative to treatment, yet without it vector control is blind — spraying the wrong place or continuing a failing insecticide.
Sources: WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### WASH interventions
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/wash-interventions/
TL;DR: Clean water, safe toilets and hygiene promotion that stop the worms, flukes and bacteria spread through water, stool and soil.
Summary: For schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, dracunculiasis and the foodborne trematodiases, drugs reduce the burden but cannot stop reinfection where sanitation and water are unsafe. WASH interventions — safe water supply, latrines, handwashing, shoe-wearing and safe food handling — attack the transmission route itself. WHO now recommends integrating WASH with preventive chemotherapy and vector control, since the two together can achieve what neither can alone.
Sources: WHO — WASH and NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Wolbachia mosquito method
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/wolbachia-method/
TL;DR: Releasing mosquitoes that carry a common bacterium so that they can no longer transmit dengue, chikungunya or Zika — and so that their offspring cannot either.
Summary: The World Mosquito Program's method infects Aedes aegypti with the wMel strain of Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses from replicating well inside the mosquito. Because Wolbachia is passed from mother to eggs, the bacterium spreads through the wild mosquito population and persists without repeated releases — a replacement rather than a suppression strategy. The evidence base is strong: a cluster-randomised trial in Yogyakarta found 77% fewer dengue cases and 86% fewer hospitalisations, and city-scale deployments in Brazil and Colombia have reported reductions of 60–90%, sustained through the severe 2024 outbreak. By 2025 the programme reported 16.1 million people protected across fifteen countries, with an estimated 1.5 million cases prevented. It is not a vaccine and does not stop every case, but no other dengue intervention has produced reductions this large and durable at city scale.
Sources: World Mosquito Program <https://www.worldmosquitoprogram.org/>; AWED trial results (NEJM) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2030243>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Xenomonitoring
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/xenomonitoring/
TL;DR: Testing the vectors themselves for infection, rather than testing people, to see whether transmission is still happening.
Summary: Xenomonitoring examines trapped mosquitoes, flies, bugs or snails for the parasite's DNA. Because many NTD infections are asymptomatic, human surveys can miss low-level transmission; testing the vector detects it directly. It has become a key tool for verifying whether lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis transmission has actually stopped, which is exactly the question elimination programmes must answer.
Sources: WHO — xenomonitoring for NTD elimination <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>


## Trials

### Acoziborole single-dose trial for sleeping sickness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/acoziborole-hat/
TL;DR: A trial of a single oral dose of acoziborole that reported cure rates above 95% in Gambiense sleeping sickness, including late-stage disease.
Summary: DNDi and partners tested acoziborole, a benzoxaborole, as a single oral treatment for Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea. Reported cure rates were very high across both early and late-stage disease without the lumbar puncture staging that older treatments required. If registration follows, treatment could be given in a village clinic with one tablet — no hospital, no infusions, no cold chain.
Sources: DNDi — acoziborole for sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; DNDi — DRC approves acoziborole <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2026/drc-approves-use-acoziborole-breakthrough-one-day-oral-treatment-against-sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### AWED: Wolbachia to eliminate dengue
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/awed-wolbachia/
TL;DR: The gold-standard randomised trial that showed Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes cut dengue by 77% and hospitalisations by 86%.
Summary: The AWED trial was a cluster-randomised controlled trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in which Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were released across part of the city and dengue incidence compared with untreated areas. It found a 77% reduction in virologically-confirmed symptomatic dengue and an 86% reduction in hospitalisations — a result of a size and rigour rarely seen for a vector-control intervention. The trial is the foundation of the World Mosquito Program's case for scaling the method, and subsequent city-scale deployments in Brazil and Colombia have reported reductions of similar magnitude. Yogyakarta recorded only 67 dengue cases in 2023, a fraction of its historical burden.
Sources: Efficacy of Wolbachia-infected mosquito deployments (NEJM) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2030243>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Azithromycin for yaws eradication
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/yaws-azithromycin/
TL;DR: The trial showing a single oral dose of azithromycin cures yaws as well as an injected penicillin, enabling mass eradication.
Summary: A landmark study in Papua New Guinea found that a single oral dose of azithromycin was non-inferior to injected benzathine penicillin for curing yaws. That result made community-wide mass treatment possible, and in 2012 WHO launched the Morges strategy to eradicate yaws. Progress has been slowed by resurges and by the difficulty of reaching the last affected communities.
Sources: WHO — yaws eradication <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/yaws>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Azithromycin mass treatment for trachoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/trachoma-azithromycin/
TL;DR: Trials showing that single-dose azithromycin reduces the eye infection that causes trachoma, forming the 'A' in the SAFE strategy.
Summary: Randomised trials in Tanzania and elsewhere showed that single-dose oral azithromycin dramatically reduced the prevalence of the chlamydial eye infection that leads to trachoma, compared with topical treatment. This established the 'A' in WHO's SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement) and turned trachoma from an intractable cause of blindness into an elimination target.
Sources: WHO — trachoma elimination <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### BE-PEOPLE: bedaquiline as leprosy prophylaxis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/be-people-leprosy/
TL;DR: A trial testing whether bedaquiline, with its very long half-life, protects contacts of leprosy patients better than a single dose of rifampicin.
Summary: BE-PEOPLE tests bedaquiline as post-exposure prophylaxis for leprosy contacts. The rationale is pharmacological: bedaquiline has a half-life of around five and a half months and greater activity against Mycobacterium leprae than rifampicin, so a single dose might protect for far longer. If it works, it would be the first genuinely new preventive agent for leprosy since single-dose rifampicin, and could be particularly valuable in high-burden settings where repeated contact screening is impractical.
Sources: Leprosy research updates — bedaquiline prophylaxis <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12010777/>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### BENEFIT: benznidazole in chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/benefit-chagas/
TL;DR: The largest Chagas treatment trial, which found that benznidazole cleared the parasite but did not clearly improve heart outcomes.
Summary: BENEFIT randomised thousands of patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy to benznidazole or placebo. The drug reduced detectable parasite DNA, but after years of follow-up it did not significantly reduce cardiac deterioration. The result reshaped the field: it showed that treating late-stage disease is not the same as curing it, and that the priority is finding patients earlier and developing better drugs.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease treatment <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Butantan-DV single-dose dengue vaccine trial
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/butantan-dv-dengue/
TL;DR: A Brazilian single-dose dengue vaccine trial reporting strong efficacy across serotypes and age groups.
Summary: Butantan-DV is a single-dose, live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine developed in Brazil. A large randomised trial reported substantial efficacy against symptomatic dengue across all four serotypes and in both younger and older participants, with a good safety profile. A single-dose vaccine removes a major logistical obstacle for mass programmes in middle-income countries.
Sources: WHO — dengue vaccines <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### DNDi-0690 for visceral leishmaniasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/dndi-0690-leishmaniasis/
TL;DR: A non-profit-developed oxaborole tested as a new oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis.
Summary: DNDi-0690 is an oxaborole that emerged from DNDi's discovery pipeline, associated with inhibition of the parasite enzyme N-myristoyltransferase. It entered clinical testing for visceral leishmaniasis as part of the effort to find an oral treatment that avoids the toxicity of antimonials and the logistics of infusions. It illustrates the non-profit pipeline filling a gap the market left empty.
Sources: DNDi — leishmaniasis portfolio <https://dndi.org/diseases/leishmaniasis/>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Ebola ring vaccination trial (Guinea)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ebola-ring-vaccination-trial/
TL;DR: The trial that proved a vaccine could protect the contacts of Ebola cases, and gave outbreak response its most powerful tool.
Summary: Run in Guinea during the 2014–2016 West African outbreak, this trial used ring vaccination — vaccinating the contacts and contacts-of-contacts of each new case — and was designed so that efficacy could be estimated from cases occurring before vaccination took effect. It found the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine highly protective, with no cases among vaccinated contacts after the ten-day window. The result licensed the vaccine and established ring vaccination as the standard response to Ebola, later used at scale in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Emodepside for onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/emodepside-oncho/
TL;DR: Clinical development of a veterinary dewormer as a new human treatment with a mechanism different from ivermectin.
Summary: DNDi and partners advanced emodepside into human trials for onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths. Because it acts on the SLO-1 potassium channel rather than the ivermectin channel, it could be used where ivermectin is contraindicated — notably areas where Loa loa circulates and ivermectin risks severe reactions — and provides a second mechanism if resistance emerges.
Sources: DNDi — emodepside <https://dndi.org/diseases/onchocerciasis/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Emodepside Phase II part 2 for river blindness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/emodepside-part2-oncho/
TL;DR: The dose-selection stage of emodepside's clinical development, after part 1 showed it works against adult as well as juvenile worms.
Summary: The final analysis of part 1 of emodepside's Phase II trial confirmed a favourable safety profile and efficacy against both juvenile and adult Onchocerca volvulus worms, meeting the criteria to proceed. Part 2 will investigate selected doses and their safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics, with recruitment planned to begin in the third quarter of 2026. The significance is the adulticidal signal: ivermectin does not reliably kill adult worms, so a drug that does would shorten the fifteen-year treatment horizon that currently defines onchocerciasis elimination.
Sources: DNDi — emodepside for river blindness <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/emodepside/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### eWHORM basket trial of oxfendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ewhorm-oxfendazole/
TL;DR: An African-European partnership testing one drug against several worm infections at once, including river blindness and loiasis.
Summary: The eWHORM partnership runs a basket trial — a single protocol testing oxfendazole across multiple helminth infections simultaneously — with clinical sites in Africa. Recruitment for trichuriasis was completed in Tanzania and sites for onchocerciasis and loiasis opened, alongside a Phase IIa dose-escalation study for loiasis in Gabon. The design is a response to a practical problem in NTD research: running one trial per infection is unaffordable, and a drug that works against several worms at once is exactly what a mass-treatment programme would want.
Sources: eWHORM — African-European partnership <https://www.ewhorm.org/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Fexinidazole for chronic Chagas disease
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fexinidazole-chagas/
TL;DR: The trial that ended fexinidazole's Chagas candidacy: tolerated by patients, but unable to eliminate the parasite.
Summary: Fexinidazole is an oral drug that transformed sleeping sickness, so testing it in chronic Chagas disease — caused by a related trypanosome — was a reasonable bet. An early Phase 2 study was encouraging enough to generate real hope, reporting high efficacy at treatment durations of less than three days, but it was interrupted for tolerability reasons. A follow-up study confirmed that the drug was well tolerated and found that it did not eliminate Trypanosoma cruzi. The negative result closed this line of work and pushed DNDi's Chagas programme toward a new candidate, with a Phase II proof-of-concept study planned to begin in Latin America in late 2026.
Sources: DNDi — fexinidazole for Chagas disease <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/fexinidazole-chagas/>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>

### Fexinidazole for sleeping sickness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fexinidazole-hat/
TL;DR: The trial that produced the first all-oral cure for sleeping sickness, covering both stages of Gambiense disease.
Summary: The pivotal fexinidazole study, run by DNDi with Sanofi and national programmes, showed that a 10-day oral course cured Gambiense sleeping sickness patients, including those with late-stage disease, without the need for hospital infusions. It led to approval in 2019 and to the drug's addition to the WHO essential medicines list. A follow-on study tested an adjusted regimen in patients with more severe disease.
Sources: DNDi — fexinidazole <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Fosravuconazole versus itraconazole for eumycetoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fosravuconazole-mycetoma/
TL;DR: The world's first randomised clinical trial for mycetoma, run in Sudan, which found fosravuconazole safe and simpler but not more effective.
Summary: This Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial at a single centre in Sudan compared two once-weekly doses of fosravuconazole with daily itraconazole, each combined with surgery at six months, in patients with moderate eumycetoma. Neither fosravuconazole dose was superior to itraconazole, and both had numerically lower efficacy. The trial nevertheless established that a rigorous randomised study is possible in one of the world's hardest settings, that once-weekly dosing is safe and tolerable, and it built the infrastructure and the international collaboration on which the next mycetoma trial will depend.
Sources: Trial results (The Lancet Infectious Diseases) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39098321/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### High-dose ivermectin for onchocerciasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ivermectin-dose-oncho/
TL;DR: A trial showing that a higher dose of ivermectin kills more adult worms, strengthening the push toward elimination.
Summary: Because standard ivermectin suppresses microfilariae but does not kill adult worms efficiently, a higher-dose regimen was tested to see whether it could sterilise or kill more adults. The trial reported improved efficacy, which matters for elimination — a treatment that harms adult worms shortens the years of repeated mass administration a programme must sustain.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis elimination <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Intradermal dose-sparing rabies PEP
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/rabies-dose-sparing/
TL;DR: Trials showing that giving rabies vaccine into the skin uses far less product and stretches scarce supplies.
Summary: Intradermal regimens for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis use a fraction of the dose of intramuscular regimens while producing adequate immunity, which WHO has recommended since 2018. For countries where vaccine supply and cost limit access, dose-sparing can mean many more bite victims are treated from the same stock. The remaining obstacle is rabies immunoglobulin, which has no dose-sparing equivalent and remains the scarce, expensive component.
Sources: WHO — rabies post-exposure prophylaxis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### IVM-KIDS: paediatric ivermectin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ivm-kids-paediatric/
TL;DR: A consortium working out the right ivermectin dose for children under 15 kg and developing a dispersible formulation for them.
Summary: Ivermectin dosing was never properly established for the youngest and smallest children — those under 15 kilograms — and the tablet is hard for them to take, so very young children have largely been excluded from mass treatment for river blindness and lymphatic filariasis. The IVM-KIDS consortium, led by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, is generating the dosing data and developing a novel oral dispersible formulation; DNDi joined in 2025. The work is unglamorous and closes the same kind of gap that arpraziquantel closed for schistosomiasis.
Sources: DNDi — paediatric ivermectin <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/paediatric-ivermectin/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### M72/AS01E tuberculosis vaccine trial
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/m72-as01e-trial/
TL;DR: The most promising tuberculosis vaccine candidate, which reported partial protection against progression to disease.
Summary: M72/AS01E is a subunit vaccine against two mycobacterial antigens. Its phase 2b trial in people with latent tuberculosis infection reported around 50% protection against progression to active pulmonary disease — the first vaccine candidate in decades to show a signal of this kind. A confirmatory phase 3 trial is under way. If it holds up, it would be the first new tuberculosis vaccine since BCG a century ago, and it is designed to be used alongside preventive treatment rather than replacing it.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Miltefosine and combinations for visceral leishmaniasis in South Asia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/miltefosine-vl-india/
TL;DR: Trials that brought oral miltefosine and short combination regimens to visceral leishmaniasis in India, then saw efficacy slip.
Summary: Miltefosine was developed as the first oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis and was deployed at scale in Bihar after antimonials failed. Later studies tested combinations of liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine and paromomycin to shorten treatment and stretch drug supply. Over time, cure rates with miltefosine fell, evidence of emerging resistance that makes combination therapy and new drugs essential.
Sources: WHO — visceral leishmaniasis elimination <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Mosnodenvir dengue prevention study
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/mosnodenvir-dengue/
TL;DR: The field study of a promising dengue antiviral that was discontinued in 2025 despite encouraging early results.
Summary: This Phase 2 field study tested mosnodenvir, formerly JNJ-1802, for the prevention of dengue after the drug showed it could protect volunteers in a controlled human infection model — an unusually strong early signal for a dengue antiviral. It was safe and well tolerated in Phase 1 and 2a studies. In 2025 the developer discontinued the field study, a decision driven by commercial and strategic considerations rather than a safety signal. The result is that dengue still has no approved antiviral, and that a challenge-model result — however encouraging — does not by itself produce a usable medicine.
Sources: Johnson & Johnson — discontinuation announcement <https://www.jnj.com/media-center/press-releases/johnson-johnson-to-discontinue-phase-2-field-study-evaluating-investigational-antiviral-for-the-prevention-of-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Moxidectin for river blindness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/moxidectin-oncho/
TL;DR: The trial showing moxidectin suppresses river-blindness microfilariae longer than ivermectin, leading to its approval in 2018.
Summary: The pivotal moxidectin study, run with DNDi and WHO, compared a single dose against ivermectin and found better and more sustained suppression of skin microfilariae. That supported FDA approval in 2018, making moxidectin the first new onchocerciasis medicine in decades. It has not widely displaced ivermectin, which remains donated free for mass treatment.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis treatment <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### NECT: nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/nect-hat/
TL;DR: The trial that showed combining two older drugs made late-stage sleeping sickness far easier to treat.
Summary: NECT combined oral nifurtimox with fewer eflornithine infusions and was shown to be easier to deliver and at least as effective as eflornithine alone for second-stage Gambiense sleeping sickness. It became the WHO-recommended treatment for late-stage disease and was a landmark in making treatment practical in resource-limited hospitals. It has since been overtaken by fexinidazole and, potentially, acoziborole.
Sources: DNDi — sleeping sickness history <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### One versus two doses of ivermectin-based mass treatment for scabies
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/scabies-mda-one-vs-two/
TL;DR: A cluster-randomised trial finding that a single round of community ivermectin treatment may be as effective as two.
Summary: This cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial compared one round of ivermectin-based mass drug administration with two for the control of scabies. If one round is sufficient, programmes can reach far more communities for the same money, because the second round is a large share of the cost and the logistical burden. The result supports the case for single-round campaigns as a first response in high-prevalence settings, with surveillance to detect whether scabies returns and a second round needed.
Sources: One versus two doses of ivermectin-based MDA (PLOS NTD) <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371/journal.pntd.0011207>; WHO — scabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/scabies>

### Oxfendazole Phase IIa for lymphatic filariasis (India)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/oxfendazole-lf/
TL;DR: A proof-of-concept trial asking whether oxfendazole can treat lymphatic filariasis by killing the adult worms.
Summary: In 2025 the Indian Council of Medical Research initiated a Phase IIa proof-of-concept trial of oxfendazole for lymphatic filariasis in India, with DNDi supplying the investigational product and providing technical support and co-monitoring. India carries the largest single share of the global filariasis burden, so a trial there tests the drug where it matters most. If oxfendazole shows macrofilaricidal activity it would address the core limitation of the current programme: every existing drug suppresses microfilariae without reliably killing adults, which is why treatment must continue for years.
Sources: DNDi — oxfendazole for lymphatic filariasis <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/oxfendazole-for-lymphatic-filariasis/>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### PALM: randomised trial of Ebola therapeutics
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/palme-ebola-trial/
TL;DR: The trial during the DRC outbreak that identified the two antibody treatments able to save lives.
Summary: PALM was a randomised controlled trial of four investigational treatments for Ebola, run during the 2018–2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. An interim analysis showed that two monoclonal antibody products — ansuvimab and the REGN-EB3 cocktail — reduced mortality substantially compared with the other arms, and the trial was stopped early so that all patients could receive them. It was the first time a trial demonstrated that any treatment changed the outcome of Ebola, and it was conducted in an active outbreak zone with armed conflict.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### PEOPLE: double-dose rifampicin prophylaxis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/people-leprosy-pep/
TL;DR: A trial in the Comoros and Madagascar showing that double-dose rifampicin prophylaxis cut leprosy incidence by 40% at population level.
Summary: The PEOPLE trial tested whether giving a second dose of rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis, at population scale, could reduce leprosy incidence rather than only protecting individual contacts. Run in the Comoros and Madagascar, it reported a 40% reduction in leprosy incidence — evidence that chemoprophylaxis can shift transmission in a community, not just lower one person's risk. It is the strongest support so far for scaling prophylaxis beyond household contacts to neighbourhoods and social contacts, as WHO now recommends.
Sources: Leprosy research updates — PEOPLE trial <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12010777/>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Praziquantel in preschool-aged children
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/praziquantel-pediatric/
TL;DR: Studies establishing a paediatric praziquantel formulation and dosing so that young children can be treated for schistosomiasis.
Summary: Preschool-aged children were long excluded from schistosomiasis treatment because the standard tablet was hard to give them and dosing was unestablished. Trials of a paediatric dispersible formulation, and pharmacokinetic studies to set the right dose, showed treatment is safe and effective in this group. That matters because very young children carry a high burden and were systematically left out of mass campaigns.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis in children <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### R21/Matrix-M malaria vaccine trial
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/r21-matrix-m/
TL;DR: A trial of a second malaria vaccine with comparable efficacy and far greater manufacturing capacity.
Summary: R21/Matrix-M is a circumsporozoite protein vaccine with a saponin adjuvant. Its phase 3 programme reported solid protection against clinical malaria in young children with a good safety profile, and — critically — it can be produced at large scale and low cost, using a manufacturing platform already established for another vaccine. R21 received WHO recommendation in 2023, and its availability is what makes wide malaria vaccination programmes realistic.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — Global Malaria Programme <https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme>

### Rabies monoclonal antibody in category III exposures
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/rabies-monoclonal-antibody/
TL;DR: A phase 4 study of an engineered antibody that could replace scarce, plasma-derived rabies immunoglobulin.
Summary: For severe (category III) bites, post-exposure prophylaxis needs antibodies as well as vaccine, and the standard product — human rabies immunoglobulin — is plasma-derived, expensive and chronically short. Monoclonal antibodies against the rabies glycoprotein offer a scalable, consistent alternative, and two are licensed in India. A 2025 phase 4 study reported outcomes for a monoclonal antibody in patients with category III exposure, and antibody cocktails are being evaluated as a second-line option when immunoglobulin is unavailable. If adopted, these products attack the single most stubborn obstacle in the rabies treatment pathway: the cost and scarcity of immunoglobulin.
Sources: Lancet — rabies monoclonal antibody PEP <https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(25)00735-4/fulltext>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### RTS,S malaria vaccine pilot programme
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/rts-s-malaria-pilot/
TL;DR: A large pilot introduction in three countries that generated the evidence for recommending the first malaria vaccine.
Summary: Before RTS,S/AS01 could be recommended, WHO ran a pilot introduction in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi to answer the operational questions a trial could not: whether the vaccine could be delivered through routine immunisation, whether parents would accept it, and whether it reduced deaths in real conditions. More than 800,000 children received it. The pilot found that delivery was feasible, that it reduced severe malaria substantially, and that it did not harm the uptake of other childhood vaccines — which is what allowed the 2021 recommendation.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### SchistoShield (Sm-p80) schistosomiasis vaccine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/schistoshield/
TL;DR: The most advanced schistosomiasis vaccine candidate, tested with a controlled human infection model that measures protection directly.
Summary: SchistoShield is a recombinant Sm-p80 antigen with a GLA-SE adjuvant, developed as a vaccine that would reduce infection intensity and reinfection — something praziquantel cannot do, since it treats but does not protect. After early-phase clinical testing, evaluation moved to a controlled human infection model, in which consented, schistosome-naive volunteers are vaccinated and then deliberately exposed to a defined number of male Schistosoma mansoni cercariae so that protection can be measured directly rather than inferred from field trials. That design is rare in parasitology and is itself a methodological milestone; the open question is how well challenge-model protection predicts what happens in a village.
Sources: Schistosomiasis challenge study (ClinicalTrials.gov) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05999825>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### STAR: azithromycin after trichiasis surgery
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/star-trichiasis/
TL;DR: The trial showing that a single dose of azithromycin after eyelid surgery cuts trichiasis recurrence by about a third.
Summary: Trachomatous trichiasis frequently returns after surgery, meaning renewed pain and renewed risk to the cornea. The STAR trial tested whether giving a single dose of azithromycin after the operation reduced recurrence, comparing it with topical tetracycline. It found that azithromycin reduced postoperative trichiasis recurrence by about one third, and that severe recurrence at one year was reduced — evidence that the surgical and antibiotic arms of the SAFE strategy work better together than either alone. It argues for combining azithromycin with trichiasis surgery as standard practice.
Sources: Single-dose azithromycin prevents trichiasis recurrence (PubMed) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16534049/>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### TAK-003 (Qdenga) dengue vaccine trial
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/tak-003-dengue/
TL;DR: A large trial of a two-dose dengue vaccine that protected against all four serotypes without needing prior-infection screening.
Summary: The TIDES trial evaluated TAK-003, a live-attenuated two-dose dengue vaccine, in more than twenty thousand children across Latin America and Asia. It showed protection against symptomatic and hospitalised dengue across serotypes, including in people with no prior dengue infection — removing the pre-vaccination screening requirement that had limited the earlier vaccine. TAK-003 is licensed in several countries.
Sources: WHO — dengue vaccines <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### TB-PRACTECAL
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/tb-practecal/
TL;DR: The trial that produced a six-month, injection-free cure for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
Summary: TB-PRACTECAL tested short all-oral regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and its BPaLM arm — bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin — produced high cure rates with far fewer deaths and better tolerability than the long regimens it replaced. WHO issued a rapid communication recommending the regimen in 2022, which changed the standard of care for a disease that had required up to two years of treatment including injectable drugs. It is one of the fastest translations of a trial result into global policy in tuberculosis.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### TREAT-BU: telacebec for Buruli ulcer
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/treat-bu/
TL;DR: A Phase 2 trial testing whether a tuberculosis drug can cure Buruli ulcer in far fewer than eight weeks of treatment.
Summary: TREAT-BU is a Phase 2 proof-of-concept study of telacebec in adults with Buruli ulcer, initiated by TB Alliance in July 2024. The endpoint is complete healing of the lesion by 52 weeks after starting treatment, without relapse. The rationale is unusually strong: telacebec has the lowest minimum inhibitory concentration of any drug tested against Mycobacterium ulcerans and sterilised the infection in mice after only sixteen doses. If it works in people, the eight-week antibiotic course that is now standard could be replaced by a regimen of a few doses — which matters most for the patients who live furthest from a clinic.
Sources: TREAT-BU trial (ClinicalTrials.gov) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06481163>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Trials of snake antivenoms and next-generation products
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/snakebite-antivenom-trials/
TL;DR: Clinical studies comparing antivenom doses and testing new products, aiming to fix a supply system that leaves most victims untreated.
Summary: Research on snakebite treatment spans dose-finding studies (how much antivenom is enough), comparisons between products from different manufacturers, and early work on recombinant antibodies. A recurring finding is that many antivenoms on the market are of uncertain quality, which is why WHO introduced a prequalification programme. The deeper problem is distribution and affordability, not a shortage of evidence.
Sources: WHO — snakebite antivenom prequalification <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO — snakebite envenoming strategy <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515993>

### TSOL18 vaccination with oxfendazole in pigs
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/pig-vaccination-oxfendazole/
TL;DR: A trial in Uganda showing that repeated pig vaccination plus deworming eliminated Taenia solium transmission by pigs.
Summary: This control trial combined three-monthly vaccination of pigs with TSOL18 and treatment with oxfendazole, on the reasoning that the vaccine prevents new cysts while the drug clears any that have already formed. It found that the combination eliminated Taenia solium transmission by pigs in the study area — the strongest evidence that the animal end of the cycle can be closed. Because pigs are the intermediate host, removing infection from pigs removes the human tapeworm cases that follow, and with them the egg contamination that causes neurocysticercosis. It is the clearest demonstration in the field that a human disease can be controlled through veterinary intervention.
Sources: Control trial of porcine cysticercosis in Uganda (PubMed) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33743828/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### WINGS-4-FGS: treating female genital schistosomiasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/wings4fgs-fgs/
TL;DR: A trial testing whether adding an anti-inflammatory to praziquantel reduces the lasting damage of female genital schistosomiasis.
Summary: Praziquantel kills the schistosomes, but in female genital schistosomiasis the inflammatory reaction the eggs provoke can leave chronic granuloma and fibrosis that the drug does not undo — and the lesions increase susceptibility to HIV. The WINGS-4-FGS consortium is running a randomised trial that adds a repurposed anti-inflammatory medicine to praziquantel for women and girls living with FGS, with the aim of halting or reducing the inflammatory damage. It is a rare example of NTD research aimed explicitly at morbidity in women, a group that has been under-studied in the field.
Sources: WINGS-4-FGS consortium <https://www.wings4fgs.eu/>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>


## Institutions

### Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/africa-cdc/
TL;DR: The African Union's own public health agency, built to give the continent its own surveillance, laboratory and emergency response capacity.
Summary: Africa CDC was established in 2016 as the African Union's specialised agency for public health, with a mandate to strengthen surveillance, laboratory networks and emergency response across the continent. It grew out of the recognition — sharpened by the 2014–2016 Ebola outbreak — that African outbreaks should not depend on capacity flown in from elsewhere. Its Regional Integrated Surveillance and Laboratory Networks aim to give every region the ability to detect and confirm disease, which is the same capability that NTD elimination verification requires. It runs its own manufacturing and diagnostics partnerships, and coordinates the continent's response to outbreaks including mpox and COVID-19.
Sources: Africa CDC <https://www.africacdc.org/>; Wikipedia — Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Centres_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention>

### Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/gates-foundation/
TL;DR: The largest private funder of NTD control, paying for mass treatment campaigns, diagnostics, disease mapping and product development.
Summary: The Gates Foundation is the single most influential private funder in NTDs, supporting the donation programmes' logistics, the mapping of where diseases occur, elimination campaigns for lymphatic filariasis and trachoma, and product development for diagnostics and vaccines. Its funding shapes which NTDs have momentum, and its withdrawal would leave large gaps — a structural weakness of relying on philanthropic rather than domestic financing.
Sources: Gates Foundation — neglected tropical diseases <https://www.gatesfoundation.org/our-work/programs/global-health/neglected-tropical-diseases>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Butantan Institute
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/butantan-institute/
TL;DR: The Brazilian institute that developed and won approval for the world's first single-dose dengue vaccine.
Summary: The Butantan Institute, linked to the São Paulo state health department, is one of Brazil's principal vaccine and antivenom manufacturers and a national research institution. It developed Butantan-DV, a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine that is the first in the world to require only a single dose, in partnership with Brazil's Ministry of Health and a manufacturing partner. Brazil's regulator approved it in November 2025 for people aged 12 to 59, with incorporation into the national immunisation programme planned for 2026 and more than a million doses prepared. Its significance is not only clinical: it shows an endemic country developing, testing, manufacturing and deploying a vaccine for its own largest vector-borne threat.
Sources: Butantan Institute — dengue vaccine approval <https://butantan.gov.br/>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### CASCAP (Cholangiocarcinoma Screening and Care Program)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/cascap/
TL;DR: A Thai programme that pairs liver-fluke control with ultrasound screening for the bile-duct cancer the flukes cause.
Summary: CASCAP, based at Khon Kaen University in northeast Thailand, is a screening and care programme for cholangiocarcinoma, the bile-duct cancer associated with Opisthorchis and Clonorchis infection. It links parasite control with systematic ultrasound screening and follow-up, on the reasoning that a cancer caused by a treatable infection should be detectable before it becomes symptomatic. It is one of the few places where a neglected parasitic disease is managed explicitly as a cancer-prevention problem, and it provides a model for combining NTD control with oncology in the same programme.
Sources: Cholangiocarcinoma Screening and Care Program <https://cascap.kku.ac.th/>

### CIDEIM (Centro Internacional de Entrenamiento e Investigaciones Médicas)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/cideim/
TL;DR: A Colombian research centre focused on leishmaniasis, contributing clinical trials and immunology from Latin America.
Summary: CIDEIM, based in Cali, is a leading centre for leishmaniasis research, running clinical trials of treatments, studying the immune response and training researchers from across the region. It represents the kind of endemic-country institution whose work is essential to making treatment guidance fit the local epidemiology rather than importing it from elsewhere.
Sources: CIDEIM <https://www.cideim.org.co/>; WHO — leishmaniasis (a focus of this institute's work) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/cepi/
TL;DR: The funder created after the West African Ebola outbreak to develop vaccines for epidemic threats before they are needed.
Summary: CEPI was founded in 2017 after the 2014–2016 Ebola outbreak showed how long it took to develop a vaccine during an emergency. It funds vaccine development for epidemic-prone diseases — including Lassa fever, Nipah, Rift Valley fever, Chikungunya and Ebola — with an approach that prepares candidates, platforms and manufacturing capacity in advance so that a response can start in weeks rather than years. It was central to the COVID-19 vaccine response, and its model is the main institutional answer to the problem that outbreaks occur in poor countries and therefore attract little commercial vaccine development.
Sources: CEPI <https://cepi.net/>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### CUIDA Chagas
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/cuida-chagas/
TL;DR: A Unitaid-funded project testing simpler ways to stop Chagas passing from mother to newborn in four Latin American countries.
Summary: CUIDA Chagas — Communities United to Integrate and Deliver Chagas Care and Treatment — is a project implemented with PAHO in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia and Paraguay and funded by Unitaid. It targets congenital transmission with a practical goal: find a shorter, simpler pathway than the current one, which requires two confirmatory serological tests and a sixty-day treatment course, and along which most patients are lost. The project is testing new diagnostic and treatment options and, crucially, implementation models that can be replicated by national programmes — because elimination of congenital Chagas is achievable with existing tools, and the obstacle is the health system.
Sources: Unitaid — new tests and treatments to prevent Chagas in newborns <https://unitaid.org/project/new-treatments-and-diagnostics-to-prevent-chagas-transmission-from-mother-to-child/>; PAHO — Chagas disease <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chagas-disease>

### Doherty Institute
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/doherty-institute/
TL;DR: An Australian research institute at the centre of Buruli ulcer transmission research and the tool that predicts hotspots years ahead.
Summary: The Doherty Institute in Melbourne conducts the research that has reshaped understanding of Buruli ulcer in Australia, where the disease is emerging and spreading. Its work implicated mosquitoes and possums in transmission and produced an early-warning approach that flags emerging hotspots two to six years before human cases. Australia is unusual in having a well-resourced public health system dealing with an NTD, which makes it a natural laboratory: transmission routes that are impossible to disentangle in a rural African setting can be studied with genomic and entomological tools here, and the findings then tested against the African epidemiology.
Sources: Doherty Institute — Buruli ulcer hotspot early warning <https://www.doherty.edu.au/articles/early-warning-tool-detect-buruli-ulcer-hotspots-before-human-cases-occur/>; WHO — Buruli ulcer (a focus of this institute's work) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/buruli-ulcer>

### Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/dndi/
TL;DR: The non-profit drug developer that has brought new medicines for sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, leishmaniasis and filarial infections.
Summary: DNDi is the clearest example of the product development partnership model. Founded in 2003 by Médecins Sans Frontières and research institutions, it develops treatments for diseases with no commercial market and then works to make them available and affordable. Its portfolio includes fexinidazole and acoziborole for sleeping sickness, DNDi-0690 and emodepside, and access programmes for benznidazole and miltefosine. It publishes its portfolio openly and reports on progress annually.
Sources: DNDi — portfolio <https://dndi.org/portfolio/>; DNDi — diseases <https://dndi.org/diseases/>

### FIND
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/find-dx/
TL;DR: A non-profit that develops and helps introduce diagnostics for neglected diseases, from rapid strips to molecular tests.
Summary: FIND works across the diagnostic pipeline: it defines what a test must do, brokers development with manufacturers, runs field evaluations, and supports countries in adopting tests. In NTDs it has worked on tests for visceral leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, filariasis and drug-resistant tuberculosis. Its role fills one of the least commercially attractive parts of the NTD toolbox, where a diagnostically empty field leaves programmes unable to know who is infected.
Sources: FIND — diagnostics for neglected diseases <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — diagnostics for neglected tropical diseases (context) <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### GALVmed
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/galvmed/
TL;DR: The alliance that works to make livestock vaccines and medicines available in the countries that need them, including the pig vaccine against cysticercosis.
Summary: GALVmed — the Global Alliance for Livestock Veterinary Medicines — works to make animal vaccines, medicines and diagnostics accessible in low- and middle-income countries, where livestock are central to livelihoods but veterinary products are often unavailable. Its work on Taenia solium cysticercosis promotes the combination of the TSOL18 pig vaccine and oxfendazole treatment, which prevents and clears the cysts that lead to human tapeworm infection and neurocysticercosis. Its role is a reminder that zoonotic NTD control is a veterinary-market problem as much as a medical one: a vaccine that exists but is not distributed to backyard pigs changes nothing.
Sources: GALVmed — breaking the cycle of neurocysticercosis <https://www.galvmed.org/breaking-the-cycle-of-the-zoonotic-disease-neurocysticercosis/>; WHO — taeniasis/cysticercosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/taeniasis-cysticercosis>

### Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/gavi/
TL;DR: The alliance that funds and procures vaccines for low-income countries, including malaria, Ebola and tuberculosis candidates.
Summary: Gavi pools demand and funding so that low-income countries can buy vaccines at prices they could never negotiate alone, and it has financed immunisation for hundreds of millions of children since 2000. In this corpus it matters mainly for the newer vaccines: it is a co-funder of malaria vaccine rollout, it holds an Ebola vaccine stockpile for outbreak response, and it is the likely purchaser of any successful tuberculosis vaccine. Its model — advance market commitments plus pooled procurement — is the closest thing global health has to a mechanism for making a vaccine for poor countries commercially viable.
Sources: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance <https://www.gavi.org/>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Global Onchocerciasis Network for Elimination (GONE)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/gone/
TL;DR: A network of national programmes and partners coordinating the final push to eliminate river blindness, with a focus on Africa.
Summary: GONE brings together national onchocerciasis programmes, WHO, donors, non-governmental organisations and researchers to coordinate the transition from controlling river blindness to eliminating it. Its work is unglamorous but decisive: aligning treatment and surveillance protocols across borders, sharing the evidence needed for a country to be verified as free of transmission, advocating for the funding that elimination requires beyond control, and supporting the countries now attempting what Niger achieved in 2025. Networks like this matter in the endgame, when progress depends on the weakest link in a region rather than the strongest.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis elimination networks <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### Global Partnership for Zero Leprosy (GPZL)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/gpzl/
TL;DR: A coalition coordinating the push to interrupt leprosy transmission, including the scale-up of post-exposure prophylaxis.
Summary: The Global Partnership for Zero Leprosy brings together national programmes, WHO, non-governmental organisations, researchers and people affected by leprosy to coordinate the goal of interrupting transmission. Its work is largely operational: supporting countries to introduce contact screening and single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis, harmonising how programmes measure transmission, advocating for the funding and surveillance that elimination requires, and keeping stigma and disability on the agenda rather than treating them as secondary. It is hosted by the Task Force for Global Health.
Sources: Global Partnership for Zero Leprosy <https://zeroleprosy.org/>

### icddr,b
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/icddrb/
TL;DR: A Bangladeshi research institute with a long record on cholera, dengue and enteric disease, and on delivering health in low-resource settings.
Summary: icddr,b in Dhaka is internationally known for work on diarrhoeal disease and for pioneering oral rehydration therapy, and it has become a centre for dengue and other arboviral research in South Asia as well as for implementation research on delivering health interventions at scale. Its history shows how an endemic-country institution can produce globally important results.
Sources: icddr,b <https://www.icddrb.org/>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (a focus of this institute's work) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Ifakara Health Institute
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/ifakara/
TL;DR: A Tanzanian research institute that is a global leader in vector biology and vector-control trials.
Summary: Ifakara runs research on mosquitoes, malaria and other vector-borne diseases, tests new vector-control tools in field conditions, and trains African scientists and entomologists. It has been central to evaluating insecticide-treated nets, new active ingredients and, more recently, genetic approaches to vector control.
Sources: Ifakara Health Institute <https://ihi.or.tz/>; WHO — Global vector control response (context) <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/icmr/
TL;DR: India's apex biomedical research body, which carries the world's largest lymphatic filariasis burden and runs the trials trying to end it.
Summary: The ICMR is India's national medical research agency, funding and running research across infectious disease, including the country's large lymphatic filariasis and visceral leishmaniasis programmes. In 2025 it initiated a Phase IIa proof-of-concept trial of oxfendazole as a treatment for lymphatic filariasis, with DNDi providing the investigational product and technical support — significant because India accounts for the single largest share of the global filariasis burden, so an Indian trial of a potential macrofilaricide is the trial that matters most for the endgame.
Sources: Indian Council of Medical Research <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>; WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Infectious Diseases Data Observatory (IDDO)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/iddo/
TL;DR: An Oxford data platform that pooled the noma evidence and called for standardised reporting and better surveillance.
Summary: IDDO, based at the University of Oxford, builds platforms that pool and standardise clinical data across studies so that evidence can answer questions no single study can. Its noma work with WHO produced a systematic scoping review of the global noma evidence base, which found large gaps in understanding of causation and treatment and called for standardised reporting, increased surveillance and improved early detection. For a disease only recently recognised by WHO, creating a usable evidence base is the first step toward measuring anything.
Sources: IDDO — global action needed to tackle noma <https://www.iddo.org/news/global-action-needed-tackle-noma-disease>; WHO — noma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/noma>

### Innovative Vector Control Consortium (IVCC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/ivcc/
TL;DR: A partnership that develops new insecticides and vector-control products, especially for insecticide-resistant mosquitoes.
Summary: IVCC was created to address the gap left when the agrochemical industry stopped investing in public-health insecticides. It works with industry, academia and programmes to develop new active ingredients, net and indoor-spray formulations, and to get them through regulatory approval and into WHO policy. Its work is a direct response to the resistance crisis and to the fact that the market alone will not supply public-health insecticides.
Sources: IVCC <https://www.ivcc.com/>; WHO — Global vector control response (context) <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Institut Pasteur
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/institut-pasteur/
TL;DR: The Paris-based research foundation whose network of institutes across the world studies parasites, vector-borne disease and immunology.
Summary: Institut Pasteur in Paris is a foundational biomedical research institution and the hub of an international network of Pasteur institutes, several in NTD-endemic countries. Its researchers work on parasite biology, vector-pathogen interactions and immunology, providing the basic science that underpins new diagnostics, drugs and vaccines, and its network gives that work a presence in the countries where the diseases occur.
Sources: Institut Pasteur <https://www.pasteur.fr/en>; WHO — rabies (the vaccine was developed in this network) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>

### Institut Pasteur de Dakar
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/ipd/
TL;DR: A Senegalese reference laboratory that produces vaccines and diagnostics and tracks arboviral and parasitic diseases in West Africa.
Summary: Institut Pasteur de Dakar is a WHO collaborating centre with vaccine manufacturing capacity and a reference laboratory for arboviruses including dengue and chikungunya, as well as malaria and other parasitic diseases. Its position as a producer, not only a researcher, matters: it is one of the few African institutions able to manufacture vaccines and diagnostics regionally, which reduces dependence on global supply chains.
Sources: Institut Pasteur international network (includes Dakar) <https://www.pasteur.fr/en>

### International Coalition for Trachoma Control (ICTC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/ictc/
TL;DR: The coalition coordinating NGOs, researchers and donors behind the global trachoma elimination effort.
