Summary: The International Coalition for Trachoma Control brings together the non-governmental organisations, academic institutions and donors delivering trachoma programmes, and coordinates their work with WHO's elimination goals. Its role is practical: aligning approaches across organisations, publishing gap analyses that estimate what the final push will cost, and advocating for the funding needed to finish. Coalitions like this matter most in the endgame, when the remaining districts are the hardest to reach and no single organisation has the reach to finish alone.
Sources: International Coalition for Trachoma Control <https://www.trachomacoalition.org/>; WHO — trachoma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### International Trachoma Initiative (ITI)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/iti/
TL;DR: The organisation that manages Pfizer's donation of azithromycin and has distributed more than a billion trachoma treatments.
Summary: The International Trachoma Initiative, part of the Task Force for Global Health, has managed Pfizer's donation of azithromycin for trachoma since 1998, allocating and distributing more than one billion treatments and supporting countries to deliver the full SAFE strategy. It is the logistical backbone of the trachoma elimination programme: a donated antibiotic is only useful if someone forecasts demand, orders, ships and accounts for it, and that is ITI's work. Pfizer has extended the donation to 2030, and as countries eliminate trachoma the freed supply is redirected to those still endemic.
Sources: International Trachoma Initiative <https://www.trachoma.org/>; WHO — trachoma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/kemi/
TL;DR: Kenya's national health research institute, running field studies, trials and surveillance on multiple NTDs.
Summary: KEMRI conducts biomedical and operational research across Kenya's infectious disease burden, including schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, leishmaniasis, lymphatic filariasis and dengue. It runs field stations and clinical trial capacity in endemic regions, making it a core partner for multi-country NTD studies and a model of research capacity located where the disease is.
Sources: KEMRI <https://www.kemri.go.ke/>

### Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/lstm/
TL;DR: The research institute that identified a previously unknown bacterium strongly associated with noma.
Summary: Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine is a long-established centre for tropical disease research, and in 2024 its researchers identified a previously unknown bacterium strongly associated with noma and showed that the disease severely disrupts the oral microbiome. The finding is significant because noma has no single known cause and no diagnostic test; a microbial marker could allow recognition before the disease becomes gangrenous. LSTM also works on scabies, snakebite and other diseases in the NTD portfolio.
Sources: LSTM — noma research <https://www.lstmed.ac.uk/>; WHO — noma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/noma>

### London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/lshtm/
TL;DR: A leading academic centre for tropical disease research, epidemiology and NTD programme evaluation.
Summary: LSHTM is one of the world's largest centres of research on infectious diseases of poverty, contributing epidemiological studies, clinical trials, mathematical modelling and health-economics analyses that shape NTD policy. Its researchers work across endemic countries, and its teaching programmes train much of the global NTD workforce.
Sources: LSHTM — neglected tropical diseases research <https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/>

### Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/msf/
TL;DR: The medical humanitarian organisation that runs the world's largest noma surgical programme and treats snakebite, Chagas and leishmaniasis.
Summary: MSF treats neglected diseases where health systems have failed, and its fingerprints are on several of them. In Sokoto, northern Nigeria, it has run the world's largest noma programme since 2014, performing over 1,200 reconstructive operations on more than 800 patients and providing nutrition, physiotherapy and speech therapy alongside surgery. It also runs snakebite treatment and antivenom access projects, Chagas and leishmaniasis programmes in Latin America, and sleeping-sickness work in Central Africa. Because it operates at the point of care, MSF's experience often exposes the gap between what guidelines recommend and what patients can actually receive.
Sources: MSF — noma <https://www.msf.org.uk/issues/noma>; WHO — Ebola disease (context) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/medicines-for-malaria-venture/
TL;DR: A non-profit that develops new antimalarials, including the first new mechanism in decades and child-friendly formulations.
Summary: MMV is a product development partnership created in 1999 to develop antimalarial drugs that the market would not deliver, particularly medicines suitable for children and for a single-dose cure. It has brought forward artemisinin combination therapies including child-friendly dispersible formulations, single-dose tafenoquine with GSK and 60 Degrees, and new candidates acting on non-artemisinin mechanisms such as PfATP4. It is the clearest parallel in malaria to DNDi in the NTD field, and the two collaborate.
Sources: Medicines for Malaria Venture <https://www.mmv.org/>; WHO — Global Malaria Programme <https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme>

### Mycetoma Research Centre (University of Khartoum)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/mrc-khartoum/
TL;DR: The world's leading centre for mycetoma, whose work was disrupted when war broke out in Sudan in 2023.
Summary: The Mycetoma Research Centre at the University of Khartoum has been the global hub for mycetoma for decades — diagnosing and treating patients, training clinicians from other endemic countries, running the world's largest case series, and hosting the first randomised clinical trial for a eumycetoma drug with DNDi and Eisai. When war broke out in Sudan in 2023, its clinics, follow-up and research were paralysed and staff displaced. The loss illustrates how concentrated expertise in a neglected disease can be, and why the field has been trying to build capacity in other parts of the mycetoma belt.
Sources: A balancing act: the pioneering mycetoma trial in Sudan <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371/journal.pntd.0013000>; WHO — mycetoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>

### Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/noguchi/
TL;DR: Ghana's flagship biomedical research institute, contributing to NTD diagnostics and surveillance in West Africa.
Summary: Based at the University of Ghana, the Noguchi Institute conducts research on parasitic and bacterial diseases of West Africa, including Buruli ulcer, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis and yaws. It supports national programmes with laboratory capacity and has been a base for Buruli ulcer research and diagnostic development in the region.
Sources: Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research <https://noguchi.ug.edu.gh/>; WHO — Buruli ulcer (a focus of this institute's work) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/buruli-ulcer>

### Noma Children's Hospital, Sokoto
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/noma-children-hospital/
TL;DR: The hospital in northern Nigeria at the centre of the world's noma surgical and rehabilitation work.
Summary: The Noma Children's Hospital in Sokoto, northern Nigeria, is the largest facility dedicated to noma in the world, treating children in the acute phase and providing reconstructive surgery and rehabilitation to survivors. Nigeria carries the highest burden of noma and led the request for WHO to recognise it as a neglected tropical disease, and the hospital's work with MSF — more than 1,200 operations since 2014 — is the clearest demonstration of what surgical care can achieve and how many more patients need it.
Sources: MSF — our work in Nigeria, including noma surgery in Sokoto <https://www.msf.org/nigeria>; WHO — noma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/noma>

### NTD Support Center (Task Force for Global Health)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/ntd-support-center/
TL;DR: The operational hub that helps national programmes run mass treatment campaigns and disease mapping.
Summary: The NTD Support Center, part of the Task Force for Global Health, supports ministries of health with the practicalities of running NTD programmes: mapping where diseases occur, planning and financing mass administration, supplying donated medicines, and monitoring coverage. Much of the field's delivery capacity runs through this kind of technical-support body rather than through research institutions.
Sources: Task Force for Global Health — NTD Support Center <https://taskforce.org/our-programs/neglected-tropical-diseases/>; WHO — preventive chemotherapy <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (Fiocruz)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/fiocruz/
TL;DR: Brazil's national public health research institution, central to Chagas disease, leishmaniasis and dengue research and manufacturing.
Summary: Fiocruz combines research, public health service and manufacturing. It is a global centre for Chagas disease and Leishmania biology, produces diagnostics, and has developed and tested the Butantan-DV dengue vaccine (with the Butantan Institute). It is also a model of a national institution that both generates evidence and supplies products to its own health system.
Sources: Fiocruz <https://portal.fiocruz.br/en>; PAHO — Chagas disease (a focus of this institute's work) <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chagas-disease>

### Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/paho/
TL;DR: The regional health agency for the Americas, which runs the elimination initiative covering Chagas disease and dengue.
Summary: PAHO is the regional office of WHO for the Americas and the body that coordinates the region's disease-elimination agenda. Its Elimination Initiative targets a set of communicable diseases including Chagas disease, and it has published a monitoring framework and a set of costed 'best buys' for accelerating them. On Chagas disease it coordinates sub-regional control initiatives, supplies nifurtimox to countries free of charge, makes benznidazole available through its Strategic Fund, and co-implements the Unitaid-funded CUIDA Chagas project on congenital transmission. On dengue it issues the regional epidemiological alerts that national programmes respond to.
Sources: PAHO — Chagas disease <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chagas-disease>; PAHO — dengue alerts <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/dengue>

### Pediatric Praziquantel Consortium
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/pediatric-praziquantel-consortium/
TL;DR: The public-private partnership that developed arpraziquantel, the first schistosomiasis treatment designed for preschool-aged children.
Summary: The Pediatric Praziquantel Consortium was formed to solve a specific, long-ignored problem: the standard schistosomiasis drug could not practically be given to children under about six, so the age group with the heaviest infection intensity in many communities went untreated. Its partners — including Merck KGaA, Astellas, the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute and European and African research institutions, with public funding — took arpraziquantel from formulation through clinical trials, a European Medicines Agency positive scientific opinion in 2023 and WHO prequalification in 2024, and supported the implementation study in which the first child was treated in Uganda in 2025.
Sources: Pediatric Praziquantel Consortium <https://www.pediatricpraziquantelconsortium.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Sabin Vaccine Institute
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/sabin-vaccine-institute/
TL;DR: The non-profit that has carried the human hookworm vaccine programme, one of the few attempts at a vaccine for a parasitic worm.
Summary: The Sabin Vaccine Institute is a non-profit vaccine developer whose human hookworm vaccine programme has taken candidate antigens through early clinical trials. A hookworm vaccine matters because deworming treats infection without preventing reinfection, so a vaccine that reduced infection intensity would add something albendazole cannot. The scientific difficulty is that hookworm has evolved to modulate the human immune response, making durable protection hard to induce, and the commercial case is weak. Sabin's work is therefore a test of whether a vaccine for a parasite of poverty can be developed at all through non-profit funding.
Sources: Sabin Vaccine Institute — hookworm <https://www.sabin.org/>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Stop TB Partnership
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/stop-tb-partnership/
TL;DR: A coalition hosted by the UN that coordinates the global response to tuberculosis and runs a pooled drug procurement facility.
Summary: The Stop TB Partnership brings together more than 1,500 organisations to coordinate tuberculosis work, and it operates the Global Drug Facility, which pools procurement of tuberculosis medicines and diagnostics so that countries can buy them at lower prices and more reliably. Its role is both political and practical: it sets targets, publishes progress, and runs the supply chain that makes quality-assured treatment available where resistance is highest.
Sources: Stop TB Partnership <https://www.stoptb.org/>; WHO — Global Programme on Tuberculosis and Lung Health <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health>

### TB Alliance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/tb-alliance/
TL;DR: A non-profit tuberculosis drug developer whose pipeline is being mined for Buruli ulcer — including the telacebec trial.
Summary: TB Alliance is a not-for-profit product development partnership that develops new tuberculosis regimens. Its relevance to NTDs is indirect but important: because Buruli ulcer and leprosy are caused by mycobacteria, drugs developed for tuberculosis can be tested against them. TB Alliance initiated the Phase 2 TREAT-BU trial of telacebec for Buruli ulcer in 2024, after the compound showed exceptional potency against Mycobacterium ulcerans and sterilised the infection in mice after sixteen doses. It is the clearest example of how investment in one disease can deliver candidates for others.
Sources: TB Alliance — telacebec for Buruli ulcer <https://www.tballiance.org/news-new-clinical-trial-examines-use-novel-compound-telacebec-buruli-ulcer-patients/>; WHO — tuberculosis (context) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### TDR (Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/tdr/
TL;DR: A WHO-hosted programme that funds research and builds research capacity in countries where NTDs are endemic.
Summary: TDR is cosponsored by UNICEF, UNDP, the World Bank and WHO. It funds and coordinates research on infectious diseases of poverty — diagnostics, treatment, vector control and implementation — and invests heavily in training researchers and institutions in endemic countries so that research is done where the disease is. It also supports the evidence base behind WHO guidance.
Sources: TDR — research on infectious diseases of poverty <https://tdr.who.int/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### The Carter Center
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/carter-center/
TL;DR: The organisation that has led the Guinea worm eradication campaign since 1986, taking the disease from millions of cases to ten.
Summary: The Carter Center, founded by former U.S. President Jimmy Carter and Rosalynn Carter, has led the global Guinea worm eradication programme since 1986 in partnership with WHO, UNICEF, CDC and national ministries of health. The campaign has reduced human cases from an estimated 3.5 million a year to ten in 2025 — the lowest ever recorded — without a drug or a vaccine, using safe water, case containment and surveillance. It also works on river blindness, trachoma and lymphatic filariasis, and it is the model of what a sustained, single-minded eradication effort looks like over four decades.
Sources: The Carter Center — Guinea worm disease <https://www.cartercenter.org/programs/guinea-worm/>; WHO — dracunculiasis (guinea-worm disease) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dracunculiasis-(guinea-worm-disease)>

### The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/the-global-fund/
TL;DR: The largest funder of tuberculosis and malaria programmes, and the reason treatment reached scale after 2002.
Summary: The Global Fund is a financing mechanism that pools donor money and disburses it to country programmes fighting HIV, tuberculosis and malaria. Since 2002 it has disbursed tens of billions of dollars, and it is the single largest external funder of tuberculosis and malaria programmes — the reason that diagnosis, treatment and prevention reached the scale they did in the 2000s. It also runs the procurement platforms through which many countries buy antimalarials, tuberculosis medicines and nets. Its funding cycles shape what is possible in the field, and when its replenishment falls short, programmes contract.
Sources: The Global Fund <https://www.theglobalfund.org/en/>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Unitaid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/unitaid/
TL;DR: A global health funder that accelerates access to new tests and treatments, including the CUIDA Chagas project on mother-to-child transmission.
Summary: Unitaid is an international organisation hosted by WHO that invests in introducing new health products and approaches in low- and middle-income countries, with a mandate to make them affordable and available quickly. In Chagas disease it funds CUIDA Chagas, implemented with PAHO in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia and Paraguay, which is testing simpler ways to screen pregnant women and treat newborns in order to eliminate congenital transmission. Unitaid's role is characteristic: it does not discover products, it buys down the gap between a product existing and people receiving it.
Sources: Unitaid — CUIDA Chagas <https://unitaid.org/project/new-treatments-and-diagnostics-to-prevent-chagas-transmission-from-mother-to-child/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Uniting to Combat Neglected Tropical Diseases
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/uniting-ntds/
TL;DR: An advocacy coalition that holds governments, donors and drug companies to the NTD commitments they have made.
Summary: Uniting to Combat NTDs coordinates advocacy and accountability around the London Declaration and the WHO NTD roadmap. It publishes the scorecards and progress reports that track whether pledges — of donated drugs, of funding, of domestic investment — are actually being met. Its role is political and reputational pressure, which matters in a field where the science is often ahead of the delivery.
Sources: Uniting to Combat NTDs <https://unitingtocombatntds.org/>; WHO — NTD road map and targets <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/cdc/
TL;DR: The US public health agency that supplies technical expertise, reference diagnostics and field support to NTD programmes worldwide.
Summary: CDC's parasitic disease division provides reference laboratory services, technical assistance, outbreak investigation and field epidemiological support for NTDs, and maintains widely used guidance for diagnosis and treatment. It also runs domestic surveillance for parasitic infections and plays a central role in the guinea worm eradication programme and in Chagas disease screening in the United States.
Sources: CDC — parasitic diseases <https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/>

### Wellcome Trust
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/wellcome/
TL;DR: A major biomedical research funder that supports NTD science, from basic parasite biology to clinical trials and public engagement.
Summary: Wellcome funds infectious-disease research with a long horizon, including parasite biology, immunology, diagnostics and drug discovery relevant to NTDs, in the UK and in endemic countries through its international programmes. Its emphasis on open research and on supporting scientists where the disease is endemic complements the operational work that other funders support.
Sources: Wellcome — infectious disease research <https://wellcome.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### World Health Organization (WHO)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/who/
TL;DR: The UN health agency that sets the NTD list, the treatment guidelines and the elimination targets every programme works to.
Summary: WHO's Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases coordinates the global strategy: it publishes the 2021–2030 NTD roadmap with its elimination and eradication targets, maintains the preventive chemotherapy guidance, sets diagnostic and treatment recommendations, prequalifies medicines and diagnostics, and grants the donation programmes their framework. When a programme says 'elimination', it usually means a threshold WHO defined.
Sources: WHO — Control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; WHO — neglected tropical diseases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/neglected-tropical-diseases>

### World Mosquito Program
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/world-mosquito-program/
TL;DR: The organisation that releases Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes and has protected over 16 million people across fifteen countries.
Summary: The World Mosquito Program, based at Monash University, developed and scales the Wolbachia method: infecting Aedes aegypti with a bacterium that blocks dengue, chikungunya and Zika transmission, and releasing them so the trait spreads through the wild population and persists. Its evidence runs from a gold-standard randomised trial in Yogyakarta to city-scale deployments in Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia and beyond. By its 2025 review it reported 16.1 million people protected across fifteen countries, around 1.5 million dengue cases prevented and US$455 million in avoided healthcare costs, with new deployments beginning in Peru and Timor-Leste.
Sources: World Mosquito Program <https://www.worldmosquitoprogram.org/>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/woah/
TL;DR: The intergovernmental body for animal health, which is central to controlling the NTDs that live in animals.
Summary: WOAH — founded as the OIE and renamed in 2022 — sets international standards for animal health and works with WHO and FAO under the One Health banner. It matters for echinococcosis, rabies, taeniasis/cysticercosis and the foodborne trematodiases, all of which cycle through animals and cannot be controlled by human medicine alone. Its standards on dog vaccination, livestock slaughter hygiene and veterinary drug use are what make a One Health programme operational rather than aspirational — and its role in veterinary anthelmintic stewardship is directly relevant to the triclabendazole resistance problem.
Sources: World Organisation for Animal Health <https://www.woah.org/>

### ZeroNoma initiative
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/institutions/zero-noma/
TL;DR: A Nigerian-led initiative campaigning for the early detection and elimination of noma.
Summary: The ZeroNoma initiative works to put noma on the agenda in Nigeria and beyond, campaigning for early detection, training health workers to recognise the disease in its treatable stage, and linking families to surgery. It marks World NTD Day and works with WHO's new NTD framework for noma. Its importance is that noma's solution is largely operational — recognition, antibiotics and referral — so advocacy that raises awareness among primary health workers and communities is itself an intervention.
Sources: WHO — noma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/noma>; WHO — noma <https://www.who.int/health-topics/noma>


## Countries

### Angola
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/angola/
TL;DR: A country where guinea worm persists in dogs, alongside onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis and a heavy rabies burden.
Summary: Angola is one of the countries still reporting guinea worm infections, predominantly in dogs, which keeps it in the small group standing between the world and eradication. It also carries onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, lymphatic filariasis, soil-transmitted helminths, leprosy and a substantial rabies burden from dog bites. Its health system is recovering from decades of conflict, and much of its NTD work depends on partnership support.
Sources: WHO — Angola <https://www.who.int/countries/ago>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/angola>

### Bangladesh
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/bangladesh/
TL;DR: The first country in the world validated for eliminating visceral leishmaniasis, and a pioneer of dengue and cholera research.
Summary: Bangladesh was the first country in the world to be validated as having eliminated visceral leishmaniasis as a public health problem, in 2023, capping a two-decade regional effort built on rapid diagnostic testing and single-dose liposomal amphotericin B. It has also eliminated lymphatic filariasis and trachoma. Dengue is a growing problem, and icddr,b in Dhaka is one of the world's leading institutions for enteric and arboviral research.
Sources: WHO — Bangladesh <https://www.who.int/countries/bgd>; WHO — leishmaniasis (visceral leishmaniasis was eliminated here) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Bolivia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/bolivia/
TL;DR: A country at the centre of Chagas disease, and the setting for long-running fascioliasis work on the Altiplano.
Summary: Bolivia has the highest Chagas disease prevalence in the world and is one of the countries where congenital transmission is the focus of elimination efforts, including through the Unitaid-funded CUIDA Chagas project. Cutaneous and mucosal leishmaniasis are endemic in the lowlands, and the Altiplano has been one of the most important settings for human fascioliasis research and for the triclabendazole treatment failures that now worry the field.
Sources: WHO — Bolivia (Plurinational State of) <https://www.who.int/countries/bol>; Unitaid — CUIDA Chagas (implemented here) <https://unitaid.org/project/new-treatments-and-diagnostics-to-prevent-chagas-transmission-from-mother-to-child/>

### Botswana
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/botswana/
TL;DR: A southern African country whose main infectious-disease burden is tuberculosis and HIV, with a strong national research and public health record.
Summary: Botswana's burden is dominated by HIV and tuberculosis rather than by the classical neglected tropical diseases, and it has run one of Africa's most effective antiretroviral programmes. It appears in this corpus mainly through the people it has produced in global health — including a WHO Regional Director for Africa and a former UNAIDS regional director — and as an example of a country whose health system is strong enough to run its own research. Schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths occur in the north, particularly around the Okavango and Chobe river systems.
Sources: WHO Regional Office for Africa — Botswana country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/botswana>; WHO — Botswana country page <https://www.who.int/countries/bwa>

### Brazil
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/brazil/
TL;DR: The country that eliminated lymphatic filariasis, developed a single-dose dengue vaccine, and carries most of the Americas' Chagas and leishmaniasis burden.
Summary: Brazil is the most consequential NTD country in the Americas. It was validated as having eliminated lymphatic filariasis as a public health problem in 2024, it has the region's largest Chagas disease burden alongside leishmaniasis in its many forms, and it developed and approved Butantan-DV, the world's first single-dose dengue vaccine. Leprosy remains a large burden, and schistosomiasis is endemic in the northeast. Its public research and manufacturing institutions — Fiocruz and Butantan — are among the few in the world that combine research, development and production for neglected diseases.
Sources: WHO — Brazil <https://www.who.int/countries/bra>; PAHO — Chagas disease (the region's largest burden) <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chagas-disease>

### Cameroon
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/cameroon/
TL;DR: A Central African country where dog infections have made guinea worm harder to finish, and a centre of onchocerciasis and filariasis.
Summary: Cameroon has become the most important country for guinea worm animal infections, reporting the largest number of infected dogs in recent years after a lapse in surveillance allowed transmission to be re-established from across the Chad border. It also carries a heavy burden of onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths and trachoma, and it was one of the countries where large-scale total community treatment for yaws was implemented.
Sources: WHO — Cameroon <https://www.who.int/countries/cmr>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/cameroon>

### Chad
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/chad/
TL;DR: The epicentre of guinea worm animal infections, where the parasite appears to use fish and frogs as paratenic hosts.
Summary: Chad is the country where guinea worm eradication has become hardest to finish. It reports the largest number of human cases of any country and, until recently, the largest animal burden; infections have been linked to fish and frogs acting as paratenic hosts, which breaks the assumption that transmission runs only through drinking water. It has also made genuine progress, with animal infections falling for six consecutive years. The country carries schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths and trachoma as well.
Sources: WHO — Chad <https://www.who.int/countries/tcd>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/chad>

### Democratic Republic of the Congo
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/dr-congo/
TL;DR: The last great stronghold of sleeping sickness and a centre of onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis and schistosomiasis.
Summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo reports more than half of all human African trypanosomiasis cases in Africa — 330 of roughly 600 in 2024 — which makes its national programme the decisive one for eliminating the disease. It also carries a heavy burden of onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, leprosy and rabies. Its size, weak road network and areas of conflict make delivery and surveillance exceptionally difficult, and it was the first country to register acoziborole after its European approval, a signal of how central it is to the endgame.
Sources: WHO — Democratic Republic of the Congo <https://www.who.int/countries/cod>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/democratic-republic-congo>

### Ethiopia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/ethiopia/
TL;DR: A high-burden country across almost the whole NTD list, and the site of the world's first large-scale snakebite and podoconiosis work.
Summary: Ethiopia has one of the broadest NTD portfolios in Africa: soil-transmitted helminths and schistosomiasis at huge scale, trachoma and lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, visceral leishmaniasis in the lowlands, and rabies and snakebite. It is also one of the countries where guinea worm still appears, with dog, cat and baboon infections complicating the final push. Its research institutions and field programmes are among the strongest on the continent, which is why it is a trial site for several new treatments.
Sources: WHO — Ethiopia <https://www.who.int/countries/eth>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/ethiopia>

### Ghana
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/ghana/
TL;DR: A West African country that has eliminated trachoma and runs strong Buruli ulcer, yaws and filariasis programmes.
Summary: Ghana has eliminated trachoma as a public health problem and is working toward elimination of lymphatic filariasis and yaws. It carries onchocerciasis and schistosomiasis, and it is one of the most important countries for Buruli ulcer research and treatment, with the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research providing laboratory capacity and field support for West Africa.
Sources: WHO — Ghana <https://www.who.int/countries/gha>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/ghana>

### Guinea
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/guinea/
TL;DR: A West African country that eliminated sleeping sickness as a public health problem in 2025 and helped test the single-dose cure.
Summary: Guinea was validated by WHO in January 2025 as having eliminated human African trypanosomiasis as a public health problem, one of only four countries to have reached that status, and it was one of the settings where acoziborole was clinically tested. The achievement is notable because Guinea's health system was devastated by the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic, which killed health workers and eroded trust in clinics — and it rebuilt enough surveillance and case-finding capacity to drive a parasitic disease to elimination within a decade. The country also carries onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths.
Sources: WHO — Guinea eliminates human African trypanosomiasis as a public health problem <https://www.who.int/news/item/29-01-2025-guinea-eliminates-human-african-trypanosomiasis-as-a-public-health-problem>; WHO — Guinea country page <https://www.who.int/countries/gin>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/guinea>

### India
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/india/
TL;DR: The world's largest leprosy and lymphatic filariasis burden, and the country that has driven kala-azar and trachoma to elimination.
Summary: India accounts for the largest single share of global leprosy and lymphatic filariasis, and it has been the site of some of the field's biggest successes: visceral leishmaniasis has been driven to the elimination threshold across the endemic districts of Bihar and neighbouring states, and trachoma has been eliminated and validated. It also carries substantial soil-transmitted helminth, schistosomiasis-adjacent and dengue burden, and a very large snakebite burden concentrated in rural agricultural communities.
Sources: WHO — India <https://www.who.int/countries/ind>; WHO — leprosy (the disease this country leads on) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Indonesia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/indonesia/
TL;DR: The country with the third-largest leprosy burden, and a vast archipelago where lymphatic filariasis and dengue are endemic.
Summary: Indonesia reports more than 10,000 new leprosy cases a year — one of only three countries to do so — and faces lymphatic filariasis, soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis in a single valley in Sulawesi, dengue and yaws. Its geography, with thousands of inhabited islands, makes elimination programmes logistically formidable, and it is one of the countries where the Brugia species of filarial worm is important, which is why a Brugia-specific diagnostic was developed.
Sources: WHO — Indonesia <https://www.who.int/countries/idn>; WHO — leprosy (one of three highest-burden countries) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>

### Kenya
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/kenya/
TL;DR: A country that eliminated sleeping sickness as a public health problem in 2025 and leads on vector control research.
Summary: Kenya was validated by WHO in August 2025 as having eliminated human African trypanosomiasis as a public health problem, one of only four countries to have reached that status. It also carries visceral leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, lymphatic filariasis and dengue, and its research and vector-control institutions are central to the East African response. It has used triple-drug therapy to accelerate its lymphatic filariasis programme.
Sources: WHO — Kenya <https://www.who.int/countries/ken>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/kenya>; WHO — Kenya achieves elimination of sleeping sickness as a public health problem <https://www.who.int/news/item/08-08-2025-kenya-achieves-elimination-of-human-african-trypanosomiasis-or-sleeping-sickness>

### Malawi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/malawi/
TL;DR: A southern African country that has eliminated trachoma, lymphatic filariasis and is pressing on with schistosomiasis control.
Summary: Malawi has been one of the most successful southern African countries in NTD elimination, validated for both trachoma and lymphatic filariasis as public health problems. Schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths remain widespread, particularly around Lake Malawi, and the country's community health worker networks are among the strongest in the region — which is why its programmes have performed well even with limited resources.
Sources: WHO — Malawi <https://www.who.int/countries/mwi>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/malawi>

### Mali
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/mali/
TL;DR: A West African country with a broad NTD burden whose research centre has shaped understanding of malaria drug resistance.
Summary: Mali carries malaria, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, onchocerciasis and leprosy, and has a history of guinea worm and human African trypanosomiasis. Its Malaria Research and Training Centre at the University of Bamako has been a leading source of work on malaria parasite genetics and antimalarial drug resistance in Africa, which is the science that makes molecular resistance surveillance possible. Much of the country's NTD work is delivered through donor-supported campaigns in a difficult security environment.
Sources: WHO Regional Office for Africa — Mali country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/mali>; WHO — Mali country page <https://www.who.int/countries/mli>

### Nepal
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/nepal/
TL;DR: A country that has eliminated trachoma and visceral leishmaniasis and is close on lymphatic filariasis, despite difficult terrain.
Summary: Nepal has reached the elimination threshold for trachoma, visceral leishmaniasis and lymphatic filariasis, which is a notable achievement for a country whose mountainous terrain makes delivery hard. Leprosy and soil-transmitted helminths remain, and snakebite envenoming is a significant and under-recognised cause of death in rural agricultural districts.
Sources: WHO — Nepal <https://www.who.int/countries/npl>; WHO — trachoma (eliminated here) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Nigeria
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/nigeria/
TL;DR: The country with the largest NTD burden in Africa, and the one whose programmes shape the continent's elimination prospects.
Summary: Nigeria carries the heaviest concentration of neglected tropical diseases in Africa: lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths and trachoma are all endemic at scale, and it has the world's highest burden of noma and one of the highest of snakebite. With roughly a fifth of Africa's population, its programme performance determines whether continental elimination targets are met. It also has genuine strengths: a national NTD programme that runs mass administration at very large scale, a specialist noma hospital in Sokoto, and research institutions that lead on Buruli ulcer and yaws.
Sources: WHO — Nigeria <https://www.who.int/countries/nga>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/nigeria>

### Papua New Guinea
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/papua-new-guinea/
TL;DR: The country where azithromycin-resistant yaws emerged, threatening the eradication strategy.
Summary: Papua New Guinea has one of the world's largest yaws burdens and is the place where azithromycin-resistant yaws was reported, with evidence of local transmission of resistant strains — the single most serious threat to the global eradication strategy. It also carries lymphatic filariasis, leprosy, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, a heavy burden of snakebite and Buruli ulcer, across terrain and a health system that make delivery very difficult.
Sources: WHO — Papua New Guinea <https://www.who.int/countries/png>; WHO — yaws (resistant strains were first reported here) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Philippines
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/philippines/
TL;DR: An archipelago where schistosomiasis, lymphatic filariasis, leprosy and rabies are all endemic across thousands of islands.
Summary: The Philippines carries schistosomiasis in the Visayas and Mindanao, lymphatic filariasis in many provinces, leprosy and soil-transmitted helminths, and a significant rabies burden addressed through dog vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis. Yaws was historically endemic and is no longer a major problem. Its geography makes uniform coverage difficult and gives its programmes a strongly decentralised character.
Sources: WHO — Philippines <https://www.who.int/countries/phl>; WHO — schistosomiasis (endemic here) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Senegal
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/senegal/
TL;DR: A West African country that has eliminated trachoma, is close on onchocerciasis, and hosts a regional vaccine and diagnostic manufacturer.
Summary: Senegal has eliminated trachoma as a public health problem and is among the countries closing in on onchocerciasis elimination, while continuing to control malaria, schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths. It is also unusual in the region for its manufacturing capacity: the Institut Pasteur de Dakar produces vaccines and diagnostics, which matters for a continent that has historically depended on imported supply. Its research and public health institutions have produced several of the figures in this corpus.
Sources: WHO Regional Office for Africa — Senegal country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/senegal>; WHO — Senegal country page <https://www.who.int/countries/sen>

### South Africa
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/south-africa/
TL;DR: The country with one of the world's heaviest tuberculosis and HIV burdens, and a research system that has shaped the evidence for both.
Summary: South Africa carries a very large share of the global tuberculosis burden, including a substantial share of its drug-resistant cases, and has one of the largest HIV epidemics — a combination that makes tuberculosis the country's leading cause of death and gives its treatment programme global significance. It also has the strongest biomedical research base on the continent, which is why so many of the trials and policy decisions described in this corpus involve South African institutions and researchers. Malaria transmission is limited to the north-east and is a target for elimination.
Sources: WHO Regional Office for Africa — South Africa country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/south-africa>; WHO — South Africa country page <https://www.who.int/countries/zaf>

### South Sudan
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/south-sudan/
TL;DR: One of the last countries with guinea worm, and a place where conflict and flooding make every NTD programme harder.
Summary: South Sudan is one of only three countries still reporting human guinea worm cases, with two in 2025, and it carries a heavy burden of visceral leishmaniasis, onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, trachoma and soil-transmitted helminths. Conflict, displacement and seasonal flooding repeatedly interrupt programmes and move populations through areas where surveillance is absent, which is why it appears in almost every difficult-elimination story in the field.
Sources: WHO — South Sudan <https://www.who.int/countries/ssd>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/south-sudan>

### Sudan
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/sudan/
TL;DR: The world centre of mycetoma and a major visceral leishmaniasis burden, whose health system has been devastated by war.
Summary: Sudan is the country with the greatest burden of mycetoma, home to the Mycetoma Research Centre at the University of Khartoum that was for decades the global hub for the disease. It also carries a large visceral leishmaniasis burden, schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma and snakebite. Since war began in 2023, clinics, research and surveillance have been disrupted, patients displaced, and the first randomised mycetoma trial reported into a country whose health system was collapsing around it.
Sources: WHO — Sudan <https://www.who.int/countries/sdn>; WHO EMRO — Sudan country page <https://www.emro.who.int/countries/sdn/>

### Tanzania
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/tanzania/
TL;DR: A high-burden East African country with strong research capacity on schistosomiasis, filariasis and vector control.
Summary: Tanzania carries lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma and leishmaniasis, and it hosts the Ifakara Health Institute, one of the world's leading centres for vector biology and field trials of vector-control tools. Its research capacity means several of the field's most important trials — from net technologies to drug combinations — have been run here, and it is a site for the eWHORM basket trial of oxfendazole.
Sources: WHO — United Republic of Tanzania <https://www.who.int/countries/tza>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/united-republic-tanzania>

### Uganda
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/uganda/
TL;DR: The only country with both forms of sleeping sickness, and the first to treat a child with the new paediatric schistosomiasis medicine.
Summary: Uganda is unusual in having both Gambiense and Rhodesiense sleeping sickness, which makes its national programme a test of two different control problems at once. It also carries schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, onchocerciasis, trachoma and rabies, and it was where the first preschool-aged child was treated with arpraziquantel in 2025 — a milestone for the youngest children with schistosomiasis. Its vector-control and vaccine trials, including TSOL18 pig vaccination for cysticercosis, have shaped practice well beyond its borders.
Sources: WHO — Uganda <https://www.who.int/countries/uga>; WHO Regional Office for Africa — country page <https://www.afro.who.int/countries/uganda>

### Yemen
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/countries/yemen/
TL;DR: A country at war that has nonetheless eliminated lymphatic filariasis and trachoma, while fighting leishmaniasis and dengue.
Summary: Yemen has eliminated lymphatic filariasis and trachoma as public health problems despite a devastating conflict, which says as much about the resilience of its health workers as about the interventions. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a major burden — the conflict has produced large outbreaks in displacement settings — and dengue and soil-transmitted helminths are widespread. It is one of the clearest examples of a country achieving elimination targets while its health system is under extreme strain.
Sources: WHO — Yemen <https://www.who.int/countries/yem>; WHO EMRO — Yemen country page <https://www.emro.who.int/countries/yem/>


## People

### Aaron Motsoaledi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/aaron-motsoaledi/
TL;DR: The South African physician and health minister whose tenure shaped the country's TB and HIV treatment scale-up.
Summary: Aaron Motsoaledi is a South African physician who served as Minister of Health from 2009 to 2019 and returned to the post in 2024, a period covering South Africa's large tuberculosis and HIV treatment programmes. He is also a former chair of the Stop TB Partnership's board. The relevance to this corpus is that the countries with the largest tuberculosis burdens are governed by health ministries whose choices about diagnosis, treatment and drug procurement determine whether resistance is contained.
Sources: Wikipedia — Aaron Motsoaledi <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Motsoaledi>

### Abdoulaye Djimdé
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/abdoulaye-djimde/
TL;DR: The Malian scientist whose work on malaria parasite genetics underpins how the world tracks drug resistance.
Summary: Abdoulaye Djimdé is a Malian molecular biologist at the University of Bamako's Malaria Research and Training Centre who has worked on the genetics of antimalarial drug resistance and on malaria genomics in Africa. Understanding how resistance mutations arise, spread and can be detected is what makes molecular surveillance possible, and it is the same logic applied to artemisinin resistance and to the kelch13 marker used in the field today.
Sources: Wikipedia — Abdoulaye Djimdé <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdoulaye_Djimd%C3%A9>

### Adetokunbo Lucas
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/adetokunbo-lucas/
TL;DR: The Nigerian physician and parasitologist who built the international research programme behind tropical disease control.
Summary: Adetokunbo Oluwole Lucas was a Nigerian physician and parasitologist who directed the WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR) and held chairs in tropical public health at Ibadan and Harvard. TDR is the programme that funded much of the research and built much of the research capacity that NTD control now rests on, and its founding generation — including Lucas — created the position that research on diseases of poverty should be done in the countries where they occur.
Sources: Wikipedia — Adetokunbo Lucas <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adetokunbo_Lucas>; TDR — the programme he directed <https://tdr.who.int/>

### Ahmed Hassan Fahal
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/ahmed-fahal/
TL;DR: The Sudanese surgeon who built the Mycetoma Research Centre and made a neglected disease visible to the world.
Summary: Ahmed Hassan Fahal is a Professor of Surgery at the University of Khartoum and the founding Director of the Mycetoma Research Centre, which he established in the early 1990s and built into the world's leading centre for the disease — treating patients, training clinicians across the mycetoma belt, running the largest case series, and hosting the first randomised clinical trial of a eumycetoma drug. He also directs the Sudanese national mycetoma control programme. Recognition of mycetoma as a neglected tropical disease in 2016 owed much to the case he and his colleagues assembled from a single hospital in Khartoum, and the war that began in 2023 has devastated the institution he built.
Sources: Professor Ahmed Hassan Fahal — about <https://www.ahmedfahal.net/index.php/about>

### Awa Marie Coll-Seck
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/awa-marie-coll-seck/
TL;DR: The Senegalese physician who led the global malaria partnership and her country's health ministry.
Summary: Awa Marie Coll-Seck is a Senegalese physician and former Minister of Health of Senegal who served as Executive Director of the Roll Back Malaria Partnership, the coordinating body for the global malaria response, and later as a United Nations Assistant Secretary-General. She represents the coordination layer that determines whether the tools described in this corpus — nets, diagnostics, combination therapy, and now vaccines — reach the populations that need them.
Sources: Wikipedia — Awa Marie Coll-Seck <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awa_Marie_Coll-Seck>

### Bongani Mayosi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/bongani-mayosi/
TL;DR: The South African cardiologist whose research on rheumatic heart disease and cardiomyopathy defined the African burden.
Summary: Bongani Mawethu Mayosi (1967–2018) was a South African cardiologist and dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences at the University of Cape Town who worked on rheumatic heart disease, tuberculous pericarditis and cardiomyopathy in Africa. Rheumatic heart disease is the long-term consequence of the streptococcal skin infection that follows scabies — which makes his work part of the downstream case for treating scabies as a serious disease rather than a nuisance.
Sources: Wikipedia — Bongani Mayosi <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongani_Mayosi>

### Carlos Chagas
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/carlos-chagas/
TL;DR: The Brazilian physician who discovered the parasite, the insect vector and the human disease that now bear his name.
Summary: In a single body of work between 1907 and 1909, Carlos Chagas described Trypanosoma cruzi in the gut of triatomine bugs, identified the parasite in a child, and established the disease as a distinct clinical entity — an achievement with few parallels in medical history, since it is rare for one investigator to identify a pathogen, its vector and the disease it causes. The condition he described still affects millions of people across Latin America and has no safe, short, reliably curative treatment.
Sources: PAHO — Chagas disease <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chagas-disease>

### Chikwe Ihekweazu
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/chikwe-ihekweazu/
TL;DR: The Nigerian epidemiologist who built the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control into a functioning outbreak agency.
Summary: Chikwe Ihekweazu is a Nigerian epidemiologist and the founding Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control, which he built into an institution capable of detecting and responding to outbreaks — Lassa fever, cholera, mpox and COVID-19 among them. He later joined WHO as Assistant Director-General for Health Emergency Intelligence. The capability he represents is exactly the bottleneck this corpus describes: outbreaks and elimination programmes both depend on a national agency that can test, count and respond.
Sources: Wikipedia — Chikwe Ihekweazu <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chikwe_Ihekweazu>

### David Molyneux
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/david-molyneux/
TL;DR: A long-standing figure in the neglected tropical diseases field who helped build the case for treating them as a single, fundable group.
Summary: David Molyneux spent much of his career at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, which he directed, and has been one of the most persistent advocates for treating neglected tropical diseases as a coherent group rather than a scatter of unprofitably obscure infections. That framing — adopted by WHO and by donors — is the reason a single mass treatment campaign can now address several diseases at once, and it underpins the push for integrated delivery that most programmes rely on.
Sources: Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine — Professor David Molyneux <https://www.lstmed.ac.uk/about/people/professor-david-molyneux>

### Donald Hopkins
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/donald-hopkins/
TL;DR: The Carter Center leader who built the scientific and operational case that Guinea worm could be eradicated without a drug or a vaccine.
Summary: Donald Hopkins led health programmes at the Carter Center for decades and was central to the strategy that made Guinea worm eradication credible: water treatment, cloth filters, case containment, reporting rewards and relentless surveillance, none of which depended on a new medicine. He also worked on smallpox eradication earlier in his career, which makes him one of the few people to have worked on two eradication programmes. Eradication of a disease without a vaccine or a drug is a claim that rests on the architecture he and his colleagues built.
Sources: The Carter Center — Guinea worm disease <https://www.cartercenter.org/programs/guinea-worm/>

### Erick Mwamba Miaka
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/erick-miaka/
TL;DR: The Congolese physician who directs the national programme for the country that reports more than half of Africa's sleeping sickness.
Summary: Erick Mwamba Miaka directs the Democratic Republic of the Congo's national human African trypanosomiasis control programme, which carries the largest share of the world's remaining sleeping sickness burden — 330 of roughly 600 cases across Africa in 2024. That position makes the DRC programme the decisive one for eliminating the disease, and it is why the country's registration of acoziborole in June 2026 mattered so much: a single-dose oral cure becomes usable at scale first where the cases are. His programme combines active case-finding with tsetse control under conditions of conflict and weak infrastructure that make both difficult.
Sources: DNDi — DRC approves acoziborole (statement by Dr Miaka) <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2026/drc-approves-use-acoziborole-breakthrough-one-day-oral-treatment-against-sleeping-sickness/>

### Gerhard Armauer Hansen
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/armauer-hansen/
TL;DR: The Norwegian physician who identified the bacterium that causes leprosy in 1873 — the first pathogen shown to cause human disease.
Summary: Armauer Hansen identified Mycobacterium leprae in 1873, at a time when leprosy was widely attributed to heredity or moral failing. The finding was the first demonstration that a bacterium causes a human disease, and it reframed leprosy as an infectious condition that could in principle be treated — though that took another century. Hansen's later attempt to transmit the disease by inoculating a patient cost him his post, and the disease is still often called Hansen's disease in an effort to reduce the stigma attached to the word leprosy.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>

### Glenda Gray
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/glenda-gray/
TL;DR: The South African vaccinologist who led HIV vaccine research and then Africa's COVID-19 vaccine trials.
Summary: Glenda Gray is a South African paediatrician and vaccinologist, former president of the South African Medical Research Council and head of the HIV Vaccine Trials Network's Africa programme. She was among the first to raise the alarm about mother-to-child HIV transmission, led vaccine trials in South African communities, and directed the country's COVID-19 vaccine trials. Africa's ability to run its own vaccine trials is a precondition for the vaccines this corpus depends on being tested where the diseases are.
Sources: Wikipedia — Glenda Gray <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Gray>

### Hoosen Coovadia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/hoosen-coovadia/
TL;DR: The South African paediatrician whose research on mother-to-child HIV transmission changed global prevention policy.
Summary: Hoosen Mahomed Coovadia (1940–2023) was a South African paediatrician and researcher at the University of KwaZulu-Natal whose work established how HIV is transmitted from mother to child and how to prevent it, contributing directly to the global policy of preventing vertical transmission. His career is also a record of research conducted under apartheid and of building a medical school in Durban, and of the principle that African populations must be studied rather than extrapolated to.
Sources: Wikipedia — Hoosen Coovadia <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoosen_Coovadia>

### Ibrahima Socé Fall
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/ibrahima-soce-fall/
TL;DR: The Senegalese epidemiologist who directs the WHO programme responsible for the world's neglected tropical disease strategy.
Summary: Ibrahima Socé Fall is a Senegalese epidemiologist who has led the World Health Organization's Global Programme on Neglected Tropical Diseases, having previously directed WHO's health emergencies work in Africa. In this role he oversees the 2021–2030 NTD road map and its elimination and eradication targets — the framework almost every programme in this corpus works to — and the technical support WHO gives to national programmes. He is the counterpart, in the current period, to Mwele Malecela's tenure.
Sources: Wikipedia — Ibrahima Socé Fall <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahima_Soc%C3%A9_Fall>; WHO — the NTD programme he directs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Jean Kaseya
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/jean-kaseya/
TL;DR: The Congolese public health leader who directs Africa CDC, the continent's own agency for disease surveillance and laboratory networks.
Summary: Jean Kaseya is a Congolese medical doctor and public health specialist who became Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in 2023, succeeding its founding director John Nkengasong. Africa CDC works on surveillance, laboratory networks and emergency response across the continent — the same infrastructure that NTD programmes depend on for case-finding, confirmation and elimination verification. Its emphasis on regional laboratory capacity is directly relevant to one of the field's persistent bottlenecks: the shortage of diagnostic and sequencing capacity where the diseases actually occur.
Sources: Wikipedia — Jean Kaseya <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Kaseya>

### Jean-Jacques Muyembe-Tamfum
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/jean-jacques-muyembe/
TL;DR: The Congolese virologist who identified Ebola virus in 1976, and whose work led to one of the first effective Ebola treatments.
Summary: Jean-Jacques Muyembe-Tamfum was part of the team that investigated the first known Ebola outbreak in 1976 in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and he is credited with identifying the virus. He went on to lead the DRC's National Institute of Biomedical Research and to direct the country's response to successive outbreaks, including the 2018–2020 epidemic. The monoclonal antibody ansuvimab, one of two treatments shown to reduce Ebola mortality, was developed from an antibody isolated from a survivor of the 1995 Kikwit outbreak that he led the response to.
Sources: Wikipedia — Jean-Jacques Muyembe <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Jacques_Muyembe>

### Jimmy Carter
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/jimmy-carter/
TL;DR: The former US president whose Carter Center has led the Guinea Worm Eradication Program since 1986, taking cases from millions to ten.
Summary: Jimmy Carter founded the Carter Center in 1982 and made Guinea worm disease its signature campaign, leading the global eradication programme from 1986 in partnership with WHO, UNICEF, CDC and national ministries of health. Under his leadership the campaign reduced human cases from an estimated 3.5 million a year to ten in 2025 — achieved without a vaccine or a drug, using safe water, case containment and surveillance. He said he wanted to outlast the last Guinea worm, and the disease is now close to being the second human disease ever eradicated.
Sources: The Carter Center — Guinea worm disease <https://www.cartercenter.org/programs/guinea-worm/>

### John Nkengasong
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/john-nkengasong/
TL;DR: The Cameroonian virologist who founded Africa CDC, arguing that Africa needed its own disease surveillance capacity.
Summary: John N. Nkengasong is a Cameroonian-American virologist whose doctoral research was the first to characterise the genetic subtypes of HIV in Africa, and who went on to found and lead the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention as its inaugural director from 2016 to 2022. He has been a persistent advocate for African-owned laboratory and surveillance systems — the argument that the continent should be able to diagnose and track its own outbreaks rather than sending samples abroad. That capability is precisely what NTD elimination verification requires, and the same argument now underpins calls for regional genomic surveillance and manufacturing.
Sources: Wikipedia — John Nkengasong <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Nkengasong>

### Louis Pasteur
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/louis-pasteur/
TL;DR: The French chemist whose 1885 post-exposure vaccination saved a boy bitten by a rabid dog, founding modern rabies prevention.
Summary: Louis Pasteur developed the first rabies vaccine, and in 1885 he used it after a bite — a post-exposure intervention that had never been attempted in a person. The patient survived, and the approach became the basis of rabies prevention worldwide: vaccinate before the virus reaches the central nervous system. Rabies is still incurable once symptoms begin, so Pasteur's intervention remains the entire strategy more than a century later; what has changed is that it is now highly effective and almost universally available in wealthy countries, and still out of reach for many of the people who need it.
Sources: Institut Pasteur — international network <https://www.pasteur.fr/en>

### Malegapuru Makgoba
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/malegapuru-makgoba/
TL;DR: The South African immunologist who led the country's medical research council and its scientific response to HIV denialism.
Summary: Malegapuru William Makgoba is a South African immunologist, former president of the South African Medical Research Council and former vice-chancellor of the University of KwaZulu-Natal. He was among the scientists who publicly opposed the South African government's HIV denialism in the 2000s, at a cost to his own position — a reminder that the biggest obstacle to a disease programme is sometimes policy rather than science, which is a recurring theme in this corpus.
Sources: Wikipedia — Malegapuru Makgoba <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malegapuru_Makgoba>

### Mamadou Camara
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/mamadou-camara/
TL;DR: The Guinean coordinator whose national programme helped test acoziborole and is now preparing to use it.
Summary: Mamadou Camara coordinates Guinea's national human African trypanosomiasis control programme, one of the countries where acoziborole was clinically tested. Guinea reached elimination of sleeping sickness as a public health problem and was validated by WHO in January 2025, which makes its programme one of the four to have achieved that status. Its experience is directly relevant to the rest of the region: a country with a small remaining burden that has to keep looking, using a treatment simple enough to be given where the last cases occur.
Sources: DNDi — DRC approves acoziborole (statement by Mamadou Camara) <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2026/drc-approves-use-acoziborole-breakthrough-one-day-oral-treatment-against-sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — Guinea eliminates human African trypanosomiasis as a public health problem <https://www.who.int/news/item/29-01-2025-guinea-eliminates-human-african-trypanosomiasis-as-a-public-health-problem>

### Marshall Lightowlers
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/marshall-lightowlers/
TL;DR: The University of Melbourne veterinary scientist who developed the pig vaccine that breaks the Taenia solium cycle.
Summary: Marshall Lightowlers, a professor at the University of Melbourne, developed TSOL18, the recombinant vaccine against Taenia solium in pigs. It is the first licensed vaccine against porcine cysticercosis and, in combination with oxfendazole, has been shown to eliminate transmission by pigs — which removes the step that creates the human tapeworm carriers who contaminate the environment with the eggs that cause neurocysticercosis. It is one of the clearest cases in the NTD field of a human brain disease being controlled by a veterinary vaccine.
Sources: GALVmed — first licensed vaccine against porcine cysticercosis <https://www.galvmed.org/news/first-ever-licenced-vaccine-major-cause-epilepsy-developing-world/>; TSOL18 vaccine and oxfendazole for control of Taenia solium (PLOS NTD) <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371/journal.pntd.0008785>

### Matshidiso Moeti
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/matshidiso-moeti/
TL;DR: The Botswanan physician who led WHO's Africa region for a decade, covering the NTD programmes of 47 countries.
Summary: Matshidiso Rebecca Natalie Moeti is a Botswanan physician and public health specialist who served as WHO Regional Director for Africa from February 2015 to February 2025 — the first woman to hold the post. The regional office she led oversees the NTD programmes of 47 member states, which is where most of the world's neglected tropical disease burden sits, and its technical support is a large part of why countries in the region have been able to reach elimination thresholds for lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, sleeping sickness and onchocerciasis. She was succeeded in 2025 by Mohamed Yakub Janabi of Tanzania.
Sources: Wikipedia — Matshidiso Moeti <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matshidiso_Moeti>

### Miriam Were
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/miriam-were/
TL;DR: The Kenyan public health physician who turned community health work into national policy.
Summary: Miriam Khamadi Were is a Kenyan public health physician and former professor of community health at the University of Nairobi who built the case for community-based health care as national policy and chaired the Global Fund's technical evaluation reference group. Community health workers are the delivery mechanism for nearly every intervention in this corpus, and her work is the reason that model exists as policy rather than as a project.
Sources: Wikipedia — Miriam Were <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miriam_Were>

### Mohamed Yakub Janabi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/mohamed-janabi/
TL;DR: The Tanzanian who took over WHO's Africa region in 2025, inheriting the NTD elimination targets for the continent.
Summary: Mohamed Yakub Janabi of Tanzania was elected WHO Regional Director for Africa in 2025, succeeding Matshidiso Moeti. The office is responsible for the technical support behind the continent's NTD programmes, and he inherits the 2030 targets for eliminating lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, onchocerciasis and sleeping sickness across the region — with the remaining high-burden countries, Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of the Congo among them, determining whether those targets are met.
Sources: Wikipedia — Mohamed Yakub Janabi <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Yakub_Janabi>

### Moses Kamya
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/moses-kamya/
TL;DR: The Ugandan physician-researcher behind a long series of malaria and HIV trials run in African communities.
Summary: Moses Robert Kamya is a Ugandan physician and infectious-disease researcher at Makerere University, associated with the Infectious Diseases Research Collaboration, and has led clinical trials of malaria treatment, prevention and vector control in Uganda. Trials run in the communities where transmission actually happens are what generate evidence that transfers — the reason Uganda features repeatedly in malaria and HIV research and in the trials that change guidelines.
Sources: Wikipedia — Moses Kamya <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Kamya>

### Muhammad Ali Pate
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/muhammad-ali-pate/
TL;DR: The Nigerian physician who has led health policy at national, Global Fund and global levels, including NTD and immunisation financing.
Summary: Muhammad Ali Pate is a Nigerian physician and former Minister of State for Health who went on to lead Big Win Philanthropy and to chair the Global Fund board, and who returned as Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health. His relevance here is financing and delivery: the decisions that determine whether money reaches NTD, malaria and immunisation programmes in the country with one of the world's largest burdens are made at this level, and Nigeria's performance shapes whether continental elimination targets are met.
Sources: Wikipedia — Muhammad Ali Pate <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Pate>

### Mwele Ntuli Malecela
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/mwele-malecela/
TL;DR: The Tanzanian scientist who directed WHO's neglected tropical diseases department and pushed the field toward elimination targets.
Summary: Mwele Ntuli Malecela was Director of the World Health Organization's Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases from 2018 until her death in February 2022. A Tanzanian researcher by background, she had earlier led Tanzania's national institute for medical research and the country's lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis programmes. Her tenure at WHO coincided with the development of the 2021–2030 NTD road map, with its explicit elimination and eradication targets, and she was widely recognised as a champion for women and girls within the field. A mentorship programme for women in NTDs was named in her memory.
Sources: WHO — mourning Dr Mwelecele Ntuli Malecela <https://www.who.int/news/item/11-02-2022-who-mourns-dr-mwelecele-ntuli-malecela>; Uniting to Combat NTDs — tribute <https://unitingtocombatntds.org/en/news-and-views/tribute-dr-mwele-ntuli-malecela/>

### Quarraisha Abdool Karim
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/quarraisha-abdool-karim/
TL;DR: The South African epidemiologist who established how HIV spreads among young women in Africa and how to prevent it.
Summary: Quarraisha Abdool Karim is a South African epidemiologist and associate scientific director of CAPRISA whose research described why young women in southern Africa carry a disproportionate share of HIV infection, and tested prevention approaches tailored to that. Her work is a model for the gendered epidemiology that NTD programmes have been slower to adopt — establishing who is actually at risk, and why, before deciding what to do.
Sources: Wikipedia — Quarraisha Abdool Karim <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarraisha_Abdool_Karim>

### Rose Leke
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/rose-leke/
TL;DR: The Cameroonian immunologist and malaria researcher who has shaped African research capacity and vaccine policy.
Summary: Rose Gana Fomban Leke is a Cameroonian immunologist and parasitologist at the University of Yaoundé I who has worked on malaria, particularly in pregnancy, and on the immunology of infectious disease in African populations. She has been central to building African research institutions and to the committees that make vaccine and immunisation policy for the continent — the kind of institutional work that determines whether a tool developed elsewhere is actually used where the burden is.
Sources: Wikipedia — Rose Leke <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Leke>

### Salim Abdool Karim
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/salim-abdool-karim/
TL;DR: The South African epidemiologist whose HIV prevention trials changed policy, and who helped steer Africa's COVID response.
Summary: Salim S. Abdool Karim is a South African epidemiologist, director of the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa (CAPRISA) and a professor at Columbia and KwaZulu-Natal. He led the trial that showed a tenofovir gel could reduce HIV acquisition in women, and co-chaired South Africa's ministerial advisory committee on COVID-19. His work matters to this corpus through the shared infrastructure of African clinical research and the precedent that trials run in African communities produce results that change global guidelines.
Sources: Wikipedia — Salim Abdool Karim <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salim_Abdool_Karim>

### Shabir Madhi
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/shabir-madhi/
TL;DR: The South African vaccinologist whose trials in African infants changed pneumococcal and COVID vaccine practice.
Summary: Shabir Mahdi is a South African vaccinologist at the University of the Witwatersrand who led the trials showing that pneumococcal conjugate vaccine reduced pneumonia in African infants, and who ran some of the first COVID-19 vaccine trials on the continent, including against the Beta variant. His work is the clearest demonstration in this corpus that vaccines must be evaluated in the populations that will use them, because efficacy varies with the local epidemiology.
Sources: Wikipedia — Shabir Madhi <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabir_Madhi>

### Sheila Tlou
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/people/sheila-tlou/
TL;DR: The Botswanan nurse and academic who led UNAIDS' work in Africa and Botswana's health ministry.
Summary: Sheila Dinotshe Tlou is a Botswanan nurse, academic and former Minister of Health of Botswana who directed the UNAIDS Regional Support Team for Eastern and Southern Africa. Her career is a reminder that the health workforce delivering disease programmes is largely nursing and community health work, and that the people who shape those systems are not always the researchers who appear in the literature.
Sources: Wikipedia — Sheila Tlou <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheila_Tlou>


## Roadmaps

### AI in NTDs roadmap: pattern recognition → foundation models → agents across the pipeline
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/roadmaps/ai-ntd-roadmap/
TL;DR: From reading microscope images to designing molecules and shaping field operations, AI is entering NTD work at every stage.
Summary: AI entered NTDs through image analysis: reading microscope slides to count parasites and identify vectors, tasks that suffered from scarce and tired expert eyes. It has since spread through the pipeline — predicting parasite protein structures, generating and prioritising drug candidates, and now forecasting outbreaks and supporting programme decisions. The promise is disproportionate for NTDs, because a small team can now do work that once required industrial resources. The risk is equally real: models trained on thin data, deployed without local validation, or bought at the expense of the basic laboratory and surveillance capacity that generates the data they depend on.
Sources: TDR — research and innovation for infectious diseases of poverty <https://tdr.who.int/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Elimination roadmap: mass treatment → surveillance and response → verification
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/roadmaps/elimination-roadmap/
TL;DR: How NTD programmes move from treating everyone to proving that transmission has actually stopped.
Summary: Elimination programmes follow a recognisable arc. Mass treatment first drives prevalence down, working best for diseases with safe single-dose medicines and no animal reservoir.
